3.1.1   Necessity of Binders for an AMC Process﻿

Most current AMC processes focus on plastics and metals. Other types of engineer­
ing material, ceramics and ceramics-based composites, are severely limited in cur­
rent AMC processes. To overcome such material limitations, researchers have studied
AMC processes using high-performance ceramic powders. A developed method
based on SLS is to use a high-energy laser beam to locally sinter ceramic particles
such that they will bond with each other. However, due to the high sintering tempera­
ture of ceramics, a low-melting-point medium such as a polymeric binder is usually
added with ceramic powders. As shown in Figure 3.1a, the low-melting-point parti­
cles bind ceramic particles together in the SLS process. Finally, some post-processing
procedures are performed to burn out the added binder and fuse the ceramic particles.
  Due to the good properties of SLA, such as high accuracy and good surface finish,
efforts to apply SLA in ceramics fabrication have been made. In such an AMC pro­
cess, a photosensitive resin is used to bind ceramic particles together (Figure 3.1b).
That is, liquid resin is mixed in ceramic suspension and selectively solidified by con­
trolled light-induced photopolymerization. Consequently, green parts with different
shapes can be fabricated using a ceramic suspension that is a mixture of ceramic
powders and photosensitive resin. Post-processing of the fabricated green parts is
needed to burn out the organics in the photosensitive resin and fuse ceramic particles
together to get dense ceramic components (Song et al., 2015).
  To sum up, the necessity of binders for an AMC process arises from several key
functions they serve during the printing and post-processing stages. Here are the
primary reasons why binders are used in AMC processes:

   •  Binding Powder Particles Together: In AMC processes like binder jetting
      (BJ), robocasting (direct ink writing [DIW]), and fused deposition modeling
     (FDM), the feedstock material is typically a powder (ceramic, metal, or pol­
     ymer). The binder acts as a glue, holding the powder particles together dur­
      ing the early stages of the printing process, before sintering or curing occurs.
     Without binders, the powder particles would not adhere to each other, and
      the printed part would collapse or fail to maintain its shape. The binder
      ensures that each layer of powder stays intact as the print builds up.
   •  Maintaining Green Body Integrity: A green body is the term for the part
       after it has been printed but before it is sintered (for ceramics) or fully

   •  Facilitating Post-Processing: After printing, most AMed parts require
      post-processing steps like sintering (for ceramics and metals) or curing
      (for polymers). The binder helps ensure that the printed part holds its shape
      during these processes. During sintering, for example, the binder is usually
     burned off, leaving behind a denser, stronger part. Without the binder, the
     powder particles would not adhere sufficiently to survive the sintering or
      curing stages. In some processes, the binder is gradually removed during
      these stages, ensuring controlled shrinkage and final densification of the
       part.
   •  Enabling Multi-Material Printing : In some advanced AM processes, mul­
       tiple materials may be used in a single print job. The binder can be used
      selectively to print different materials with varying properties, such as
      creating gradients of material or combining different types of ceramic or
     metal powders. The binder helps maintain structural integrity when different
      materials are used in the same part. It can also be tailored to promote bond­
      ing between dissimilar materials, allowing for complex multi-material parts
      that might be impossible to manufacture using traditional methods.
   •  Providing Flexibility in BJ for Ceramics and Metals: In BJ, where the
      part is built by selectively dispensing binder onto powder material, the
      binder plays an essential role in determining the final part’s quality. For
     ceramic and metal parts, the binder is essential for holding the powder
      in place while the part is still in its “green” state. The binder is typically
     removed in a post-processing stage (such as thermal debinding) before sin­
       tering, but, without it, the printed part would not hold its shape.
   •  Cost-Effective Material Handling : The binder can help reduce the cost of
     manufacturing by allowing for the use of less expensive raw materials or
      enabling the reuse of unsintered powder. For example, in BJ or FDM pro­
      cesses, the binder can be tailored to support low-cost ceramic or metal pow­
      ders, while the part quality is achieved during post-processing. This allows
      for the production of high-quality, cost-effective parts.

3.1.1.1   Challenges with Binders
While binders are essential, their use also presents challenges, particularly during
the post-processing phase:

   •  Binder Removal: The binder must be effectively removed without dam­
     aging the part, which can be challenging, especially in intricate or high-
      resolution parts.
   •  Material Properties: Some binders can leave residues that may affect the
       final properties of the part, such as strength or thermal performance.
   •  Residual Stresses: The removal of binder, especially during processes like
     debinding and sintering, can introduce residual stresses that may distort the
      part if not carefully controlled.

Therefore, binders are critical in AMC processes for materials that start in powder
form. They enable the handling, shaping, and cohesion of powder particles, ensuring

ing high-quality, functional parts.

3.1.2   Necessity of Using Powder-Based Feedstock
       Material in AMC Processes﻿

Ceramic powder is used as feedstock material in additive manufacturing (AM) pro­
cesses of advanced ceramics for several reasons:

   •  Ease of Shaping and Precision: Ceramic powders can be easily shaped
      into complex geometries with high precision when used in AMC processes
      like selective laser sintering (SLS), stereolithography (SLA), or BJ. Pow­
      ders allow for fine control over layer-by-layer deposition, making it ideal for
      creating intricate ceramic components that would be difficult to form using
      traditional methods.
   •  Homogeneity: Powders can be mixed and blended to achieve uniform mate­
       rial properties throughout the part. The consistent particle size and distribu­
      tion help to ensure the resulting ceramic material has predictable mechanical
     and thermal properties.
   •  Customization of Material Properties: By controlling the type, size, and
     shape of the ceramic powder particles, as well as the additives and binders
      used, manufacturers can tailor the material properties of the final part. This
      includes mechanical strength, thermal conductivity, porosity, and more.
   •  Sintering Capability: In many AMC processes, ceramic powders are
      deposited layer by layer, and then they are sintered to fuse the particles
      together. The powder form makes it easier to achieve the required densifi­
      cation during sintering, which is crucial for developing the final ceramic’s
      strength and structural integrity.
   •  Reduced Waste: Powder-based AMC processes generally use only the
      material needed for the part, reducing material waste compared to tradi­
      tional subtractive manufacturing methods, where material is often cut away.
   •  Material Flexibility: AMC processes allow the use of a wide variety of
     ceramic powders, including oxides, nitrides, carbides, and composite mate­
       rials. This gives manufacturers the ability to produce parts with specific
      properties, such as wear resistance, high temperature tolerance, and electri­
      cal insulation.
   •  Post-Processing Capability: After the ceramic part is created, it can be fur­
      ther processed, such as by infiltrating it with another material or post-sin­
      tering to achieve specific characteristics, such as improving density or
     enhancing surface finish.

These factors together make ceramic powders an ideal feedstock material in AMC
processes for advanced ceramics, allowing for the creation of high-performance,

struggle to produce.

3.1.3  Forms of Feedstocks Used in AMC Processes﻿

Feedstock forms for additive manufacturing (AMC) of advanced ceramics are crit­
ical in ensuring the precision and quality of the printed ceramic structures. The
feedstock, essentially the material used in the 3D printing process, has to meet spe­
cific requirements for AMC techniques like BJ, material extrusion (ME), and DIW,
among others. Here are the most common feedstock forms used for AM of advanced
ceramics:

    1. Powder-Based Feedstock: Ceramic powders are widely used as feedstock
      for ceramic AM. These powders are often combined with a binder or sol­
      vent to form a printable slurry or paste. Common ceramic materials include
     alumina, zirconia, silicon carbide, titanium carbide, and various oxide and
     non-oxide ceramics. In processes like BJ and SLS, powders are printed
      layer by layer and later sintered to achieve the final material properties. In
     powder bed fusion (PBF), a laser or electron beam is used to fuse (sinter or
      melt) the powder at pre-defined positions in the ceramic powder bed. Once
     a layer is completed, the building platform is lowered, and a new layer of
     powder is deposited. PBF processes can be divided into three subcatego­
       ries: electron beam melting (EBM), selective laser melting (SLM), and SLS,
     although EBM and SLM are used mainly in AM of metals. BJ is a process
     where the binder is deposited on a ceramic powder bed. As the binder is
      selectively jetted on the powder bed, it solidifies and bonds the powder in
      those areas.
   2. Filament-Based Feedstock :  Filament  feedstocks  are  used  in  extru­
      sion-based AM processes, like FDM. The filament is typically made by
      extruding a mixture of ceramic powders and a polymer binder. This method
     can be used for ceramic materials such as alumina, zirconia, and others. The
     ceramic filament is heated and extruded through a nozzle to build up the part
      layer by layer. After printing, the binder is removed, and the part is sintered.
        Fused filament fabrication (FFF), also referred to as fused deposition
     modeling (FDM), is a ME process where the feedstock in the form of a
      filament is fed to the extruder, melted (allowing plastic deformation), and
      deposited to manufacture the desired part. The feedstock for FFF of ceram­
      ics is composed of ceramic powder, high-melting-point backbone thermo­
      plastic polymer, low-molecular-weight support binder, and other additives
     such as tackifiers, plasticizers, and surfactants. There are two main ME AM
      processes: FFF and DIW, also referred to as robocasting, which is an AM
     method developed for processing ceramics. In FFF a thermoplastic filament
       is prepared with a high solids loading of ceramic particles.

     shown in Figure 3.2. First, mixing of the binder system and the ceramic

3.1.3.1   Considerations for Feedstock Selection
    1. Viscosity and Flow Properties: The feedstock needs to have appropriate
      viscosity for the printing process. For example, filaments need to flow easily
     through the nozzle without clogging, while slurries should have a consis­
      tency that allows for precise deposition.
   2. Particle Size: The size of the ceramic powder particles is essential to
      achieve good resolution and avoid issues like clogging in the printer nozzle
      or nozzle blockages.
   3. Binder Removal and Sintering: After printing, the binder used in the feed­
      stock must be removed, and the part must be sintered to achieve full density
     and strength.
    4. Material Compatibility: The feedstock must be compatible with the AM
      process chosen. For example, inkjet processes require stable inks, while
      extrusion processes require filaments with appropriate thermal properties.

It is worth pointing out that, for all AMC processes of advanced ceramics, the
ceramic powder is a main constituent (core material) of the aforementioned ceramic
feedstock forms. The contribution of the ceramic powder in the AMC processes can
be summarized as follows:

   • SLA: While this technique uses resin-based feedstocks, the resin is often
       filled with ceramic powders (e.g., alumina or zirconia) to enable the creation
      of advanced ceramic parts after photopolymerization and sintering.
   • PBF: Powdered ceramic materials (such as alumina, zirconia, or silicon car­
      bide) are directly used in this technique, where layers of powder are sintered
      using a laser or electron beam.
   • BJ: This process relies on ceramic powders that are bound together with a
      liquid binder. The powder is the core material, while the binder holds it in
      place during printing.

3.1.4  Advanced Ceramic Powder﻿

3.1.4.1  Ceramic Powders and Their Preparation
Commonly, ceramic materials can be divided into two main categories: traditional
and advanced (or technical). Traditional ceramics are those made from natural mate­
rials, such as clay and sand. In contrast, advanced ceramics are typically synthesized
using advanced manufacturing techniques, and examples include silicon carbide
(SiC) , silicon nitride  (Si 3 N 4) , boron nitride (BN) , aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3) ,
­zirconium oxide (ZrO2) , composites, and many others.
  Ceramic powder is prepared with controlled chemical composition and particle
size. There are many different methods for the production of powders. The choice
of production method depends on the required particle characteristics. A key goal
in the production of ceramic powders for advanced ceramic applications is attaining
a fine particle size, typically less than 1 µm in diameter. The fine size is required
for two reasons. First, powder processing of ceramics requires a high-temperature
treatment to make a dense material. The sintering process is greatly enhanced with
fine particles. Sintering is also required for most powder metallurgy operations.
Second, the mechanical properties, as well as many other properties, of the final
ceramic are enhanced with fine grain size. The dimensions of the grains in the
final microstructure cannot be smaller than the size of the original particle; there­
fore, fine particles are needed for a fine-grained polycrystalline ceramic. Ceramic
powder processing consists of powder production by milling/grinding and sieving,
followed by the fabrication of the green product, which is then consolidated to
obtain the final product.
  The ceramic particles are mostly very irregular. Particle shape is an important
issue because of the following reasons:

   •  Irregular particles “key” together well and so, when pressed together, tend
      to adhere, leading to stronger “green” components than rounded particles.

52           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   •  Rounded particles flow more easily than irregular particles and can pack
      together more uniformly and densely than irregular particles. For the highest
     packing density, use mainly rounded particles with a range of particle sizes
      (small ones to fill up the gaps between big ones). With a single size, highly
      controlled porosity can be achieved.

Most ceramic components are made through powder processing, starting with
ceramic powders. Generally speaking, the flow for ceramic components includes:
raw materials → powder processing/mixing → forming → firing/sintering → final
ceramic component (https://www.preciseceramic.com/blog/).
 AM enables the production of ceramics of tailored structures with controlled
macro and microscale properties (e.g., controlled pore shape and size). Selective
deposition and densification during AM also enables the combination of different
materials into one component, leading to the production of multifunctional com­
ponents with unprecedented properties, such as combining electrically conductive
metals and electrically isolating ceramics, as well as creating functionally graded
microstructures throughout the part.
   Powder-based AM techniques, shown in Figure 3.3, rely on the deposition of a uni­
form powder layer (powder bed), which is either directly densified by a heat source
(e.g., laser) or bound together by a selectively deposited binder system, as in the case
of BJ. To ensure uniform deposition and high packing density of the powder bed, the
properties of the powder, especially the size and shape, are of high importance.
   In powder-based ceramic AM technologies, a powder bed including loose ceramic
particles as feedstock material is processed in each layer. These ceramic particles are
bonded together using a spread of liquid binders or powder fusion through thermal
energy provided by a laser beam.

Some advanced ceramics cannot be easily processed using the conventional (suspen­

A photopolymer product can be applied as a thin coating, as in liquid photoresists, or
formed into a large model, as in stereolithographic/3D printing equipment (https://

   Photopolymer formulations comprise polymers, oligomers, monomers, and addi­

and additives. Polymers usually function as binders and determine processing charac­
teristics as well as the final physical properties of cured photopolymer compositions.
Liquid compositions such as those used for printing plates and stereolithographic
resins usually do not incorporate polymers as a significant component. However,
liquid photoresists may contain a polymer dissolved in a solvent carrier. The first
photopolymers developed and marketed were based on polyvinyl cinnamates and
sensitizers dissolved in solvents and marketed as photoresists by Eastman Kodak
Company.
   Photopolymers undergo curing, where oligomers are crosslinked upon exposure
to light, forming what is known as a network polymer. The result of photocuring is
the formation of a thermoset network of polymers.
   Photosensitive materials are made up of polymers that can undergo rapid
physical and chemical changes in a relatively short period after being irradiated
by light. Photosensitive materials are advanced by high production efficiency,
high-energy utilization rate, low organic volatile matter emission, and enhanced
flexibility in coating various substrates, such as paper, plastic, leather, metal, glass,
and ceramics.

curing time and low pollution (https://www.pharmiweb.com/).

3.1.7   Additives﻿

Each of these additives plays an important role in the preparation, printing, and
post-processing of advanced ceramic parts using AM technologies. The choice of
additive and its chemical formula depend on the specific AM process, the type of
ceramic material being printed, and the desired properties of the final product.

3.1.7.1   Photoinitiators
These compounds absorb light and initiate the polymerization process in photopoly­
mer resins. Camphorquinone is a popular photoinitiator (PI) that works in combina­
tion with amine-based co-initiators. The PI is responsible for initiating the chemical
reaction by converting the energy from a UV source into a free radical or cationic
initiating species. This initiating species causes the reactive chemistry to polym­
erize to give a cured ink or coating. A PI is a molecule that creates reactive spe­
cies when exposed to UV. Synthetic PIs are key components in photopolymers. The
chemistry behind the photo polymerization process (free radical) is rather simple:
photons of a specific wavelength in the UV range provide the required energy to the
PI (Figure 3.4) so that the photocuring process propagates and builds a crosslinked
polymeric network.

3.1.7.2   Surfactants
Surfactants are cleaning detergents. The word “surfactant” means surface-active
agent. Surfactants stir up activity on the cleaning surface to trap and remove dirt
from the surface. These reduce surface tension, ensuring that the ceramic particles
are well-dispersed in the liquid binder or photopolymer matrix. Sodium dodecyl sul­
fate is commonly used to improve dispersion and flowability in ceramic suspensions.
Surfactants have a hydrophobic (water-hating) tail and a hydrophilic (water-loving)
head (Figure 3.5). The hydrophobic tail of each surfactant surrounds soils. The
hydrophilic head is surrounded by water (https://www.ipcol.com/).

Surfactants are chemical compounds that decrease the surface tension or interfacial
tension between two liquids, a liquid and a gas, or a liquid and a solid. The word
“surfactant” is a blend of surface-active agents, coined in 1950. As they consist of a
water-repellent and a water-attracting part, they enable water and oil to mix; they can
form foam and facilitate the detachment of dirt. Today, one of the most commonly
used anionic surfactants, linear alkylbenzene sulfates, is produced from petroleum
products. However, surfactants are increasingly produced in whole or in part from
renewable biomass, like sugar, fatty alcohol from vegetable oils, byproducts of bio­
fuel production, or other biogenic material.
  When there is a sufficient amount of surfactant molecules present in a solution,
they combine together to form structures called micelles. As the micelle forms, the
surfactant heads position themselves so they are exposed to water, while the tails are
grouped in the center of the structure protected from water (Figure 3.6).
  The micelles work as a unit to remove soil. The hydrophobic tails are attracted
to soils and surround them, while the hydrophilic heads pull the surrounded soils
off the surface and into the cleaning solution. Then the micelles reform with the
tails suspending the soil in the center of the structure. The hydrophilic head of each
surfactant is electrically charged. The charge can be negative, positive, or neutral.
  Depending on the charge of the hydrophilic head, the surfactant is classified as
anionic, nonionic, cationic, or amphoteric (Figure 3.7).

    c. Cationic Surfactants: Cationic surfactants have a positive charge on their
      hydrophilic end. The positive charge makes them useful in anti-static prod­
      ucts, like fabric softeners. Cationic surfactants can also serve as antimicro­
      bial agents, so they are often used in disinfectants. They cannot be used with
      anionic surfactants. If positively charged cationic surfactants are mixed
     with negatively charged anionic surfactants, they will fall out of solution
     and no longer be effective. Cationic and nonionic surfactants, however, are
      compatible. Examples of some common cationic surfactants include alkyl
    ammonium chlorides.
    d. Amphoteric Surfactants: Amphoteric surfactants have a dual charge on
       their hydrophilic end, both positive and negative. The dual charges cancel
     each other out, creating a net charge of zero, referred to as zwitterionic.
     The pH of any given solution will determine how the amphoteric surfac­
      tants react. In acidic solutions, the amphoteric surfactants become positively
     charged and behave similarly to cationic surfactants. In alkaline solutions,
      they develop a negative charge, similar to anionic surfactants. Amphoteric
      surfactants are often used in personal care products such as shampoos and
      cosmetics. Examples of some frequently used amphoteric surfactants are
      betaines and amino oxides.

3.1.7.3   Plasticizers
Plasticizers are organic compounds that reduce the viscosity of the feedstock materi­
als and improve their flow characteristics, particularly in materials like filaments or
pastes. They improve extrusion and printing characteristics, making it easier to print

62           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

with high ceramic load and ensuring smoother deposition during AM processes like
material extrusion. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate is a commonly used plasticizer in AM
filaments and slurries.

3.1.7.4   Stabilizers
Stabilizers are additives that prevent the premature precipitation or settling of
ceramic particles in liquid suspensions or slurries. They ensure that ceramic par­
ticles stay evenly dispersed in liquid- or paste-based feedstocks and help maintain
uniformity in feedstock viscosity and properties. Sodium hexametaphosphate is used
to maintain stable dispersions.

3.1.7.5   Dispersants
Dispersants are chemicals (surfactants or polymers) that improve the dispersion of
ceramic particles in liquids by reducing agglomeration. They are especially useful in
suspension-based AM processes. They help ceramic powders to remain evenly sus­
pended in liquids or slurries, resulting in more uniform parts with consistent proper­
ties. Polyvinylpyrrolidone is often used to stabilize ceramic slurries.

3.1.7.6   Crosslinkers
These chemicals form covalent bonds between polymer chains, strengthening the
polymer matrix. Crosslinkers are used in photopolymer-based feedstocks (e.g., in
SLA) to form chemical bonds between polymer chains, enhancing the structural
integrity of the printed part. They provide additional stability and mechanical
strength to the printed object and prevent deformation or shrinkage during post-
processing. Ethylene glycol dimethacrylate is a common crosslinker used in photo­
polymer-based AM processes.

3.1.7.7   Rheological Modifiers
These additives control the flow properties (viscosity) of the feedstock materials.
Rheological modifiers alter the flow characteristics of the feedstock materials, espe­
cially for slurries, pastes, and inks used in ceramic AM processes. Viscosity control
ensures that the feedstock is suitable for the specific AM process (e.g., proper flow for
extrusion or jetting). Consistency in printing ensures that the material can be depos­
ited smoothly during the AM process. Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose is commonly
used to adjust the viscosity in pastes and slurries.

3.1.7.8  De-Binders
These are chemicals that aid in the removal or breaking down of the binder during
post-processing to ensure proper sintering of ceramic parts. They are often used
in binder-based AM processes. These de-binders help ease the binder removal step
before sintering by chemically breaking down or dissolving the binder. Ammonium
carbonate is one of the de-binders used in ceramic AM processes to break down
organic binders.

3.2  PRECERAMIC POLYMERS AS FEEDSTOCK MATERIAL FOR AMC

3.2.1   Preceramic Polymers and Polymer-Derived Ceramic﻿

AM technologies are promising for the fabrication of ceramic components. However,
printing ceramics directly from their raw powders is a daunting task and requires
multi-step processing. Preceramic polymers (PCPs) offer an attractive pathway
toward AM of preceramic structures featuring heterogeneous architectures and their
direct conversion to polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs).
  The AM processes with PCPs involve feedstock materials that usually consist of
organic compounds and possess excellent processability, which allows them to be
easily shaped into desired geometric structures. After pyrolysis, the AM-fabricated
preceramic physical objects will be further converted into functional ceramic compo­
nents. AM processes using preceramic feedstock materials have been demonstrated
to be effective and versatile approaches for manufacturing functional advanced
ceramic materials with complex geometric structures. They have been investigated
for various applications, especially in the last decade. However, the use of PCPs as a
starting material for 3D printing is still developing.
  Compared to ceramic powders, PCPs offer much more flexibility for effectively
fabricating ceramic components with complex geometric structures and shapes using
a wide range of processes, such as casting, molding, and AMC. PCPs can have dif­
ferent configurations/microstructures, which can affect the composition, microstruc­
ture, porosity, yield, and properties of fabricated ceramics.
  PDCs represent a relatively new class of materials within AM. They enable the
development of ceramic parts patterned via low-cost polymer 3D printing methods,
followed by pyrolysis in a high-temperature process in which the polymer itself forms a
ceramic, often in the absence of any ceramic filler. PDCs have served as a feedstock for
various 3D printing techniques, for which a wide range of physicochemical factors can
be tailored to optimize the ceramic manufacturing processes. In particular, the silicon
and carbon-rich polymeric microstructure of PDCs offers a high degree of tunability
and potential to achieve a closely defined combination of functional, thermomechani­
cal, and chemical properties (Lacelle et al., 2023). The introduction of PDC techniques
has drawn significant attention due to their ability to overcome the limitations and
challenges associated with conventional fabrication methods (Han et al., 2023).
  The PDC technology has some significant advantages over conventional pow­
der-based ceramic processing and forming techniques, since:

   •   it can be a completely liquid-based process, avoiding the issues arising with
      the use of ceramic powders,
   •   it provides better shaping ability enabled by the soluble and crosslinkable
      precursors,
   •   it enables flexible tailoring of microstructures and compositions at the
     molecular level, affording novel functionalities,

Feedstock Materials for AMC                                          65

   •  the polymer-to-ceramic transformation occurs at relatively lower temper­
      atures (800–1200°C), in comparison to conventional ceramic processing,
     which can reduce energy consumption and cost, and
   •  provides design  flexibility, allowing the creation of complex, intricate
     ceramic parts with features that would be challenging to produce with tradi­
      tional ceramic processing techniques.

The aforementioned advantages led to the consideration of PCPs as highly
suitable materials for AM processes, and the combination of AM and PDC
technologies has emerged to open up a pathway toward the possible solution
to the challenges faced in conventional ceramic synthesis and manufacturing
(Chaudhary et al., 2022). Moreover, it has become the next technological fron­
tier, not only expanding the range of complex-structured advanced ceramic
components but also making novel functionalities and properties available for
cutting-edge applications.
  The utilization of PCPs to produce both oxide and non-oxide ceramics has caught
significant interest, owing to their exceptional characteristics. Diverse types of PDCs
synthesized by using various PCPs have demonstrated remarkable characteristics
such as:

   •  exceptional thermal stability,
   •  resistance to corrosion and oxidation at elevated temperatures,
   •  biocompatibility,
   •  notable dielectric properties, among others,
   •  excellent processibility and tunability,
   •  ease of processing them into complex shapes,
   •  tailorable composition for fabricating high-performance ceramic components,
   •  control over microstructure and composition,
   •  flexibility in the selection of AM technique.

The application of AM techniques to produce PDCs opens up new opportunities
for manufacturing complex and unconventional ceramic structures with complex
designs that might be challenging or impossible to achieve using traditional AM
methods. This is particularly advantageous in industries like aerospace, automotive,
electronics, and others. The future of producing ceramics using preceramic feed­
stock materials for AM processes is a promising new technology.

3.2.1.1  Drawbacks of the PDC Route
However, the main drawback of the PDC route lies in the polymer-to-ceramic trans­
formation by pyrolysis itself. The high-temperature pyrolysis is characterized by
the release of substantial amounts of volatile gaseous species (H 2 O, CO2, H2, CH4),
which results in high mass loss and significant dimensional shrinkage of 30% to
50%. This tends to prevent the use of PCPs for making ceramic components with
a bulk volume greater than a few millimeters without the formation of pores and
cracks. Moreover, some challenges are related to the application of the PDCs must be
carefully considered and managed. These are:

    1. Post-Processing Challenges
       •  Shrinkage (30–50%) during pyrolysis can lead to dimensional distortion.
       •   Potential porosity in the final ceramic product may reduce mechanical
          strength.
   2. Material Limitations﻿
       •  Limited range of polymer precursors available compared to traditional
         ceramics.
       •   Properties can vary depending on processing conditions, making consis­
         tency a challenge.
    3. Limited Tooling and Support Infrastructure
       •  Limited infrastructure for processing PDCs in AM (specialized printers,
          post-processing tools).
       •  Emerging field, infrastructure still developing.

However, AM technologies based on the PDC approach can fabricate complex
ceramic components featuring highly detailed, dense lattice structures – from the
microscale down to the nanoscale. In this context, PDCs act as an enabling technol­
ogy, especially given that ceramic materials exhibit greater thermodynamic stability
than metals and polymers.

3.2.2   Basic Concept of PDC Technology﻿

3.2.2.1  Polymer-Derived Ceramics
PDCs are intrinsically complex nanostructured materials, for which it is possible to
create chemical compositions uniquely which cannot be created by other techniques.
The macroscopic properties of PDCs heavily depend on the structure and the compo­
sition of the PCP, which is why the study of the synthesis and properties of the PCPs
is crucial in the design and optimization of PDCs (Rivera et al., 2019).

3.2.2.2   Si-Based PCPs
A PCP consists of various small organic molecules, of which the characteristics
determine the microstructure of the ceramic. PCPs are inorganic polymers that can
be converted into ceramics with high yield, of which the most commonly used ones
are silicon-based polymers. In Figure 3.8, a general chemical formula is presented
for a silicon-based precursor. The presence of organic groups is noted by R¹ and R²,
which are attached to the inorganic backbone of the silicon-based precursor. These
organic groups generate a combination of unique properties, resulting in a wide
range of engineering applications. The presence of organic groups is furthermore
essential to controlling the content of carbon in the resulting ceramic material, which
defines the polymer properties, such as thermal stability, solubility, and viscosity.
Substitution of group X in Figure 3.8, for example, –O–, leads to different classes of
organosilicon precursors (Francis, 2018).
  Due to the flexibility of polymers being able to be processed in a liquid, solid, or
molten state, the PCPs can be shaped into films or 3D frameworks directly by various
methods, such as extrusion molding and AM, which is a great advantage as opposed to
the shaping limitations of traditional ceramics. After shaping, crosslinking methods

such as thermal or light curing are used to polymerize the material, connecting the
polymer backbone. Highly crosslinked PCPs can retain shape better due to a higher
ceramic yield. This is generally done through temperature control in combination
with a curing agent. During cross-linking, covalent bonds among molecules and sub­
networks lead to branched structures, while forces (van der Waals, etc.) generate
reversible molecular associations (Rivera et al., 2019). The occurrence of both chem­
ical and physical cross-linking leads to the formation of three-dimensional networks
that significantly alter the PCP’s rheological behavior by inducing a phase transition
from liquid to solid (Rivera et al., 2019).
  The transformation of the material from organic to inorganic is completed by
pyrolysis, which induces changes in its internal structure and properties. During
pyrolysis, the organic groups of the polymer (phenyl, vinyl, etc.; Francis, 2018) grad­
ually vanish using decomposition and gaseous byproducts (Lacelle Thomas et al.,
2023), and the polymer transforms into an amorphous ceramic at a typical tempera­
ture of 900–1100°C (Rivera et al., 2019). Amorphous structures formed by pyroly­
sis show high-temperature stability, excellent semiconducting properties, oxidation
and corrosion resistance, and light transmission. As the heat treatment temperature
increases, the amorphous structure gradually crystallizes between 1200°C and
1800°C. During this transformation, the disordered structure is rearranged by the
rupture of chemical bonds. With increasing temperature and time, the formed crystal
nuclei gradually grow and form a crystalline structure. Mechanical properties such
as strength, modulus, and hardness can be enhanced using the gradual structural
evolution and modifying the structure and distribution of ceramic nanoparticles. An
overview of the entire process of ceramization is given in Figure 3.9.
   During pyrolysis, the elimination of organic groups leads to a significant weight
loss and volume shrinkage in the material, often resulting in a ceramic structure
that contains a high amount of pores and cracks. To overcome these shortcomings,
fillers can be added to preserve the integrity of the ceramic material. The fraction of
shrinkage in the polymer phase is then reduced according to the filler volume effect,
and the filament toughness is increased (Francis, 2018). Although many studies have
already been dedicated to the addition of fillers, research on the rheology and ceram­
ization of PDCs without added fillers or particles is limited. Vidakis et al. (2022)
have, for example, studied the effect of several DIW printing parameters, such as the
infill density and nozzle temperature, on the dimensional accuracy of the samples
but have tested this with a common PLA. Pierin et al. (2016) have studied the effect
of fillers on a similar PDC but with a different crosslinking agent, limited rheology,

3.2.3   Characteristics of Important Classes of PCPs﻿

Only high-molecular-weight polymers that are capable of crosslinking can be used
for the fabrication of PDC (Yajima et al., 1978). A brief description of the import­
ant classes of PCPs, including PSis, PCSs, PSZs, PSOs, and polysilsesquioxanes
(PSSQs), is summarized in the following subsections.

3.2.3.1   Polysilanes
These are polymers containing a backbone of alternating silicon and carbon atoms
 – Si – C – Si – C . They are typically liquid or low-viscosity, making them suitable
for 3D printing and other AM techniques. They can be used to create a wide range
of ceramic materials, particularly silicon carbide (SiC), which is desirable in appli­
cations requiring high thermal and mechanical stability. After pyrolysis, they pro­
vide a high yield of ceramic products, which is crucial for achieving dense, durable
ceramics. Silicones generally exhibit good mechanical properties at elevated tem­
peratures, especially when converted to SiC. However, the produced SiC ceramics,
while strong, can be brittle after processing, which may limit their use in certain
applications.
   PSis having a one-dimensional silicon backbone are basic precursors for the
synthesis of SiC ceramics. Each silicon atom is attached to R¹ and R² substituents,
whereas the substituents are presenting molecules with different combinations of
C, H, S, N, and O atoms. This synthetic approach involves the reaction of chlo­
rosilanes with sodium or lithium dispersion, resulting in a reduction process that
leads to the formation of PSi. The reaction occurs within a high-boiling-point inert
solvent, such as toluene, benzene, or tetrahydrofuran, under reflux conditions.
   PSis have been proposed for various applications such as photoresists, photocon­
ductors, and semiconductors (Fu et al., 2019). Their σ-conjugation due to electron
delocalization on silicon–silicon bonds results in distinctive optoelectronic and
photoelectric properties. The properties of PSis stem from two primary factors: the
side chain groups attached to the backbone and the molecular weight of the polymer
(Chaudhary et al., 2022).

3.2.3.2   Polycarbosilanes
Their composition is similar to PSis but with a higher carbon content  ( Me 3SiH ),
with more carbons being incorporated into the polymer backbone. They are of better
processability than PSis. PCSs offer better viscosity and stability, making them eas­
ier to work with in the PDC-AM process. PCSs yield silicon carbide ceramics upon
pyrolysis with minimal carbon residues. They can be tailored for producing various
forms of silicon carbide or silicon carbonitride, offering a versatile route to advanced
ceramic materials. However, PCSs are more difficult to synthesize than PSis, requir­
ing more precise conditions for preparation. Moreover, while the high carbon content
is beneficial for SiC formation, it can limit the production of ceramics like silicon
nitride or oxide-based ceramics.
  PCSs with a  Si – C  backbone contain branched chains such as methylene,
vinylidene, and phenylene, which make them more complex compared to PSis. The
most common way to synthesize these polymers is thermal decomposition of PSis

under pressure using the Kumada mechanism. However, the accumulation of decom­
position gaseous products [e.g., Methane, Trimethylsilane ( Me 3SiH ) , Silane (SiH4)]
can lead to a dangerous increase in pressure in the autoclave. Synthesis of PCSs using
pyrolysis of polydimethylsilane in a nitrogen atmosphere was performed at ambient
pressure through catalytic processes (using polyborodiphenylsiloxane) in a reflux
condenser (Yajima et al., 1978). This class of organosilicon polymers has been widely
used for the fabrication of SiC-based components like fibers, composites, powders,
and other non-oxide ceramic structures.

3.2.3.3   Polysilazanes
These are polymers with a backbone of alternating silicon and nitrogen atoms
 – Si – N – Si – N . They produce high yields of ceramic materials, particularly sil­
icon nitride  Si 3 N 4  ceramics, which are highly valued in high-temperature appli­
cations. Silicones and silicon nitrides offer excellent thermal stability and resistance
to oxidation at high temperatures. PSZs offer high flexibility in material design. By
modifying the PSZ structure, various ceramic materials, such as silicon nitride, can
be targeted. However, PSZs tend to produce less dense ceramics compared to PCSs,
often leading to lower mechanical strength. Additionally, their synthesis can be more
complex and expensive compared to other PCPs, and PSZs might not be as widely
available commercially.
   Using PSZs with carbon-containing side chains attached to a Si – N backbone,
SiCN ceramics are synthesized. If a C-free PSZ polymer like perhydridopolysilazane
is utilized, Si 3 N 4 ceramics can be produced. Fabrication of SiCN fibers from poly­
carbosilazanes was first demonstrated by Verbeek et al. in the 1970s (Kleebe et al.,
2001), where oxidation resistance up to 1200°C and a significant strength and elastic
modulus were achieved. Remarkable thermal stability, scratch resistance, corrosion
resistance, and high hardness of PSZs make them ideal for various applications,
including protective and heat-resistant coatings in industries such as electronics,
automotive, and aerospace, as well as heat exchanger barriers and for protecting steel
against oxidation (Günthner et al., 2009).

3.2.3.4  PSOs and PSSQs
PSOs are polymers based on a silicon–oxygen backbone  – Si – O – Si – O . PSOs are
generally stable at elevated temperatures and can produce ceramics with excellent
thermal properties. The versatility of the Si – O backbone allows the production of
a variety of ceramic types, including silica (SiO 2 ), silicon carbide (SiC), and sili­
con nitride (Si 3 N 4). PSOs are often low-viscosity, making them easier to process in
AM techniques. However, ceramics derived from PSOs often have lower mechanical
strength than those from PCSs. Moreover, SiO2-based ceramics may not achieve
the same density and mechanical properties as those derived from more carbon-rich
precursors like PCSs.
  PSOs (Figure 3.10) with a general formula of [R2SiO]n are an inexpensive, widely
used class of Si-based PCPs for the synthesis of silicone oxycarbide and oxynitride­
ceramics (Chaudhary et al., 2022).

Crosslinked PSOs and PSSQs can be obtained using the sol–gel process via hydroly­

on their functional side chain.
  PSSQs  are  hybrid  polymers  with  a  silicon–oxygen–carbon  backbone
 – Si – O – Si – O – Si  with additional organic functional groups. PSSQs are highly
flexible in terms of tailoring the material properties, allowing the production of a
wide range of ceramics (liquid, crystalline, or amorphous powder), and due to their
hybrid nature. Due to their inorganic–organic nature, these polymers often exhibit
better properties compared to purely organic PCPs. PSSQs generally exhibit lower
shrinkage, leading to more precise and controlled ceramic structures after sintering.
However, synthesis can be more complex than other PCPs. PSSQs produce limited
ceramic types. The main products are typically silica-based or silicon carbide com­
posites, which might not be suitable for all applications.
  PSSQs with a chemical formula of [RSiO3/2]n, as implied by their name, con­
sist of a silicon atom (sil-), bonded to one and a half (-sesqui-) oxygen atoms (-ox-),
and a hydrocarbon group (-ane) (Fan et al., 2021). R can be either an H atom or an
organic functional group such as methyl, phenyl, ethoxy, or hydroxyl. The nature of
the organic ligands attached to the Si atoms determines the packing of the molecules
and the intermolecular forces between them, which ultimately determine the physi­
cal state of the material. As a result, pure PSSQs can be found in the form of liquid,
crystalline, or amorphous powder.

3.2.3.5  Comparison between Classes of PCPs
In conclusion, the choice of PCP depends on the desired ceramic properties, such
as thermal stability, mechanical strength, and processability. Each type of polymer
plays a distinct role in the fabrication of specific advanced ceramic materials using
the PDC-AM approach. Table 3.5 illustrates the advantages, limitations, and types of
produced ceramics for each PCP class.

3.2.4   Processing of PCPs﻿

One of the main advantages of PCPs is the ease of processing them into complex
shapes. Processing begins by ensuring that the polymers are in a liquid state, either
by using low molecular-weight precursors or by dissolving the polymers into sol­
vent. The polymers must also be formulated with appropriate additives, in particular,
an initiator or catalyst, and possess suitable functional groups for crosslinking. The
polymer resins are generally shaped using established technologies, such as resin
transfer molding, extrusion, injection molding, AM, fiber drawing, compression
molding, impregnation, casting, and tape casting (Parcianello, 2012 and Greil, 2000).

Once crosslinked, the PCPs undergo a polymer-to-ceramic conversion through
pyrolysis in an inert (e.g., Ar) or another nonoxidizing atmosphere. The environment
used in this step has important implications for the ceramic composition and proper­
ties, as an inert environment can minimize oxygen contamination. Furthermore, the
atmosphere can influence how the organic side chains decompose, thus influencing
the residual carbon content of the final ceramic (Welna et al., 2005).
  The polymer-to-ceramic transition continues up to 800–1000℃, yielding an
amorphous ceramic that has undergone significant mass and volume loss relative
to the PCPs as a result of the release of gases and the cleavage and rearrangement
of chemical bonds. The volumetric shrinkage of            and mass losses of
10–30 wt.% are typical (Greil, 2000). Densities increase accordingly, from    g/cm3for the polymer to densities ranging to 2.2–2.6 g/cm3∼20%–40%for SiO2 and 3–3.2 g/cm3 for                                                     ∼1SiC and Si 3 N 4 (Greil, 1995). The polymer-to-ceramic conversion yields amorphous
ceramics with a mixture of covalent bonds between the Si atom and C, O, N, and
C – C ; however, other bonds can be present with elements such as B, Al, Ti, and Zr,
dependent upon the ceramic precursor, and the type of covalent bond is essential
in determining the maximum service temperature of the final ceramic, typically in
the range of 1000–2000℃ (Sorarù and Suttor, 1999). The amorphous structure is
responsible for determining the attractive properties, such as oxidation, creep and
chemical resistance, and thermal stability (Greil, 2000).
  The notable loss of mass and volume associated with the transformation is the
main drawback of the PDCs approach. When gases are released, cracks and pores
may be formed inside the material. This affects the structural integrity of the compo­
nent, particularly for coatings. Porosity and cracking are not present in thin-walled
structures as there are short diffusion paths, which lead to a very limited build-up of
internal pressure (Greil, 2000). Additional exceptions where crack-free ceramic com­
ponents have been demonstrated include structures below a few hundred microme­
ters, such as thin films and fibers. To mitigate this drawback, fillers have been widely
used.
   Using PCPs to fabricate 3D ceramic structures, several steps need to be taken,
including shaping the material, followed by crosslinking and pyrolysis. After that, a
sintering step can be implemented if necessary. Figure 3.13 demonstrates the neces­
sary processing steps to achieve PDC components.
   Concluding, the conversion of a liquid or solid PCP into fully dense ceramic pro­
ceeds through three critical and sequential stages: shaping, crosslinking, and pyroly­
sis. Each stage plays a vital role in ensuring that the final material attains the required
mechanical strength, thermal stability, and controlled microstructure.

    1. Shaping: One of the advantages of PCPs is their viscoelastic behavior ris­
      ing from their polymeric nature. As a result, PCPs are well-suited for a
     wide range of thermoplastic shaping techniques such as casting, injection
     molding, pressing, tape casting, extrusion, fiber drawing, and coating. More

   2. Crosslinking: Crosslinking is the process by which polymer chains are
      linked together, forming a three-dimensional network. This process  is
      important for almost all the fabrication processes of PDC structures because
         it allows the precursor to transform from a flexible, thermoplastic organic
      material (necessary for shaping) into a rigid and insoluble thermoset and
      preserve the  structure during post-processing. Crosslinking can occur
     through a variety of mechanisms, most commonly by thermal crosslinking
      in the range of 100–250℃ under airflow, crosslinking with chlorosilane, or
      curing with radiation (Greil, 2000). With the presence of functional groups
     such as Si–H, Si–OH, and Si-vinyl, PCPs can be spontaneously crosslinked
     below 200°C using hydrosilylation (addition) or silanol–silanol reactions
      (condensation). Crosslinking in an air atmosphere has traditionally been a
     popular method for curing PCPs to provide SiO2 yield. This process, how­
      ever, is not suitable for the fabrication of non-oxide ceramics due to the
     drawback of leaving up to 15 wt% oxygen in the final PDC (Taki et al.,
       1987﻿). This residual oxygen content can adversely affect the thermal stabil­
       ity of the non-oxide PDCs, weakening their overall performance.

       The utilization of a catalyst offers the advantage of crosslinking the PCPs
       at lower temperatures. The early linking of the volatile oligomers, facilitated
     by the catalyst, contributes to shape stability. Because of the crosslinking,
      the volatile oligomers, which typically evaporate or degrade, are effectively
      incorporated into the crosslinked network and increase the yield of the
      obtained ceramic (Janakiraman and Aldinger, 2009). Crosslinking using UV
      radiation is applicable when PCP contains photosensitive functional groups
      in its backbone structure. This method can be mostly effective when utilized
      for crosslinking PCPs in the form of fibers or thin structures due to its lim­
      ited penetration depth (Schulz et al., 2004). Another common crosslinking
     mechanism called “free radical polymerization” is utilized for the vat photo­
      polymerization AM technique. This method involves the absorption of UV
     photons with a PI. This process generates highly reactive free radicals (R*)
      that react with the monomer (M), leading to the formation of polymer chains
     and the progression of the polymerization process.
    3. Pyrolysis (Ceramization): Shaping and crosslinking of PCPs are followed
     by a pyrolysis step, known as ceramization, in which the PCP is trans­
     formed into a ceramic material through various thermal processes. These
      processes include hot pressing, spark plasma sintering, CVD, plasma spray­
      ing, rapid thermal annealing, laser pyrolysis, microwave heating, and the
     most commonly used method, pyrolysis in an argon or nitrogen atmosphere.
      Pyrolysis in such inert atmospheres leads to the formation of amorphous
      covalent ceramics with the decomposition of organic side chains (methyl/
      phenyl/vinyl groups) or Si – H , Si – OH , or Si – NH x groups and the gradual
     removal of the gaseous byproducts at elevated temperatures (600–1000℃).
       The reaction mechanisms during pyrolysis have been studied using
      solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance, Fourier transform infrared spectros­
      copy, Raman spectroscopy, and a thermogravimetric analysis, coupled with
     mass spectroscopy. The use of ion irradiation to eliminate hydrogen atoms
     through the cleavage of C-H bonds is an alternative non-thermal process for
      ceramization, where any remaining carbon is transformed to diamond-like
     carbon clusters. The pyrolysis atmosphere can modify the composition
      of the final ceramic component. Pyrolysis of a PCP under an inert atmo­
      sphere (argon or nitrogen) is required to create SiC , Si 3 N 4 , Si 3 CN , SiBC ,
      or SiCBN (depending on the starting PCP composition), whereas pyrolysis
      in air can be employed for the formation of silicate ceramics using active
     metal oxide fillers (Sarraf et al., 2023).
             During the ceramization process of PCPs, important parameters such
      as heating rate, reaction atmosphere, reaction temperature, and dwell time
      influence the phase composition and microstructure of the final ceramics.
     They influence the extent of crystallization, carbothermal reduction reac­
       tions, and filler reactions within the material (Sarraf et al., 2023).

3.2.5   Future of PDCs and AM Techniques﻿

The use of PCPs as a feedstock material for AM processes has demonstrated sig­
nificant potential for producing high-performance components. Researchers are

80           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

currently exploring several key areas and will likely remain focal points of future
work (Han et al., 2023):

   •  Advanced preceramic feedstocks  for AM processes  are an emerging
      trend driven by the rapid development of AM technologies and the grow­
      ing demand for advanced ceramic materials in applications like hyper­
      sonic flight, electronic devices, thermal protection, and healthcare. The
      focus will continue on developing preceramic feedstocks, particularly
     ceramic-based nanocomposites, for the fabrication of high-performance
     ceramic components.
   •  Developing highly dense, near-net-shape advanced ceramic composites
     with low volumetric shrinkage and high performance is a key focus area.
     Volumetric shrinkage and porosity remain significant challenges for pyro­
     lyzed AM-fabricated ceramic components, particularly when PCP resins
      are used as feedstocks. Adding inert or active fillers or reinforcement mate­
       rials has been shown to effectively reduce shrinkage and enhance the prop­
       erties of the printed ceramic components after pyrolysis. Future research
      will aim to explore new composite feedstock materials for manufacturing
      high-quality ceramic components with superior performance using AM
      processes.


3.3  REVIEW QUESTIONS

3.3.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. What are the feedstock materials commonly used for additive manufac­
     turing (AM) of advanced ceramics?
     Answer: Advanced ceramic AM typically uses materials like metal oxide
     powders – such as alumina and zirconia – and non-oxide ceramics like sili­
     con carbide or silicon nitride. Composite ceramics are also common. These
      materials are chosen for their exceptional strength, thermal stability, and
      resistance to chemicals, making them ideal for demanding applications in
      aerospace, automotive, and electronics.
   2. Why are binders necessary for AM of advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Binders play a crucial role in ceramic AM by holding the ceramic
      particles together during printing and early handling. In techniques like
      binder jetting or extrusion, they prevent the powder from dispersing and
      help maintain the shape of the printed part – known as the green body –
      before it’s sintered. Binders also improve the flow of ceramic materials,
     which enhances printing precision and overall part stability.
   3. What are the advantages of using powder-based feedstock materials in
     ceramic AM?﻿
     Answer: Powder-based feedstocks offer several benefits, including the abil­
       ity to print highly complex shapes that are difficult or costly to make using
      traditional methods. They allow for efficient use of material with minimal
     waste and can be customized by tweaking the particle size or composition

Feedstock Materials for AMC                                          81

      to suit specific performance needs. This flexibility makes powder-based AM
     a powerful option for producing advanced ceramic components.
    4. In powder-based AMC processes, why is particle shape an important
      issue?﻿
     Answer: Ceramic powder processing consists of powder production by
      milling/grinding and sieving, followed by the fabrication of the green prod­
       uct, which is then consolidated to obtain the final product.
      Particle shape is an important issue for the following reasons:
       •   Irregular particles “key” together well and so, when pressed together,
         tend to adhere, leading to stronger “green” components than rounded
           particles.
       •  Rounded particles flow more easily than irregular particles and can pack
          together more uniformly and densely than irregular particles.
       •  For the highest packing density, use mainly rounded particles with a
         range of particle sizes (small ones to fill up the gaps between big ones).
       •  With a single size, highly controlled porosity can be achieved.
       •  Most ceramic components are made through powder processing, starting
         with ceramic powders.
       •   Generally speaking, the flow for ceramic components includes: raw
          materials → powder processing/mixing → forming → firing/sintering
    → final ceramic component.
   5. How does the particle size and distribution of feedstock powders influ­
     ence the AM of advanced ceramics?
     Answer: Particle size and distribution play a key role in ceramic AM. Finer
      particles typically allow for better packing density and smoother surface
       finishes, which is ideal for high-resolution printing. However, they can be
      harder to flow. Larger particles improve flowability but may compromise
       detail and cause defects. A well-balanced particle size distribution ensures a
     good compromise between printability, strength, and sintering performance.
    6. What are the different forms of feedstocks used in AM of advanced
     ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Ceramic AM uses several feedstock forms, including powders,
      pastes, slurries, and filaments. Powders are common in binder jetting and
     SLS. Slurries and pastes – ceramic powders mixed with a liquid binder –
      are used in SLA and DIW for high-resolution printing. Filaments, used in
    FDM, are made by combining ceramic powders with polymers to create a
      solid strand that can be extruded. Each form suits different processes based
     on material handling and part complexity.
    7. What are the common binder materials used in the AM of advanced
     ceramics, and why are they chosen?﻿
     Answer: Typical binders include materials like polyvinyl alcohol (PVA),
      polyethylene glycol (PEG), and wax-based compounds. These are chosen
     because they help maintain the shape and strength of printed parts (green
      bodies) during handling and printing. They also need to burn out cleanly
      during sintering to avoid defects. Good binder compatibility with ceramic
     powders is essential for a strong, cohesive final structure.

82           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   8. How does the removal of binders affect the AM process of advanced
     ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Binder removal is a critical step that must be carefully controlled.
       If binders aren’t completely removed, they can leave behind residues that
     weaken the part or disrupt sintering. This process, often done through ther­
     mal or chemical debinding, needs to be slow and even to prevent cracking,
     warping, or contamination. Successful binder removal is key to achieving
      high-quality ceramic components.
   9. What are the main challenges in the AM of advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Some of the biggest challenges include achieving high density
     and mechanical strength after sintering, managing thermal stresses that can
     cause cracks, and minimizing defects like warping. The materials them­
      selves can also be costly, and the process often involves complex steps such
      as careful binder removal and thermal post-processing. These factors make
         it difficult to produce high-performance ceramic parts consistently.
  10. What are some of the AM techniques that are particularly suitable for
     processing advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Techniques like selective laser sintering (SLS), binder jetting,
      direct ink writing (DIW), and stereolithography (SLA) are well-suited for
      ceramics. They offer high precision and the ability to produce complex
     shapes layer by layer. These methods can handle advanced ceramic powders
     and binders, making them ideal for parts that require both intricate geometry
     and strong material performance.
  11. What role do photoinitiators play in the AM of advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Photoinitiators are key additives in light-based AM processes like
    SLA and DLP. They absorb light and trigger the hardening (polymerization)
      of resin-based ceramic slurries, solidifying each printed layer. The right
      photoinitiator helps control curing speed, depth, and resolution, directly
      affecting the detail, surface quality, and strength of the final ceramic part.
  12. How do surfactants and dispersants contribute to the performance of
     ceramic feedstocks in AM?﻿
     Answer: Surfactants and dispersants help improve how ceramic powders
     mix and flow. Surfactants reduce surface tension between powders and bind­
       ers, improving flow and coating. Dispersants prevent particles from clump­
      ing, keeping them evenly distributed in the mixture. Both additives ensure
     a smoother, more uniform feedstock, which leads to better print quality and
     fewer defects.
  13. What are the functions of plasticizers, stabilizers, and crosslinkers in
     ceramic feedstocks for AM?﻿
     Answer: Plasticizers make the feedstock more flexible and easier to print by
     lowering viscosity – especially important for extrusion-based methods like
   FDM and DIW. Stabilizers prevent chemical degradation during printing
     and heat treatment, helping maintain material consistency. Crosslinkers are
     used in light-based processes to form strong bonds between polymer chains,
     improving the mechanical strength and stability of printed parts. Together,
      these additives optimize printability and the final part’s performance.

﻿Classification of 4﻿   AM Processes of
     Ceramic Materials﻿



This chapter provides an overview of the classification of additive manufacturing pro­
cesses for ceramic materials (AMC), laying the groundwork for a deeper understanding
of this versatile technology and its potential applications. A comprehensive classification
of additive manufacturing (AM) can be found in standards such as the German pro­
duction process standard (DIN 8580), the American Society for Testing and Materials
(ASTM-F42, 2009), and other specialized guidelines. While many AM techniques have
been successfully commercialized for producing polymer and metal parts, fewer systems
have been developed for manufacturing functional ceramic components. As a result,
recent research has focused on advancing AMC. Our work draws on the latest research,
utilizing data collected from studies on the classification of ceramic AM techniques.
  Based on that, AM processes for ceramic materials can be classified based on sev­
eral factors, including the technology employed, the form of the starting materials,
and the intended application or type of ceramic material used.


4.1  GENERAL CLASSIFICATION SCHEMES OF AMC

4.1.1   Classification Based on Common Ceramic AM Technologies﻿

One of the common classifications is based on ASTM-F42, 2009 committee guide­
lines, according to which AM can be classified into seven categories. These categories
are vat photopolymerization (VP), material jetting (MJ), binder jetting (BJ), mate­
rial extrusion (ME), sheet lamination (SL), powder bed fusion (PBF), and directed
energy deposition (DED). The sequence of these categories is aligned according to
their energy consumption. For example, the least energy is required in the case of VP
(typically a laser of 40–50 mW) to cure the layers, while high energy is consumed
in DED (typically 4–6 kW). This classification is adopted by Srivastav et al. (2022).
  Özden et al. (2021), Bandyopadhyay et al. (2016), and Travitzky et al. (2014)
­classified AMC according  to Common Ceramic AM Processes as shown  in
Figures 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3, respectively.
  Özden et al. (2021) organized AMC into several key categories according to
ASTM-F42, 2009 (Figure 4.1). Here’s a structured overview of their classification.

   •  Powder Bed Fusion﻿
      In PBF a laser or electron beam is used to fuse (sinter or melt) the pow­
      der together at pre-defined positions in the ceramic powder bed. Once a

      layer is completed, the building platform is lowered and a new layer of pow­
      der is deposited. The process is repeated until the part is completed. PBF
      processes can be divided into three subcategories: electron beam melting
     (EBM), selective laser melting (SLM), and selective laser sintering (SLS),
      although EBM and SLM are used mainly in AM of metals. SLS is regarded
      as a slow and costly process; however, the print quality of the formed parts
       is high.
   •  Binder Jetting﻿
      BJ, one of the pioneering techniques for AM of ceramics, is a process where
      the binder is deposited on a ceramic powder bed. As the binder is selectively
       jetted on the powder bed, it solidifies and bonds the powder in those areas.
     The next layer of powder is spread on with the help of a scraper or roller,
     and the process is repeated until the part is completed. BJ can be used for
      the production of porous parts and large products with complex geometries.
    On the other hand, the resolution and surface quality of the parts are low.
    Due to difficulty in removing the remaining powder after the process, it is
      not possible to print parts with small or closed pores with BJ. Alongside
      the aforementioned dry powder-based BJ, slurry-based BJ is also used for
      processing ceramics.
   •  Photopolymerization﻿
     Photopolymerization is one of the most used and well-developed AM pro­
      cesses. Unlike other ceramic AM processes, where thermal reactions take
      place during solidification, during photopolymerization, chemical reaction
      takes place due to radiation induced polymerization. Light, which usually

88           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

     has a wavelength within the UV range, is used to irradiate certain areas
      of the slurry to cure and polymerize the monomers which surround the
     ceramic particles. Exceptionally, the wavelength of visible light can also
     be used. One of the most commonly used photopolymerization processes
       is stereolithography (SLA). During the SLA of ceramics, ceramic pow­
      der is mixed with photopolymerizable monomers (e.g., acrylate, epoxy),
      photoinitiators, anti-scattering agents, and other non-reactive additives to
      decrease the viscosity of the slurry. Typically, a high ceramic powder load­
      ing of 40–60 vol.% is used. Ceramic suspensions possess suitable viscosity,
     good stability, and a homogeneous distribution of particles. Parts fabricated
     by SLA are characterized by high density, high resolution, and good sur­
      face quality. SLA is widely used to produce complex-shaped ceramics
     such as Al 2 O 3 , ZrO2 , and transparent laser ceramics. Lithography-based
     ceramic manufacturing (LCM) outstands in surface quality as well as pre­
      cision of parts and is used for a wide range of ceramic materials from SiOC
      to SiAlON.
   •  Material Extrusion﻿
     There are two main ME AM processes: fused filament fabrication (FFF) and
      direct ink writing (DIW), also referred to as robocasting (RC), which is an
   AM method developed for processing ceramics. In DIW, filaments of con­
      centrated colloidal suspensions or pastes are used as feedstock and processed
       at room temperature. Shape retention is due to the high solid loading and
      viscoelastic rheological properties. In FFF a thermoplastic filament is pre­
     pared with a high solid loading of ceramic particles. The filament is melted
     and extruded through a heated nozzle. Due to the thermoplastic nature of
      the feedstock, the extruded material solidifies and retains the desired shape
    when the temperature is decreased. The main advantages of extrusion-based
      techniques are low cost, high speed, and large-size capabilities. It is also
      possible to manufacture multi-material parts with complex geometries by
     combining multiple extrusion heads or using a single nozzle for multiple
      thermoplastic filaments. The main drawbacks of extrusion-based processes
      are poor mechanical properties and surface quality.
   •  Material Jetting﻿
    MJ is an AM process where the material is deposited in droplets to man­
      ufacture the part. This process is fast and offers high accuracy; however,
         it is limited in material selection due to the requirement for low feedstock
      viscosity under processing conditions. MJ has three sub-processes: inkjet
      printing, aerosol jet printing (AJP), and T3DP.
   •  Inkjet Printing﻿
      Inkjet printing in ceramic AM is a high-resolution, drop-on-demand tech­
     nique that deposits droplets of low-viscosity ceramic ink onto a substrate.
     The ink typically consists of ceramic nanoparticles suspended in water or
      organic solvents, with a viscosity suitable for inkjet nozzles (typically <30
      mPa·s). This process allows precise deposition with feature sizes in the
     range of 20–50 µm, making it ideal for fabricating fine structures, thin films,
     and functional ceramic layers. However, the low solid loading limits green

Classification of AM Processes of Ceramic Materials                       89

      part density, requiring extensive post-processing, including drying, binder
      removal, and sintering to achieve dense ceramic components.
   •  Aerosol Jet Printing﻿
    AJP uses a mist of aerosolized ceramic ink to deposit material onto flat or
      non-planar surfaces. It accommodates inks with higher viscosities (up to
     ~1000 mPa·s) and solid loadings than inkjet printing, improving deposition
      control and material variety. The aerosol is created through atomization and
     guided to the substrate by a carrier and sheath gas, allowing high-precision
      feature deposition down to 10 µm. AJP is especially useful for producing
     complex ceramic microstructures, electronic components, and coatings,
     though it requires careful process control and similar post-processing steps
      as inkjet methods.
   •  Thermoplastic 3D Printing﻿
     Thermoplastic 3D printing (T3DP) employs molten ceramic–thermoplas­
       tic suspensions in a drop-on-demand manner to build parts with high solid
      loading (up to ~60 vol%). The feedstock is heated above the binder’s melt­
      ing point and ejected as droplets that solidify upon deposition, forming a
      stable green structure with high dimensional accuracy. T3DP supports
      greater design complexity and structural integrity than other jetting methods
     due to the dense green parts it produces. Post-processing includes thermo­
      plastic debinding and high-temperature sintering, enabling the fabrication
      of strong, fully dense ceramic components suitable for structural, biomedi­
       cal, or electronic applications. Table 4.1 provides a comparison between the
      three sub-processes of AMC MJ, regarding feedstock, viscosity range, solid
      loading, resolution, post-processing, and key applications.
   •  Sheet Lamination﻿
     SL, also known as laminated object manufacturing (LOM), is a process
     where sheets of material are laid on each other with a layer of adhesive
      material in between each layer to help the interconnection of layers. The
     bonding of subsequent layers is ensured by mechanical compression or heat
      treatment. This layered structure is cut with the help of a laser beam to
      achieve the desired final shape. In the case of ceramics, tape casting is used
      to prepare sheets of material. Large parts can be produced with this process,
     and a wide range of materials are possible.

Each of these processes has its own advantages and limitations, influencing factors
like material properties, complexity of shapes, and production speed. Özden et al.
(2021) considered the DED not to be one of the dedicated technologies for AMC.
  Bandyopadhyay et al. (2016) focused on various AM techniques, exploring how
they can be applied to ceramic processing and their advantages and associated chal­
lenges. Figure 4.2 illustrates the proposed classification, which closely aligns with
the ASTM-F52, 2009 classification system.

highlighting common ceramic AM techniques, based on the ASTM-F42, 2009 clas­
sification system. In addition to the process classification, they addressed key issues
such as dimensional order, starting materials, and the type of layer formation used.

4.1.2   Classification Based on Feedstock Material Form﻿

Three feedstock materials are considered (Figure 4.4).

   •  Liquid/Slurry-Based Deposition Processes: Use of liquid resins or solu­
      tions that cure into a solid ceramic, such as vat polymerization, or MJ.
   •  Powder-Based Deposition Processes: These techniques rely on the dep­
      osition of a uniform powder layer (powder bed), which is either directly
      densified by a heat source (e.g., laser) or bonded together by a selectively
      deposited binder system, as in the case of a BJ.
   •  Bulk Solid-Based Deposition Processes: such as ME and DIW.

This will be separately treated in the next section of the chapter.

4.1.3   Classification According to Single Versus Multi-Step Processes﻿

Deckers et al. (2014), Dadkhah et al. (2023), and Özden et al. (2021) have catego­
rized technologies of AMC according to ISO/ASTM. Accordingly, complex shape
ceramic part production using the AM techniques can be classified into two groups:
direct or single-step and indirect process, also known as multi-step. In the multi-step

AM process, the manufactured green body requires post-processing steps such as
debinding and sintering treatments to consolidate the green body. SL, ME-based
techniques, BJ, VP-based technologies, direct inkjet printing (DIP), and indirect SLS
are the most available indirect AM technologies. Whereas there are currently only
two AM processes that can be used to produce complex shape advanced ceramic
parts via directly shaping and consolidating the material in a single step: laser-pow­
der bed fusion (L-PBF) and DED (Dadkhah et al., 2023).

4.1.4   Classification According to Part Quality﻿

AMC technologies can be classified according to the quality of their printed parts
(Deckers et al., 2014). For some AMC processes producing ceramic parts, cracks
are still the most critical flaws that compromise the mechanical strength. During
single-step processes, that is, DED and single-step PBF processes, thermal cracks
are generally caused by thermal shocks introduced by the laser beam heating. It is
well known that preheating the ceramic powder before laser irradiation and material
consolidations results in overcoming these cracks during single-step PBF. During
multi-step processes, cracks are generally caused during the post-processing furnace
treatment.

4.1.5   Classification Based on End-Use Applications﻿
   •  Functional Parts: Components designed for specific mechanical, thermal,
      or electrical functions such as parts in aerospace, automotive, and biomedi­
      cal fields.
   •  Prototyping : Rapid production of models for testing and validation such as
      design iterations for engineering applications.
   •  Artistic and Decorative : Creating intricate designs sculptures or ceramic
       art.

4.1.6   Classification Based on Material Properties﻿
   •  Traditional Ceramics: Commonly used clays and earthenware, such as
     stoneware and porcelain.
   •  Advanced Ceramics : Materials engineered for enhanced properties (e.g.,
      strength, thermal stability), such as zirconia, alumina, and silicon carbide.
