   Unlike polymers and metals, which can be molten or plastically deformed to obtain
the desired geometry, stress accumulation during the solidification of ceramics pre­
vents their direct shaping by certain AM processes, namely PBF, MJ, or ME. Binder
materials are added to ceramic powders to form suitable feedstocks to enable their
shaping into desired geometries by the aforementioned techniques. In these tech­
niques, processing ceramics usually requires additional post-processing steps such
as drying, debinding, and sintering, which are not needed in the case of polymers.
   According to the type of raw material supply, AMC processes can be classified
into liquid-based, solid-based, powder based Chen et al. (2018), Özden et al. (2021),
Dadkhah et al. (2023), and others.

   •  In liquid-based techniques a high powder concentration suspension or slurry
      of ceramic powder is prepared. Depending on the selected technique, the
     suspension medium and additives are optimized to ensure the optimal rheo­
      logical characteristics to enable further processing (Cano et al., 2019).
   •  Powder-based techniques rely on the deposition of a uniform powder layer
     (powder bed), which is either directly densified by a heat source (e.g., laser)
          ﻿(Zocca et al., 2013), or bonded together by a selectively deposited binder
      system, as in the case of BJ. To ensure uniform deposition and high packing
      density, the properties of the powder, especially the size and shape, are of
      importance.
   •  Solid-based techniques cover those that use solid feedstocks at room tem­
      perature, but in the case of thermoplastic materials, higher temperatures are
     used to melt and process the feedstock.

4.2.1  Özden Model﻿

According to Özden et al. (2021), there are many AMC techniques suitable for
ceramic fabrication, with their specific advantages and disadvantages (Figure 4.5).
Currently, stereolithography of ceramics (SLC) is regarded as state-of-the-art tech­
nology for ceramic AM, but for the moment its high cost, long processing time, and
limited material selection are limiting its wider industrial use. Prior to SLC, FFF, a
technique representing a cornerstone for AM of ceramics, has established a wide­
spread and cost-effective AM technology, however, with relatively low resolution and
poor surface finish limited by the inherent process limitations. It is based on model­
ing thermoplastic feedstocks and can thus benefit from existing knowledge from con­
ventional injection molding methods. The development of novel feedstock materials
will drive further development of the FFF technique to produce ceramic components.
  Most recently, T3DP emerged as a high-precision, high-surface-finish AM tech­
nology. According to Figure 4.5, solid-based techniques cover those that utilize
feedstocks which are solid at room temperature, but, in the case of thermoplastic
materials, higher temperatures are used to melt and process the feedstock. T3DP
provides easy feedstock handling and the possibility to be combined with other pro­
cesses, such as FFF, to overcome the disadvantages of individual processes. With
further development, thermoplastic feedstock-based AM processes have the potential
to take AM of ceramics to a more advanced level, which is dependent not only on

   Laser-engineered net shaping (LENS) is a DED process focused by the laser beam
and produces molten material onto the surface area. The powder material is fed
through the feeding gas that also acts as a coolant that solidifies the molten material
as soon as it is deposited on the surface. LENS is much easier to control while achiev­
ing higher cooling rates. By using different powders carried in different nozzles and
allowing them to react with different non-reactive gases, functionally graded mate­
rials can be produced. Since LENS is used only to repair and not to produce parts, it
has not been considered in this classification (Chen et al., 2018).
    It is important to note that all ceramic AM processes share a common charac­
teristic in that they use ceramic in its powder form. Moreover, most are indirect 3D
printing processes. The printed parts need to go through debinding and sintering pro­
cesses (Figure 4.7). The debinding process removes the matrix material that is used,
while the sintering process is a high-temperature thermal treatment used to densify
the part after the matrix material is removed.

4.2.3   Lakhdar Model﻿

Ceramic AM processes can be categorized according to whether they are “sin­
gle-step” or “multi-step” processes. Multi-step AM processes result in the for­
mation of a green body that requires subsequent debinding and sintering thermal
treatments to obtain the final advanced ceramic part. Most AM technologies, as
they have been implemented up until now, belong to this category. SL processes,
extrusion-based technologies such as FDC, freeze-form extrusion fabrication
(FEF) and RC, VP-based technologies, DIP, BJ, and indirect laser sintering (iLS)
have all been applied using a multi-step process. On the other hand, there are
currently only two AM processes that have been demonstrated to be capable of
directly shaping and sintering advanced ceramics in a single step: direct laser sin­
tering (dLS), commonly known as SLM and DED. The most extensive list to date
of AM technologies that have been used to shape advanced ceramics is provided
in Figure 4.8.

4.3  REVIEW QUESTIONS

4.3.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. How does the form of feedstock material influence the choice of AM
     process for advanced ceramics?
     Answer: The form of the feedstock – whether it’s powder, liquid, or filament –
      plays a big role in deciding which AM process to use for ceramics. Each
     form comes with  its own set of handling and processing needs. Pow­
      der-based materials are suited for methods like PBF, which rely on precise
      spreading and sintering. Liquid slurries are ideal for processes like SLA,
     where light is used to cure layers of material. Filaments, often used in FDM,
      are user-friendly and easy to handle but can struggle to deliver the density
     and strength required for high-performance ceramics. Choosing the right
     form is key to balancing printability with final part quality.
   2. Define material jetting of ceramics and then classify it into its three
     sub-processes: inkjet printing, aerosol jet printing, and T3DP.
     Answer: Material jetting is an AM process where the material is depos­
      ited in droplets to manufacture the part. This process is fast and accurate;
     however, it is limited in material selection due to the requirement for low
      feedstock viscosity under processing conditions. Material jetting has three
      sub-processes.
        1. Inkjet printing of ceramic AM is a high-resolution, drop-on-demand
        technique that deposits droplets of low-viscosity ceramic ink onto a sub­
          strate. This process allows precise deposition with feature sizes in the
        range of 20–50 µm, making it ideal for fabricating fine structures, thin
          films, and functional ceramic layers.
        2. AJP uses a mist of aerosolized ceramic ink to deposit material onto flat
         or non-planar surfaces. It accommodates inks with higher viscosities (up
         to ~1000 mPa·s) and solid loadings than inkjet printing, improving depo­
          sition control and material variety. AJP is especially useful for producing
       complex ceramic microstructures, electronic components, and coatings,
        though it requires careful process control and similar post-processing
         steps as inkjet methods.

102           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

        3. T3DP employs molten ceramic–thermoplastic suspensions in a drop-on-
       demand manner to build parts with high solid loading (up to ~60 vol%).
       The feedstock is heated above the binder’s melting point and ejected as
         droplets that solidify upon deposition, forming a stable green structure
        with high dimensional accuracy. T3DP supports greater design complex­
          ity and structural integrity than other jetting methods due to the dense
        green parts it produces.
   3. How does the use of filament-based feedstocks for advanced ceramic
   AM compare to powder and slurry forms?
     Answer: Filament-based feedstocks are easier to handle and process, espe­
      cially with techniques like FDM, making them appealing for more accessible
     ceramic printing. However, they often fall short when it comes to achieving
      the density and strength needed for high-performance ceramic parts. Unlike
     powders or slurries, filaments can’t be compacted as efficiently, which
      affects sintering results. They also tend to limit resolution, making it harder
      to print fine, complex geometries.
   4. How do multi-step AM processes affect the material properties of
     advanced ceramic parts?﻿
     Answer: Multi-step processes, such as printing followed by debinding and
      sintering, can significantly improve a ceramic part’s strength, density, and
     thermal stability. These steps help refine the material’s structure but also
      introduce more complexity. More stages mean longer production times,
      higher costs, and increased chances for defects like warping or cracking if
      not carefully controlled.
   5. What are the potential advantages of using a single-step process for AM
      of advanced ceramics compared to a multi-step approach?﻿
     Answer: Single-step processes offer speed and simplicity by removing the
     need for separate post-processing like sintering or curing. This makes them
     more cost-effective and lowers the risk of introducing errors during multi­
      ple steps. However, these methods often can’t match the material quality
     achieved through multi-step approaches, limiting their use in applications
      that require high-density or high-performance ceramics.
   6. In what situations would a multi-step AM process be more beneficial
     than a single-step process for advanced ceramics?
     Answer: Multi-step processes are ideal when performance matters most –
      like in aerospace, defense, or medical applications – where strength, dura­
       bility, and thermal resistance are critical. Although these processes take
     more time and effort, they allow for better control over the final properties,
     making them worth the investment for high-stakes applications.
    7. How does the medical industry benefit from ceramic AM, and which
     processes are most commonly used?
     Answer: Ceramic AM offers the medical field the ability to create custom­
      ized implants, dental prosthetics, and bone scaffolds tailored to individ­
      ual patients. Processes like SLA and direct ink writing (DIW) are popular
     because they can produce highly detailed, biocompatible parts with excel­
      lent precision – crucial for fit and function in medical applications.

Classification of AM Processes of Ceramic Materials                      103

    8. How does the type of layer formation affect the mechanical properties
      of advanced ceramic parts produced via AM?
     Answer: The method used to build up layers greatly influences a ceramic
      part’s strength and surface finish. Techniques like PBF tend to produce
      strong, well-bonded layers thanks to localized sintering. In contrast, meth-
     ods like inkjet or direct ink writing may result in weaker layer bonding,
      requiring additional post-processing to reach desirable mechanical prop-
       erties. The choice of technique has a direct impact on the final part’s
     performance.

﻿Slurry-Based Deposition 5﻿      for Advanced Ceramics ﻿



The slurry-based deposition technique includes vat photopolymerization (VP) and
material jetting technology (MJT), as shown in Figure 5.1. VP is one of the most
widely used additive manufacturing (AM) methods for producing ceramic materials.
Stereolithography (SLA) and digital light processing (DLP) are subcategories of the
VP process and other related techniques. MJT, on the other hand, involves using ink­
jet technology with thousands of micro-sized nozzles to print 3D products.
  Based on the type of feedstock materials, ceramic powder with polymer (conven­
tional) and preceramic polymers (with or without fillers) are the two most popular
materials for AM processes. AM processes with ceramic powder and polymer sus­
pension (conventional) involve mixing ceramic powders with binder polymers for
the 3D fabrication of solid objects. Once printed, objects usually undergo a sintering
process to remove the polymer and fuse the ceramic powder, and, finally, the solid
ceramic objects are produced.
  The AM processes with preceramic polymers involve feedstock materials that
usually consist of organic compounds and possess excellent processability, which
allows them to be easily shaped into desired geometric structures. After pyrolysis, the
AM-fabricated preceramic physical objects will be further converted into functional
ceramic components. AM processes using preceramic feedstock materials have been
demonstrated to be effective and versatile approaches for manufacturing functional
advanced ceramic materials with complex geometric structures. They have been
investigated for various applications, especially in the last decade. However, the use
of preceramic polymers as a starting material for 3D printing is still developing.
  Compared to ceramic powders, preceramic polymers offer much more flexibility
for effectively fabricating ceramic components with complex geometric structures
and shapes using a wide range of processes, such as casting, molding, and AMC.
Preceramic polymers have different configurations/microstructures which affect
the composition, microstructure, porosity, yield, and properties of the fabricated
ceramics.

VP uses a vat of liquid photopolymer resin, out of which the model is constructed layer
by layer. Ultraviolet (UV) light is used to cure or harden the resin where required,
while a platform moves the object being made downward after each new layer is

   There are two possible structures for a VP machine, depending on the manufac­
turer’s design: bottom-up and top-down orientations, as shown in Figure 5.2. All VP
technologies use almost similar mechanisms for curing and fabrication of structures.
Bottom-up printers have the main light engine positioned below the resin vat and
the part print upside-down. The build plate moves up from the resin vat to print the
part layer by layer. In contrast, in top-down printers, the light engine is positioned
above the built platform. The printing starts from the top of the vat in the resin and
moves down as the layers are cured to fabricate the features. The light source can be
different, such as UV lamps, laser radiation, gamma rays, light-emitting diode (LED)
screen, X-rays, or electron beams; however, UV light is commonly applied for curing
the photopolymer resin. The bottom-up VP printer is the more common method to
print microparts with finely detailed geometries.

sintering at high temperatures to obtain the final ceramic component. For alumina
and zirconia materials, the sintering temperature can be increased up to 1600°C. In
addition, ceramic parts should be sintered under a controlled temperature to reduce
thermal stresses and avoid crack formation. After sintering, the obtained samples
offer high-density and complex features (Wang J-C et al., 2019).

5.1.1.1   Stereolithography of Ceramics
Figure 5.3 shows the steps to fabricate alumina parts using stereolithography of
ceramics (SLC). Briefly, ceramic particles are added to photoreactive polymers such
as acrylate and epoxy resins to form a homogeneous ceramic–polymer suspension.
Ceramic particles are then cured with a photocurable polymer using a UV laser
beam. After the curing is completed, the organic phase is removed by an appropriate
thermal treatment cycle.
   Hinczewski et al. (1998a), reported the effects of dispersant and diluent concentra­
tions on the viscosity and rheological behavior of highly loaded alumina particles in
curable acrylate monomer solutions. Chartier et al. (2002), also reported the effects
of exposure conditions, powder characteristics, reactive system, and cured depth and
width on the SLC process.

5.1.1.1.1  SLC Printers
Printers for SLC were the first commercially available printers designed specifically
for ceramic part manufacturing. These printers are known for their exceptional char­
acteristics, which include:

   •  High accuracy
   •  Smooth surface finish
   •  Strong chemical bonding between layers

The SLC printers utilize a “top-down” approach for printing, allowing multiple small
samples to be fabricated simultaneously by positioning them next to each other on

resin vat, a model-building platform, and an UV laser, which together facilitate the
creation of precise and high-quality ceramic parts. The ceramic components are pro­
duced by laser VP successive layers of liquid resins. These resins include organic
molecules, monomers, oligomers or prepolymers, photoinitiators (PIs), and other
additives that enhance different functionalities. The resin is cured and solidified
through a chemical reaction activated by a light source (laser or LEDs) emitting UV
light to form a highly crosslinked polymer network. The UV laser is focused onto the
surface of a vat filled with liquid photopolymer, and a highly exothermic polymer­

spontaneously until the monomers cease to react or another terminating reaction
occurs. Once the first layer is fully polymerized according to the CAD model, a res­

should be like conventional SLA resins (<3 mPa.s) to achieve proper flow during
layer-by-layer processing (Griffith and Halloran, 1994). In addition, the ceramic sus­
pension should be photoactive with high cure depth and low cure width to achieve

nificant shrinkage after polymer removal (Griffith and Halloran, 1994; Hinczewski
et al., 1998a).
  Ceramic powders have negligible solubility in polymer solutions. Dispersants are
needed to achieve a homogeneous dispersion of ceramic powders in a polymer solu­
tion with high ceramic loading. Dispersants are widely used to disperse ceramic
particles in low-polar organic media through electrostatic and steric repulsion forces
(Hinczewski et  al., 1998a). Many dispersants have been introduced to improve
ceramic powder loading and homogeneity of suspension for the SLA process. Using
quaternary ammonium acetate as a dispersant allows the 50 vol.% of alumina
loading in hexanediol diacrylate (HDDA); however, 50 vol.% of alumina loading
in HDDA without a dispersant results in a stiff paste-like colloidal gel (Brady and
Halloran, 1997). Triton X-100 is another dispersant used in barium titanate-HDDA
(BT-HDDA) resin system. 6 wt.% triton X-100 is the optimized concentration for 30
vol.% BT-HDDA suspension (Jang et al., 2000).
   Viscosity is another crucial factor that decides the rheological behavior of the
suspension. The viscosity of an SLA suspension can be calculated using a modified
Krieger–Dougherty equation (Griffith and Halloran, 1994). The viscosity of the sus­
pension is usually larger than that of pure photocurable resin. The viscosity of the
suspension for SLA is generally in the range of 2–5 Pa.s to assure satisfactory layer

Slurry-Based Deposition for Advanced Ceramics                         113

recoating. Thus, decreasing the viscosity of the suspension is vital for a successful
ceramic SLA. Suspension with low viscosity can be achieved by using an appropri­
ate polymer, dispersant, and diluent (Hinczewski et al., 1998b). The initial viscos­
ity and the change in viscosity regarding shear rate play a significant role during
the SLA. By increasing the shear rate, the viscosity may decrease (shear thinning),
increase (shear-thickening), or remain unchanged (shear immunity). Shear thinning
is desired in the standard SLA process as it allows the tape casting of layers before
UV treatment (Hinczewski et al., 1998b). The viscosity of the suspension decreases
with an increase in temperature. However, the temperature should not be higher than
the polymerization temperature, as it causes undesired polymerization before UV
scanning.

5.1.1.1.4   Challenges Facing SLC
SLC faces challenges due to the complex interaction between light and the ceram­
ic-filled resin, which affects flow, resolution, and curing performance. The main
challenges facing SLC in AM are suspension rheology, particulate-induced light
scattering, and low cure depth. Here’s a brief explanation of each point:

   •  Suspension Rheology: SLA uses a photosensitive resin mixed with ceramic
       particles. The rheology (flow behavior) of this suspension must be well-con­
      trolled to ensure smooth layer spreading and printing accuracy. However,
     ceramic particles increase viscosity, making it harder to spread the material
      evenly and consistently, which can lead to print defects.
          To address rheological challenges in SLA of ceramics, Chartier et al.
     (2002) developed a novel processing method that allowed the use of photo­
      curable suspensions with ceramic loadings up to 60 vol.%. Instead of rely­
      ing on fluid flow for recoating, they employed a piston-driven dispensing
      system, combined with a doctor blade to spread uniform layers of a photo­
      curable alumina suspension. This approach enabled the formation of layers
      as thin as 25 µm. The printed parts, made from alumina with an average
      particle size of 1.5 µm, were sintered at 1700 °C and achieved relative den­
       sities of 97%, with flexural strengths of 275 MPa – comparable to those of
      conventionally processed ceramics (250–350 MPa).
          To improve densification when using coarser alumina powders, Zhang et
       al. (2021) introduced fine grains and sintering additives. Using a suspension
     with 50 vol.% ceramic content and alumina particles averaging 10.34 µm,
      sintering at 1600 °C resulted in minimal densification. However, by incor­
      porating a bimodal powder mixture – 85% of 10.34 µm and 15% of 1.05 µm
     alumina particles – along with 1 wt.% MgO and 3 wt.% TiO₂, the relative
      density improved to 93%. Although this density remains below the thresh­
      old required for structural ceramics, the results underscore the potential of
      low-cost coarse powders enhanced with fine grains and sintering aids. For
      printed zirconia components, Zhang et al. (2019) demonstrated that adding
      7.5 vol.% of 3Y-TZP (yttria-stabilized zirconia) increased the relative den­
       sity from 91.84% to 96.40%, highlighting the effectiveness of composition
      optimization in improving sintering outcomes.

114114           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   •  Particulate-Induced Light Scattering: During curing, a laser or light
      source polymerizes the resin. Ceramic particles can scatter and absorb light,
     reducing its penetration and precision. This scattering leads to blurring or
     unwanted curing, affecting resolution and feature accuracy.
   • Low Cure Depth: Because of the light scattering and absorption, the depth
      to which the resin cures (polymerizes) is reduced. This low cure depth lim-
        its layer thickness and increases print times, while also making it harder to
      fully bond layers, potentially compromising mechanical strength and part
       integrity.

particulate–loaded resin. In SLC, cured depth and width are important parameters
determining accuracy and process effectiveness. Cured depth Cd  is the thickness
of gelled resin and should be larger than 0.2 mm (Johansson et al., 2017). It can be

VP has two main parameters: the layer thickness (usually varying between 25 and
100 μm) and the light exposure energy that determines the cure depth. This key fac-
tor should be higher than the layer thickness to ensure layer integration (Johansson et
al., 2017). Conversely, if the cure depth is too high, the accuracy is reduced (Borlaf
et al., 2019). Thus, the cure depth should be between 1.10 and 1.35 times the layer
thickness (Wei et al., 2019), and the exposure energy must be defined empirically for
each photosensitive feedstock to satisfy such condition.
   However, cured width   Wc  should be low enough to ensure the high resolu-
tion and quality of SLA-printed parts. Cured width has been studied with density
of energy, PI concentration, powder concentration, particle diameter, and refrac-
tive index (RI) difference between powder and monomer. A linear relationship was
found between the mean particle diameter and cured width, with slopes depending
on energy density (Jacobs, 1992).
   Hinczewski et al. (1998a) predicted that heating the vat of photocurable suspen-
sion significantly reduces viscosity, which enables higher ceramic content. For an
alumina diacrylate photocurable suspension, viscosity was reduced by a factor of six
when the temperature was increased from 25°C to 70°C. This enabled an unusually

   Finally, this process presents outstanding surface quality, and roughness  ( Ra )
below 0.5 μm has been reported by (Borlaf et al., 2019). Research about ceramic VP
has become widespread in recent years, and over 30 research institutions published
at least ten papers indexed by the Web of Science in the past five years. For more
in-depth information about this technology, many review articles are given in the

  Ceramic VP is the most mature technology with an industrial readiness level and
several commercial machines (Chen et al., 2019). Although most related companies
emerged in the last five years, there are well-established companies with years in
the market, such as Lithoz (2022) and 3DCeram (2022), with a variety of 3D print­
ing systems and feedstock commercially available. Even systems capable of working
with multi-materials have emerged in recent years.
   Contrastingly, producing carbides and borides with this technology remains chal­
lenging due to the high RI of these materials, which would cause light scattering
due to the RI mismatch with the usual photosensitive materials, leading to poor res­
olution and reducing the photopolymerization reaction. Such materials are not yet
commercially available. One alternative approach to deal with this issue is the use
of polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs), which are converted into ceramics without the
addition of ceramic particles. It is proven to be capable of manufacturing SiOC,
SiC, SiCN, and SiBCN (Li et al., 2018), by ceramic VP. This AM technology is
relatively expensive. The raw materials are costly because they depend on high-
priced photosensitive materials. Efforts have been made to reduce feedstock waste.
Thus, machines that work with a small amount of material (60 mL) and studies about
recycling raw materials have emerged (3DCeram, 2022). These systems have a ded­
icated recoating arrangement, which allows the spreading of constant and homoge­
neous micrometric layers even for high-viscosity feedstock, such as the high ceramic
loading photosensitive suspensions, de (Camargo et al., 2022). On the other hand,
research using home-built prototypes and low-cost 3D printers (Kotz et al., 2017),
commonly used in the manufacturing of polymers, has emerged and may be a suit­
able solution for the use of the technique in laboratories and small businesses.
  SLC is perhaps the AM process that is the most preferred when it comes to ceram­
ics. Because it uses a semi-liquid material, supports are needed under all overhangs,
and these supports are made from the same material. The advantages of SLA are that
it can deal with small powder grains (that are easy to sinter), and produce parts with
fine details with a very high accuracy and surface finish, in a wide range of available
ceramic materials. Its main drawbacks are the photopolymer stability over time (being
expired), the support removal from complex structures, and the difficulties in develop­
ing new materials, which are linked to several factors inherent to this technology.
   Existing machines are made by Lithoz, 3DCeram, Prodways, Admatec, or DDM
Systems. The size of the building platform goes from about 50 to 500 mm. 3DCeram
now has a wide range of AM machines, such as the C900, a hybrid press that prints
more than one material at the same time, dedicated to the electronics and energy
industries, and two additional machines launched in 2019. These are C100 “KISS”

5.1.1.1.8   Applications, Advantages, Limitations, and Future Developments of
          Ceramic SLC Process
   •  Applications:
     The first advantage of SLC is that it’s compatible with a wide range of
      ceramics, including alumina, zirconia, ZTA/ATZ, corderite, silicon-based
      ceramics, and HAP/TCP. Second, SLA allows for printing not only very
     dense parts but also very small details, thanks to the high resolution its thin
      layers provide. Ceramic SLC also made it possible to manufacture electric
      devices in small dimensions and complex structures. Moreover, SLC 3D
      printers are an excellent choice for jewelry, dental, and other high-precision
      casting applications. Attempts should be made to increase resolution and
      repeatability and to decrease the processing time. Recently, biocompatible
     ceramics such as hydroxyapatite (HA) and bioglass have been processed via
       this technology for biomedical implants and tissue engineering scaffolds.
     With the development of this technology, it will become a more promising
   AM method for manufacturing products for different applications.
   •  Advantages:
       •  The process is efficient, flexible, and of a high readiness level.
       •   It is characterized by repeatability and accuracy.
       •  Enables the fabrication of near-net-shape, fully dense parts with a high
         geometrical complexity and an excellent surface finish.
   •  Limitations:
       •  The limited types of ceramic materials can be produced using the pho­
         topolymerization of ceramic slurries.
       •  The processes may be limited in terms of the maximum wall thickness
          that can be manufactured without the formation of porosity or cracks.
       •  Large amounts of organic compounds such as dispersants and PIs are
        added; this first results in very significant shrinkage that can lead to part
        deformation and, second, tends to complicate the debinding stage due to
         the release of gaseous species
       •  Supporting  material  is needed when producing  parts  of complex
        geometry.
       •  Parts produced are of low density and of low mechanical strength.
       •  The process is not capable of manufacturing large ceramic parts.

   •  Future Developments:
      Future developments in SLC for advanced ceramics are poised to signifi­
      cantly enhance the precision, scalability, and material versatility of the pro­
      cess. Innovations in photopolymer resin formulations are expected to enable
      higher ceramic loadings, improving the density and mechanical properties
      of final sintered parts.
           In SLC, light projection systems are used to selectively cure photosensi­
       tive ceramic-loaded resins layer by layer. Traditional systems typically use
     a single-wavelength UV light to solidify each cross-section. However, vol­
      umetric curing (or holographic 3D printing) involves curing an entire 3D
     volume at once using intersecting light patterns. This technique could dras­
       tically reduce print times compared to layer-by-layer methods and produce
     more isotropic mechanical properties, which are especially important for
      structural ceramics. Volumetric curing (also called computed axial lithog­
     raphy or CAL) is different from SLC, DLP, and continuous liquid interface
      production (CLIP). It uses a series of light projections from different angles
      into a rotating or still volume of photopolymer to cure an entire 3D object
      simultaneously, rather than layer by layer. While promising for speed and
      isotropy, it’s still in early research stages for ceramics, as adapting dense,
     opaque ceramic suspensions to this technique is challenging.
           Integration with machine learning (ML) algorithms may further opti­
     mize print parameters and reduce defects. ML can be used to analyze large
      datasets of printing parameters, resin properties, and final part qualities to
      identify patterns that a human might overlook. For instance, ML can pre­
      dict the optimal exposure time, layer thickness, and resin temperature for
     a given ceramic formulation to achieve high-quality prints with minimal
     warping, cracking, or porosity. Additionally, real-time process monitoring
       (e.g., through cameras or sensors) can be fed into ML models to detect and
      correct errors during the printing process, significantly improving yield and
       reliability, especially for complex or high-value ceramic parts.
          Hybrid systems also open the door to multi-material printing, allowing
      ceramics to be combined with metals or polymers in a single part. This is
      especially valuable in industries like aerospace, where lightweight, thermally
       resistant parts are crucial; biomedicine, where implants must match vary­
      ing tissue properties; and micro-electro-mechanical system (MEMS), which
      require microscale precision and material integration for sensors or actuators.

5.1.1.2  DLP of Ceramics
The use of the DLP as an AM for ceramic fabrication has been widely explored. DLP
is another slurry-based VP process shown in Figure 5.8. High-density (97–99%) zir­
conia and alumina structural parts have been produced using this process. Since 2012,
considerable efforts have been made by a research team at the Vienna University of
Technology using DLP to produce complex ceramic structures with very fine fea­
tures, with resulting relative densities above 90% and mechanical strength compa­
rable with conventionally processed samples (Gmeiner et al., 2015). Other ceramic

materials, such as zirconia and β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP), were successfully
printed with solid loadings of up to 50 vol.% (Schwentenwein and Homa, 2014).
  Based on the aforementioned research, the team commercialized the DLP-based
ceramic printing technique – termed lithography-based ceramic manufacturing –
through the establishment of Lithoz GmbH, with the objective of further advanc­
ing the AM of high-performance ceramics (Schwentenwein et al., 2014). Owing to
its superior efficiency relative to the conventional stereolithography (SLC) process,
DLP presents a highly promising approach for the fabrication of advanced ceramic
components.
  DLP is also considered a subcategory of the VP approach, as both use light as
the polymerizing agent. DLP is a mask-based stereolithography technique in which
a complete image is projected onto the surface of a photopolymerizable resin via a
patterned light source. The concept was initially introduced using physical masks
by Nakamoto and Yamaguchi, and later by Lee et al. (2015). In 1997, Bertsch
et al. advanced the method by employing a liquid crystal display (LCD) as a dynamic
mask generator. Since 2001, LCDs have largely been supplanted by digital micro­
mirror devices (DMDs), owing to their superior fill factor and reflectivity, which
result in enhanced resolution and contrast in the projected light pattern (Kaneko and
Takahashi, 2001). The DLP technique can print small complex geometric products
with high accuracy with liquid photopolymers as the construction material. A trans­
parent vat is filled by the photopolymer lying above a projector, which applies a
high-power LED source. This projector is based on a MEMS using a DMD, which
contains individually moving micro-mirrors for controlling the path reflection of
the UV light. During the fabrication process, the build platform (on the x–y axis)
is dipped into the resin vat with one-layer thickness. Subsequently, one layer forms
based on the CAD model through the reflection of the UV light by the DMD to the
surface of the resin vat. After building a layer, the build platform is moved to the

z-axis (upward) by one-layer thickness. These steps are repeated to complete the
product.
  Compared to SLA, printed products with DLP possess good accuracy, afford­
able cost, perfect feature resolution (several micrometers), and smooth surfaces.
Furthermore, faster light switching and image projection decrease the manufacturing
time in the DLP process compared to SLA. Therefore, most of the industry’s attention
has been paid to this technique. The DLP process can produce zirconia and alumina
structural components with a full density of 97–99% and a Vickers hardness of 13.1
and 17.5 GPa, respectively. These results are comparable with the produced parts
using the traditional methods (Zhou et al., 2016). Alumina and bioactive glass with
complex structures and suitable characteristics are printed using DLP. In addition,
ceramic structures with unique properties and characteristics can be produced by
DLP, such as honeycomb catalyst supports, heat exchangers, and negative Poisson’s
ratio metamaterial Liu and Zhang (2020). The porous scaffolds of the ZrO 2 / HA
composite, with different HA additions, were printed using the DLP technology (Cao
et al., 2020). The compressive strengths of all the printed scaffolds were enhanced
up to 20 MPa. The results indicated that all scaffolds achieved compressive strengths
comparable to those of cancellous bone, highlighting their potential suitability for
applications in bone repair.
   Rauchenecker et al. (2022) successfully fabricated aluminum nitride components
via DLP and sintered them at 1700°C. The flexural strength of the additively manu­
factured specimens ranged from 320 to 498 MPa, depending on the orientation of the
samples relative to the build direction. Additionally, the sintered parts exhibited high
thermal conductivity, reaching 160 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹. In another study, Guo et al. (2019)
employed the DLP technique to produce titanium dioxide (TiO₂) ceramic lattice
structures for applications in bone tissue engineering, filtration, and thermal man­
agement. The fabricated specimens exhibited porosity levels between 50% and 80%.
By carefully controlling process parameters such as debinding and sintering, issues
related to resin volatilization – such as cracking and structural collapse – were effec­
tively mitigated. However, despite its advantages, the DLP process remains more
costly than fused deposition modeling in terms of operational expenses.

5.1.1.3  Continuous DLP
CDLP or CLIP technology is an innovation based on DLP technology. In particular,
being different from SLA and DLP technology, CDLP employs digital projection
with LEDs and an oxygen-permeable window instead of a normal glass window.
This oxygen-permeable window forms a so-called dead zone as thick as a human
hair, which allows the liquid resin to flow between the interface of the printed part
and the window. This uncured resin flow remarkably increases the resolution of
the printed part, as well as decreasing the risk of printing failure due to the peel­
ing force. Moreover, as opposed to the layer-by-layer method, CDLP machines are
designed with continuous movement of the build platform, thus allowing for unin­
terrupted prototype printing at speeds of several hundred millimeters per hour.

trast, Figure 5.9b illustrates the layer-by-layer movement of the build platform in the
case of DLP.

5.1.1.3.1  DLP versus CDLP
DLP and CDLP or CLIP are all resin-based 3D printing technologies that utilize
a projector to cure photosensitive resin, but they differ fundamentally in how the
curing process is controlled. DLP operates in a layer-by-layer fashion, where each
layer is individually projected and cured. After each layer is cured, the build platform
pauses and moves to allow the next layer to be formed, which can introduce mechani­
cal stress and slow the process. In contrast, CDLP/CLIP employs a continuous curing
approach using an oxygen-permeable window. This window creates a thin “dead
zone” where resin does not cure due to oxygen inhibition, allowing fresh resin to flow
under the part as it is continuously drawn upward, enabling a seamless, high-speed
printing process.
  The primary advantage of CDLP/CLIP is its significantly faster print speed and
superior surface finish, as the continuous process eliminates layer lines and reduces
peeling forces that often lead to print failures in DLP. It also enables better mechan­
ical properties by producing more isotropic parts. However, CDLP systems are
typically more expensive and less flexible in resin compatibility due to the special­
ized oxygen-permeable membrane. DLP printers, while slower and more prone to
mechanical stresses during layer separation, are more cost-effective, easier to main­
tain, and widely used for high-detail prototypes and small-scale production.

5.1.1.4  Two-Photon Photopolymerization
2PP or TPP is yet another lithography-based AM process characterized by its extreme
resolution and accuracy, making it ideal for the manufacture of microscopic struc­
tures. 2PP is a highly sophisticated and precise technique that enables the creation
of complex, high-resolution 3D ceramic structures. By utilizing the simultaneous
absorption of two photons and leveraging a femtosecond laser, it allows for polym­
erization to occur only at the focal point, resulting in extraordinary control over the
material. This makes it an ideal technique for applications in advanced ceramics,
particularly where fine details, complex geometries, and high-resolution features are
required. Two-photon polymerization is particularly beneficial in the following areas:

   •  Micro- and Nanostructured Ceramics: 2PP is widely used for creating
    MEMSs, biomedical implants, and other applications that require precise
      control over the structure at the micro or nanoscale.
   •  Complex Ceramic Parts: It is useful for creating intricate ceramic parts
     with complex internal channels, lattices, or other structures that are not eas­
       ily achievable using traditional manufacturing techniques.
   •  Porous Ceramic Structures : The ability to fabricate controlled porosity
     makes 2PP ideal for applications like bone scaffolds in tissue engineering,
     where a porous structure is necessary for biological growth and integration.

5.1.2   Material Jetting of Ceramics﻿

Material jetting (MJ) is a process that employs inkjet technology with thousands of
micro-sized nozzles (ranging from 20–75 μm) to print low-viscosity ceramic suspen­
sions, referred to as “inks,” to create 3D-printed objects, as illustrated in Figure 5.10.
In the context of ceramic AM, MJ is usually called direct inkjet printing (DIP). In
DIP, the jetted ink is either (i) a well-dispersed suspension of submicron ceramic
particles in water or an organic solvent, or (ii) a wax-based ink containing submicron
ceramic particles. DIP can be performed either by jetting a constant flow of ceramic
ink or by adopting a DOD approach. In continuous stream (CS), an uninterrupted
flow of individual droplets of electrically charged ink is generated, and unwanted
droplets are caught before hitting the substrate using deflecting electrodes. These

unprinted droplets are then redistributed to the ink reservoir to be reused. DOD, on
the other hand, is a non-continuous approach where individual droplets are generated
by the pressure pulses induced by the excitation of a piezoelectric or thermal actuator
at controlled frequencies. As a result, ink droplets are deposited only when and where
required. While the building rate of DOD is slower than that of CS, its wider range
of jettable materials, lower risk for ink contamination, higher resolution, and better
accuracy make it more suited to the fabrication of 3D objects. Besides, piezoelectric
actuators are suited to a larger variety of solvents than thermal actuators, the latter
being restricted to water-based inks only. In solvent DIP, the ink typically consists
of ceramic nanoparticles suspended in water or organic solvents, with a viscosity
suitable for inkjet nozzles (typically <30 mPa·s). In wax DIP, the ceramic powders
are suspended in a low-melting-point wax, which, after ejection from the printing
nozzles at a temperature above its melting point, solidifies onto the substrate upon
impact cooling. There is therefore no solvent drying cycle in wax DIP.
   Extensive studies have focused on producing ceramic parts using inkjet technol­
ogy with thermal DOD MJ, which is also accessible via piezoelectric technology for
manufacturing 3D structures. This method can generate high-performance ceram­
ics such as alumina, zirconia, and silicon-based ceramic materials. For example

Slurry-Based Deposition for Advanced Ceramics                         125

Willems et al. (2021) manufactured zirconia stabilized with 3 mol% yttria (3Y-TZP)
by the MJ technique and investigated the microstructure and mechanical behavior
of the sintered printed objects. The printed parts using a layer thickness of 10.5 μm
had a high green density of 58%, and approximately fully dense sintered ceramics
of 99.7%. Moreover, they reported the hardness and toughness of 12.5–12.8 GPa and
3.8–3.9 MPa m1/2, respectively, independent of the printing direction. Mummareddy
et al. (2021) produced material jetted zirconia with complex geometries with an aver­
age shrinkage of 17%. They assessed the sintering process and print orientations for
solid ceramic samples and lattice structures.
   However, MJ with ceramics poses challenges because the ink formulation must
meet conflicting requirements: it needs to be sufficiently low in viscosity to prevent
nozzle clogging yet have a high enough ceramic content to allow the green body to
be sintered to full density. MJ allows for the use of ultra-fine ceramic powders (of
size less than 100 nm) that are well-dispersed as inks, which facilitates full-density
sintering after post-processing. In this process, the printer software mixes the ther­
mo-polymer material cartridges and controls the inkjet nozzles along the x/y-axis.
The deposited droplets agglomerate to form the build material, which solidifies
when exposed to an external light source (UV lamp) or by cooling. The build plat­
form is then lowered along the z-axis by one-layer thickness, and the subsequent
layer is deposited on top of the previous one, continuing until the entire part is
completed.
  Among the current available AM techniques for fabricating ceramic components,
the conventional MJ method can generate parts with highly complex geometries,
high resolution, low thickness (less than 20 μm), dense green bodies, good surface
finish, homogeneous mechanical properties, and high dimensional accuracy. In this
method, increasing the surface inclination of the printing area results in reduced
surface roughness, a benefit not observed with other AM technologies (Kim and Oh,
2008). The combination of two materials together consisting of different colors can
be achieved by this technology. The MJ technique is inexpensive, time-effective, and
office-friendly, but manufactured parts have lower strength. Besides, MJ is greatly
restricted to mostly less than 25 vol% solid loading and low-viscosity ceramic inks,
often in the range of 20–40 mPa.s−1, which causes the limitation of the widespread
adoption of this method (Fayazfar et al., 2020). In contrast to other AM processes,
MJ has low productivity (~1 mm height per hour). Also, 3D printed parts by MJ may
exhibit “coffee stains” formed in the drying step, in which solid particles segregate
from the center to the edge of the printed patterns.
  The application of MJ to printing ceramic components was first described in
the literature by Blazdell and co-workers beginning in 1995 using ZrO2 and TiO2
ceramic inks, both of volume fractions as small as 5 vol.%. Such low-volume frac­
tions would lead to long drying times. However, their earlier attempts at ceramic
printing generated only simple multilayer structures, which also exhibited poor
surface quality. Another group then successfully printed small-sized pillar arrays
based on submicron ZrO2 particles loaded at 14 vol.% in the ink (Zhao et al., 2003).
Seerden et al. (2001) reported the use of ceramic ink prepared with an Al 2 O 3 , load­
ing of up to 40 vol%, resulting in the fabrication of ceramic parts with a feature size
of less than 100 μm.

  MJ of ceramics has been frequently used in tissue engineering applications.
Hydroxyapatite (HA) scaffolds have been printed using water-based solutions as
binder (Leukers et al., 2005). Tetracalcium phosphate, dicalcium phosphate, and tri­
calcium phosphate have also been fabricated using citric acid as a binder (Vorndran,
2008). MJ printed ceramics need to be sintered to enhance densification and mechan­
ical properties. Post-processing of MJ-ed ceramics is important to achieve handle­
ability and higher mechanical strength, especially in bone tissue engineering. Due
to the low mechanical properties of porous 3D printed ceramic scaffolds, the effect
of sintering, dopant addition, and polymer infiltration on final part properties is well
studied (Tarafder and Bose, 2014).
  With attention to the advantages presented by MJ, it is an appropriate technique
for tooling purposes and rapid prototype manufacturing. This process can overcome
challenges when a part is generated using nonconventional manufacturing methods
like waterjet cutting, Electro discharge machining (EDM), laser cutting, and casting.
Furthermore, the MJT process has several applications in electronics (production of
capacitors) (Liu et al., 2003), dental prostheses, medical industry (tissue engineering
applications) (Velasco et al., 2016).

5.1.2.1  Ceramic Inks for MJT
Ceramic MJ has still been little explored. Around the early 2010s, a research group
from RWTH Aachen University (Germany), led by Prof. Telle, investigated the
development of ceramic inks and their application in the MJ process (Özkol et al.,
2012). However, few articles have been recently published on the topic. Usually, very
thin ceramic (thickness smaller than 1 mm) bodies were fabricated, aiming to pro­
duce cathodes/electrolytes for solid oxide fuel cells or dielectric resonator antennas.
There is very little information about the properties of parts produced by ceramic
MJ. Willems et al. (2021) reported having obtained zirconia parts by MJ with a den­
sity of 99.7%, surface roughness ( Ra ) of about 7 μm, and flexural strength greater
than 1000 MPa.
   For this process, the feedstock is a suspension with well-dispersed ceramic par­
ticles in the liquid solvent, with suitable stability, viscosity, and surface tensions.
Unlike the pastes used in DIW technology, the MJ’s feedstock is ink-based, ejecting
a low-viscosity (~20 mPa.s) fluid with surface tension not exceeding 60 mN/m. To
avoid clogging and blockage, the diameter of the nozzles should be 100 times bigger
than the particle size (Kosmala et al., 2012). Consequently, nanoparticles are more
desirable in formulating inks, since the nozzle diameters usually range between 20
and 30 μm (Zhu et al., 2021). On the other hand, smaller particles are more likely
to agglomerate. In addition to deionized water, some additives such as dispersants
(triethanolamine, polyethylene glycol, polyacrylic acid, glycerol, and ethanol) are
added to the suspension to adjust the ink properties and performance (Qu et al.,
2021).

5.1.2.2  Advantages and Limitations of Solvent DIP
Solvent DIP is characterized by a high resolution, thanks to the deposition of drop­
lets with a volume of a few picoliters. Moreover, fully dense components with an
excellent surface finish can be obtained. Solvent DIP enables the fabrication of green

Slurry-Based Deposition for Advanced Ceramics                         127

parts containing very low amounts of organics, providing improved sintering behav­
ior and a lower linear shrinkage upon firing. Aqueous-DIP, in particular, is desirable
for a more environmentally friendly and less hazardous alternative to organic sol­
vent-based DIP.
  The unique advantage of DIP over all other AM technologies lies in the abil­
ity to deposit droplets of multiple materials simultaneously, enabling the fabrication
of Functionally graded materials (FGMs) and voxel-wise microstructure tailoring.
Gingter et al. (2015) manufactured 3Y-TZP/ Al 2 O 3 FGM cylinders with a diameter
of 10 mm; high-sintered, dense cylinders (97.5% theoretical density–TD) made of
800 individual layers with a 2 μm thickness were printed on a substrate at 80°C.
Furthermore, the suitability of DIP for manufacturing dense, fully ceramic parts
from both oxide and non-oxide ceramic materials has already been demonstrated.
DIP can, in principle, be used to shape any ceramic material, provided that a stable
suspension of submicron powders with the necessary physical properties for jetting
can be formulated. The fact that the use of submicron or nanoparticles is required for
the ceramic ink to be jettable results in a higher particle packing during deposition
and a higher furnace sintering activity, which are both highly beneficial to the final
density of printed products.
  One of the main disadvantages of the DIP process is its relatively slow building
rate, which is the trade-off for its high resolution. Actually, each pass of the printhead
depositing pico-liter droplets results in the formation of a very thin layer, leading to
a height increment rate of only about 2 mm/h at best. Besides, defects are easily gen­
erated in DIP because of the difficulty to ensure printing consistency and reliability.
Nozzle clogging is still a major issue when jetting ceramic suspensions, which can
easily cause missing features, uneven layer thicknesses, or deposition inaccuracies.

5.1.2.3   Nano-Particle Jetting of Ceramics
This technique is based on MJT and was developed by the company XJET. After
years of work and more than 80 patents in 2016, a new technology has been launched
as the nano-particle jetting and developed for AM of metals and ceramics. The pro­
cess effectively uses well-dispersed non-aqueous suspensions of ceramic nanopar­
ticles as build material for DIP. The technology has so far been demonstrated for
zirconia, with final densities reaching 99.9% TD, a hardness of 12.3 GPa, and a
roughness range of 12.5 > Ra > 1.6. It is claimed that complex geometries can be
fabricated by simultaneously jetting a second material to build sacrificial support
structures that can be dissolved in water. By jetting pico-liter size droplets and build­
ing layers as thin as 10 μm resolution and accuracy of 20–100 μm are achieved, so
that complex parts such as those in Figure 5.11 can be built almost free of the stair­
casing effect. However, the trade-off is a relatively slow build rate of only 1 to 1.5
mm in height per hour – lower than that of the DIP process – despite employing 24
printheads, each with 512 jetting nozzles. This highlights the significant hardware
complexity required to scale up the process.
  Two machine sizes are available, which work at a high speed, with very high
accuracy and surface quality. The first machines of XJET were the Carmel 1400,

jetting technology. They print liquid ink containing a suspension of nanoparticles

5.2  SLURRY-BASED PROCESSES USING PRECERAMIC FEEDSTOCK

Material preparation for preceramic AM involves mixing the preceramic polymer
with additives, such as coupling agents like photo- or thermal initiators or reinforce­
ment materials, to create a printable mixture of starting material. Once prepared,
the material is loaded into a 3D printer to build solid parts that are called green
parts. Here, the “green” means the solidified preceramic component after printing
and before pyrolysis. After printing, the green objects are post-cured to remove any
remaining uncured resin and ensure their structural stability and integrity. This is
usually conducted by exposing the object to light or heat, depending on the cou­
pling agents used. The next step is pyrolysis, where the green objects are heated to
a specific temperature under an inert or reactive atmosphere to convert them into
ceramic objects. Finally, the pyrolyzed objects may be subjected to post-processing
(e.g., polishing and coating) or other treatments, such as chemical vapor infiltration
and polymer infiltration and pyrolysis to improve the appearance and performance.
A typical AM process for manufacturing ceramic components using preceramics is
illustrated in Figure 5.13. Theoretically, all seven AM methods can be used to pro­
duce ceramic components. However, some of them, till now, have been adopted for
use with preceramic polymers.

5.2.1  VP-Based Processes Using Preceramic Feedstock﻿

A notable alternative to loading ceramic particles into photocurable resins is the
PDC method. In this approach, photocurable preceramic resins are formed through
VP and then pyrolyzed at temperatures of 1000–3000°C to derive ceramic parts
with final properties. Significant energy savings are realized by using these rela­
tively low post-processing temperatures, compared to traditional ceramic sintering
temperatures. In addition, this method enables the production of ceramic parts with
excellent surface finish. One major advantage is that carbides, borides, and nitrides
can all be derived from preceramic resins; these materials are challenging to cure
using traditional ceramic particle-loaded resins due to their large RI differences and
high absorbance values. A variety of ceramic materials can be produced by varying
the preceramic feedstock, including SiOC using siloxane-based polymers, SiOCN
by combining siloxanes with silazanes, and SiC by adding silane-based polymers
(Colombo et al., 2010).
  An initial study by Eckel et al. (2016) demonstrated the feasibility of producing
dense SiOC microlattices that outperform ceramic foams with respect to shear and
compressive strength. O’Masta et al. (2020) used the PDC method in combination

feedstock materials. (Han et al., 2023.)

with reinforcement particles (mullite, alumina, and silicon nitride) and whiskers
(SiC) to produce ceramic matrix composites with improved toughness. Adding SiC
whiskers to the SiOC matrix increased toughness by three. Guo et al. (2019) demon­
strated an additional benefit of the PDC method, wherein elastomeric material can
be printed, stretched/deformed, and then pyrolyzed into ceramic lattices with unique
geometries that may be difficult to print in a single orientation. The main draw­
back of the PDC approach is shrinkage-induced cracking and pore formation during
pyrolysis, which imposes limits on the maximum thickness of structures. Thus, this
method shows significant promise for lattice structures with strut diameters below
approximately 1 millimeter but will face challenges for structural applications that
require dense, bulk ceramic components. The PDC method is not limited to VP
processes and has been demonstrated for powder bed fusion, binder jetting, MJ, and
material extrusion.
  Compared to other AM techniques, VP has the advantage of manufacturing
ceramic components using preceramic material. As mentioned earlier, all AM meth­
ods follow three primary steps: creation of a digital 3D model, 3D printing, and
post-processing. Additional steps may be involved depending on the type of AM pro­
cess used. VP includes preparing photosensitive preceramic polymers, fabricating a
green component layer by layer using an appropriate process (i.e., SLA, DLP, CLIP,
or 2PP), and post-processing the green component with pyrolysis and other neces­
sary treatments. Material preparation involves mixing the preceramic polymer with
specific PIs and crosslinkers. PIs are compounds that can convert light energy into
chemical energy by forming free radicals or cations when exposed to light radiation.
These free radicals and cations will enable the molecular chains of preceramics to
crosslink by activating vinyl groups, resulting in hardened and solidified structures.
The addition of crosslinkers to preceramic polymers can react with the molecular
chains and promote the efficiency and degree of crosslinking during photopolymer­
ization (Hazan and Penner, 2017).
  The choice of PIs plays an essential role in VP, where selection depends on the
specific resin and printing conditions. Literature search results indicate that diphenyl
(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl) phosphine oxide (TPO), ethyl phenyl (2,4,6-trimethylben­
zoyl) phosphinate (TPO-L), and phenylbis (2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl) phosphine oxide
(BAPO) are commonly used as PIs for preceramic materials (Ou et al. 2023 and
Al-Ajrash et al., 2021), and Figure 5.14a illustrates their chemical structures. TPO,
TPO-L, and BAPO belong to the Norrish type I category, which can effectively gen­
erate free radicals through homolytic cleavage of their C–O or C–N bonds upon
exposure to light radiation. They can efficiently facilitate the polymerization of dif­
ferent monomers and preceramic polymers to form a network structure. Figure 5.14b
shows a typical photocuring process.
   In addition to the three main components (i.e., preceramic polymers, crosslinkers,
and PIs), other chemical additives are often incorporated into the photocurable resins
to enhance print quality. To obtain precise geometrical structures with intricate fea­
tures, free radical inhibitors and UV absorbers are typically added to absorb excess
light and prevent unintended curing during VP (Eckel et al., 2016). For instance,
organic dyes, such as Sudan III or Sudan Orange G, which function as UV absorb­
ers, were used to create highly complex SiOC ceramic components. To improve the

5.2.1.3  Two-Photon Polymerization
Compared to polymers commonly used for microdevices, ceramics exhibit superior
mechanical properties, chemical stability, and thermal resistance. Harnessing the
distinct capabilities of 2PP printing, ceramic 3D microstructural components have
been produced with preceramic materials. Park et al. (2009) developed a photo­
curable resin, including AHPCS and organometallic (η5-cyclopentadienylmethyl)-
trimethylplatinum (CpPtMe3), which is a multifunctional catalyst for fabricating 3D
ceramic structures with near-zero shrinkage using 2PP (Park et al., 2009).
   Researchers found that adding CpPtMe3 could initiate dual crosslinking (photo­
curing and thermal curing), resulting in dense SiC ceramic microstructures with
near-zero shrinkage after pyrolysis (Park et al., 2009).
   Although 2PP enables high-resolution and accurate 3D printing capabilities, the
process can be time-consuming, especially for large-scale components. To address
this challenge (Schmidt et al., 2019) proposed a hybridization approach combining
DLP and 2PP to facilitate the rapid fabrication of multiscale dense and crack-free
SiOC ceramic hybrid components using resins containing acrylate polysiloxanes.
DLP was used with this approach to print 3D structures with a millimeter size, and
2PP was utilized to create microstructures at a submicron size scale.
  Pham et al. (2006) reported the fabrication of complex SiCN ceramic micro­
structures with a 210 nm resolution via nano-SLA of a preceramic polymer. The
process is based on the two-photon absorbed crosslinking of a 2-isocyanatoethyl
methacrylate-functionalized polyvinylsilazane precursor and its subsequent pyroly­
sis at 600°C under a nitrogen atmosphere. However, a highly anisotropic shrinkage
was obtained, which is detrimental to the accuracy of the process (Lakhdar et al.,
2021).

5.2.2   MJ-IJP Using Preceramic Feedstock﻿

MJ or inkjet printing (IJP) is generally operated in either continuous or DOD mode,
where the latter offers a more accurate 3D fabrication process owing to its smaller
droplet size and thus higher dimensional accuracy. Because the ink must be ejected
from narrow nozzles, optimization of ink properties, such as viscosity, dispersion
homogeneity, and stability of the ink suspension, is critical for successful IJP. This
makes PCP the only suitable ceramic-based material for IJP, as it can be liquid with
tunable rheological properties. This AM technique enables the fabrication of ceram­
ics with small features (micron scale). A quantitative method to evaluate the print­
ability of an IJP ink was developed by Fromm in 1984, based on the surface tension
(), density (), and viscosity () of the ink along with the printer nozzle diameter
(a), and it is expressed as follows:

  While the IJP of PDCs has yet to be thoroughly explored in the literature, a
study evaluated the printability of an ink formulation by mixing a SiC precursor
with a dispersant, a ceramic powder filler, and different solvents (Table 5.7). It
was found that the PCS acted as a dispersing medium for silicon carbide powder
as well as a ceramic source; however, the addition of polyisobutene succinimide
as a dispersant further improved the ink suspension and printability. While prints
were successful with just the polycarbosilane in a solvent, cracking occurred after
pyrolysis and could be avoided with the addition of the silicon carbide powder.
A series of solvents, including n-heptane, n-octane, and n-decane, were tested to
increase the ceramic powder concentration, and octane was found to be the pre­
ferred choice. The use of decane resulted in impractical printing due to long drying
times between layers, and heptane evaporated too quickly, causing the nozzle to
clog. Overall, with the optimized ink, small features with low shrinkage were 3D
printed, such as pillars printed with 200 layers and a layer thickness of 3 μm (Mott
et al., 1999).
   Aerosol jet printing was also recently used, in combination with allyl-termi­
nated hyperbranched polycarbosilane (HBPCS) and reactive silane crosslinkers,
for generating 3D printed PDCs (Baldwin et al., 2018). Using a silane crosslinker
led to excessive hydrosilylation and oxidation, which in turn improved the ceramic
yield to 80% at 100°C. Initial hydrosilylation reactions crosslinked the polymer net­
work and incorporated reactive Si–H bonds into the structure. These new bonds are
susceptible to thermal oxidation, where high-temperature curing (280°C) induces
covalent bond reorganizations. This phenomenon increases thermal  stability,
diminishes volatility, and boosts ceramic yield. It was also shown that the resulting
amorphous SiOC ceramic can be further pyrolyzed at 1800°C to produce a fully
crystalline β-SiC.

5.3  REVIEW QUESTIONS

5.3.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. Differentiate between conventional and preceramic polymers of ­slurry-
     based deposition for advanced ceramics.
     Answer﻿: Based on the type of feedstock materials, ceramic powder with
     polymer (conventional) and preceramic polymers (with or without fillers)
      are the two most popular materials for AM processes. Here is a differentia­
      tion between each:
      1.  Conventional Approach﻿
            • AM with ceramic powder and polymer suspension (conventional)
             involves mixing ceramic powders with binder polymers for the 3D
              fabrication of solid objects.
            •  Once printed, objects usually undergo a sintering process to remove
             the polymer and fuse the ceramic powder to produce the solid
            ceramic objects.
      2.  Preceramic Approach﻿
            • AM with preceramic polymers involves feedstock materials that
             usually consist of organic compounds and possess excellent pro­
               cessability, allowing them to be easily shaped into desired geometric
             forms.
            •  After pyrolysis, AM-fabricated preceramic physical objects are con­
             verted into functional ceramic components.
            • AM is using preceramic feedstock materials demonstrated to be
              effective and  versatile  for  manufacturing  functional advanced
            ceramic materials with complex geometric structures.
            •  Preceramic polymers have different configurations/microstructures
           which affect the composition, microstructure, porosity, yield, and
              properties of the fabricated ceramics.
   2. What are the key factors influencing slurry preparation for SLA and
    DLP ceramic 3Dprinting?
     Answer﻿: Successful slurry preparation depends on factors like viscosity,
      solid loading, binder type, particle size distribution, and stability. The slurry
     needs to flow smoothly while maintaining enough thickness to build strong
      layers. A well-balanced mix with the right ceramic concentration and parti­
      cle sizes ensures good print quality and fewer defects. Stability is also key –
       settling or clumping can disrupt printing. Overall, carefully controlling
      these variables is essential for consistent, high-quality ceramic parts.
    3. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using SLA and DLP for
     ceramic 3D printing?﻿
     Answer﻿: SLA and DLP offer high resolution and precision, making them
      great for printing complex ceramic parts with fine details. They allow for
      designs that traditional methods can’t easily achieve. However, they also

138138           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

    come with challenges. The need for photopolymer binders limits material
      choices, and post-processing steps like debinding and sintering can cause
      shrinkage or cracking. So, while the print quality is excellent, careful han­
      dling is needed throughout the process.
﻿   4. How  do  binder  materials  affect  the  mechanical  properties  of
      sintered ceramic parts?﻿
     Answer﻿: Binders play a key role in both shaping the ceramic during printing
     and influencing the final strength after sintering. They must burn out cleanly
      during debinding – any residue can weaken the part or cause defects. A good
      binder supports strong, uniform parts, while a poor one can lead to cracks or
      structural flaws. Choosing the right binder is critical for achieving reliable
     mechanical performance in the finished ceramic component.
﻿   5. Specify the main challenges that may be faced by stereolithography of
     ceramic materials.﻿
     Answer﻿: Some of these challenges:
       •  Suspension Rheology: The rheology (flow behavior) of the suspension
        must be well-controlled to ensure smooth layer spreading and print­
         ing accuracy. Ceramic particles increase viscosity, making it harder to
         spread the material evenly and consistently, leading to print defects.
       •  Particulate-Induced Light Scattering: During curing, a laser or light
         source polymerizes the resin. Ceramic particles can scatter and absorb
            light, reducing their penetration and precision, which leads to blurring or
        unwanted curing, affecting resolution and feature accuracy.
       •  Low Cure Depth: Because of the light scattering and absorption, the
         depth to which the resin cures (polymerizes) is reduced, which limits
          layer thickness and increases print times, while also making it harder
          to fully bond layers, potentially compromising mechanical strength and
          part integrity.
﻿   6. Differentiate between digital light processing (DLP) and continuous
      digital light processing (CDLP).﻿
     Answer﻿: DLP and CDLP or CLIP are resin-based 3D printing technologies
      that utilize a projector to cure photosensitive resin, but they differ in how the
      curing process is controlled.

    DLP

       •  Operates in a layer-by-layer fashion, where each layer is individually
          projected and cured.
       •   After each layer is cured, the build platform pauses and moves to allow
          the next layer to be formed, which can introduce mechanical stress and
         slow the process.

    CDLP/CLIP

       •  Employs a continuous curing approach using an oxygen-permeable
        window. This window creates a thin “dead zone” where resin does not
         cure due to oxygen inhibition, allowing fresh resin to flow under the part

Slurry-Based Deposition for Advanced Ceramics                         139

          as it is continuously drawn upward, enabling a seamless, high-speed
          printing process.
       •   Offer faster print speed and superior surface finish, as the continuous
         process eliminates layer lines and reduces peeling forces that often lead
          to print failures in DLP.
       •  Enables better mechanical properties by producing more isotropic parts.
       •  CDLP systems are typically more expensive and less flexible in resin
          compatibility due to the specialized oxygen-permeable membrane.
       •  DLP printers are more cost-effective, easier to maintain, and widely used
          for high-detail prototypes and small-scale production.

﻿   7. The two-photon photopolymerization (2PP or TPP) is a slurry-based
     process using conventional suspension feedstock. Briefly describe the
      process, focusing on its specific characteristics and its promising fields
      of applications.﻿
     Answer﻿: By utilizing the simultaneous absorption of two photons and a
     femtosecond laser, it allows for polymerization to occur only at the focal
      point, resulting in extraordinary control over the material, which makes it an
      ideal technique for applications where fine details, complex geometries, and
      high-resolution features are required.

      Specific characteristics:

       •    It is a lithography-based AM characterized by its extreme resolution and
         accuracy for microscopic structures.
       •  Highly  sophisticated and  precise technique  that  enables complex,
          high-resolution 3D ceramic structures.

    2PP is particularly beneficial in the following areas:

       1.  Micro- and Nanostructured Ceramics: 2PP is widely used for creating
       MEMSs, biomedical implants, and other applications requiring precise
          control over the structure at the micro or nanoscale.
       2.  Complex Ceramic Parts: It is useful for creating intricate ceramic parts
         with complex internal channels and lattices that are not easily achievable
         using traditional manufacturing techniques.
       3.  Porous Ceramic Structures: The ability to fabricate controlled porosity
        makes 2PP ideal for bone scaffolds in tissue engineering, where a porous
          structure is necessary for biological growth and integration.

    8. Differentiate between solvent DIP and wax DIP as applied in material
      jetting (MJ) of ceramics.﻿
     Answer﻿: In solvent DIP, the ink consists of ceramic nanoparticles sus­
     pended in water or organic solvents, with a viscosity suitable for inkjet noz­
      zles (typically <30 mPa·s). In wax DIP, the ceramic powders are suspended
      in a low-melting-point wax, which, after ejection from the printing nozzles
       at a temperature above its melting point, solidifies onto the substrate upon
     impact cooling. There is therefore no solvent drying cycle in wax DIP.

﻿   9. What are the potential challenges associated with sintering ceramic
     parts made using slurry-based additive manufacturing?﻿
     Answer﻿: Sintering ceramic parts presents several challenges, including manag­
      ing shrinkage, avoiding cracks, and achieving uniform density. As parts shrink
      during sintering, tight control of temperature and time is needed to prevent
     warping or distortion. Additionally, removing any leftover binder without caus­
      ing internal stresses or cracks requires careful thermal management. If these
      steps aren’t precisely controlled, the final part’s quality and integrity can suffer.
  10. How does the green body (pre-sintered part) stability affect the final
     ceramic product in slurry-based AM?
     Answer﻿: The stability of the green body is critical for ensuring the printed
      part holds its shape before sintering. If it’s too fragile or unstable, it may
      crack, warp, or collapse during handling or early post-processing. Factors
      like slurry viscosity, ceramic loading, and binder choice all impact the green
     body’s strength. A stable green body sets the foundation for a successful
       final product with good mechanical properties and dimensional accuracy.
  11. What role do post-processing techniques like debinding and sintering
     play in the mechanical properties of slurry-based printed ceramics?﻿
     Answer﻿: Post-processing steps, especially debinding and sintering, directly
     impact the strength and quality of the final ceramic part. Debinding must
      carefully remove all binder materials without damaging the structure, while
      sintering densifies the ceramic and improves mechanical strength. Poor
      control during these steps can lead to defects like porosity, cracking, or
     low strength, so precise processing  is essential for achieving reliable,
     high-performance ceramics.
  12. How does layer thickness affect surface finish and mechanical proper­
       ties in slurry-based ceramic 3D printing?
     Answer: Layer thickness plays a big role in the final part’s quality. Thinner
      layers usually produce smoother surfaces and finer detail, but they increase
      print time due to the higher number of layers needed. Thicker layers can
     speed up printing but often result in rougher finishes and weaker mechanical
      properties because of reduced interlayer bonding. Balancing layer thickness
       is key to optimizing both efficiency and performance.
  13. How do UV absorbers like Sudan dyes impact the precision of ceramic
     parts made with the PDC-AM method?﻿
     Answer: UV absorbers such as Sudan III or Sudan Orange G help improve
      printing accuracy by filtering excess UV light during the curing process.
     This reduces unwanted polymerization beyond the intended area, which
     enhances resolution and allows for the creation of more detailed and com­
      plex ceramic structures. Their use is essential in pushing the limits of preci­
      sion in polymer-derived ceramic additive manufacturing.
