Deposition  6﻿﻿Powder-Based      for Advanced Ceramics ﻿



The powder-based  deposition technique  includes  binder  jetting  (BJ), powder
bed fusion (PBF), and directed energy deposition (DED) techniques, as shown in
Figure 6.1. In powder-based ceramic additive manufacturing (AM) technologies,
a powder bed including loose ceramic particles as feedstock material is processed
in each layer. These ceramic particles are bonded together using a spread of liquid
binders or powder fusion through thermal energy provided by a laser beam. In this
chapter, different types of powder-based AM techniques are described.

6.1  POWDER-BASED PROCESSES USING
    CONVENTIONAL POWDER FEEDSTOCK

In ceramic processing, three main powder bed-based technologies are typically
applied: binder jetting technology (BJT), selective laser sintering (SLS), and L-PBF.
Depending on the particle size, the powder layer can be 20–200 μm. The fusion pro­
cess or binding mechanism mainly includes four types: solid-state sintering, chemi­
cally induced binding, liquid-phase sintering (partial melting), and full-state melting
(Kruth et al, 2005).

6.1.1   Binder Jetting/3DP Technology (BJT)
The original BJ process was invented by Emanuel Sachs et  al., US5204055;
1993 from the MIT in the late 80 s, with a patent filed in 1989. The technology –
­originally termed three-dimensional printing (3DP), a name now commonly used
to describe all AM processes – has been licensed to several companies. The BJ
process manufactures 3D structures by selectively depositing droplets of a liquid
binding agent onto a powder bed of coarse ceramic powder. As the binder pene­
trates into the powder bed by capillarity, ceramic particles are joined to form a
pattern as defined by the STL file. This process is repeated layer after layer until
a printed ceramic green body is obtained. After its removal from the unprinted
powder bed, the green part is subjected to debinding and sintering schedules, which
are potentially preceded by a binder activation heat treatment and/or followed by
additional densification steps.
  BJT is a multi-step, 3D-printing process, defined by ISO/ASTM 52,900:2015
as an “AM process in which a liquid bonding agent is selectively deposited to join
powder materials” ASTM−2012. The process consists of spreading thin layers
of powder, with the printhead selectively ejecting and depositing binder droplets on
the powder bed layer by layer to produce the object. Figure 6.2 illustrates the major

  BJT produces 3D structures by selectively depositing droplets of a liquid binder
onto a bed of coarse ceramic powder. The binder infiltrates the powder via capil­
lary action, joining particles to form a layer according to the STL-defined pattern.
This layer-by-layer process continues until a ceramic green body is fully built. Once
removed from the unbound powder, the green part undergoes debinding and sinter­
ing, often preceded by a binder activation heat treatment and/or an additional densi­
fication step.
   Understanding the powder properties (Figure 6.3) is critical for producing parts
of acceptable quality. Consequently, powder characterization techniques such as
scanning electron microscopy (SEM), laser light diffraction, X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy, and differential thermal analysis have been used to study the effect
of powder characteristics on part properties, both qualitatively and quantitatively
(Sutton Austin et al., 2016). Particle size distribution, morphology, and flowability
primarily influence the printing process as they dictate the packing density of the
powder beds and subsequently the quality of sintered parts (Chen et al., 2022).
   Figure 6.4 shows the steps of ceramic BJ. The feedstock powder should meet high
flowability and sinterability for making high-quality parts. The printed green part is
then cured by heating to around 200°C, such that the binder is thermally activated

Afterward, debinding and sintering are applied to the cured parts to improve their
material properties. In the debinding step, the binder is thermally decomposed or
burned out by heat treatment between 400°C and 800°C, producing a brown part.
The heating rate is controlled to ensure the escape of gaseous reaction products. In
the sintering step, the part is heated to a high temperature just below the melting point
of the ceramic material, followed by dwelling and furnace cooling. The sintering step
increases the density of the part by mass transport across the boundaries of ceramic
particles (Kang, 2005). Isostatic pressing and infiltration can further increase the
density and mechanical properties. Compared to PBF, BJT does not employ heat
during the build process, preventing residual stresses in the parts.
  BJT permits the creation of intricate ceramic geometries and customized shapes
that would be hard or impossible to achieve using conventional ceramic manufac­
turing techniques. It is extensively used to produce ceramic components in vari­
ous applications such as structural, biomedical, optical, and electronics. Alumina
was the first advanced ceramic investigated by the inventors of BJ. For instance,
Mariani et al. (2021) produced -Al 2 O 3 components using BJT. They reported that
the fabricated objects possess a high green relative density of 61.2% and the highest
final sintered density of 75.4% after the thermal treatment at 1750°C. Despite the
relatively large residual internal porosity (~40%), materials presented good flexural
strength and Vickers hardness of 56.1 MPa and 1.95 GPa, respectively. Kunchala et
al. (2018) assessed the effect of adding nano-particle densifiers on printing manu­
facturability, density, porosity, and compressive strength of BJT-prepared ceramics.
They found that, by increasing the amount of densifier up to 15 wt.%, the samples’

6.1.1.1  Powder-Based Binder Jetting
In powder-based binder jetting (P-BJ), a coarse ceramic powder is used as feedstock
and is typically spread into thin layers by a roller. This technology has thus been
extensively used to additively manufacture porous ceramic components, especially
for biomedical applications such as scaffolds for tissue engineering. However, P-BJ
does not enable the manufacture of monolithic ceramic parts since coarse powders
result in a highly porous powder compact upon spreading, and it usually yields final
relative densities of between 20% and 70%, although higher densities have been
achieved using high binder saturations, warm isostatic pressing (WIP), uniaxial and
cold isostatic pressing, or infiltration. WIP was applied to 3D printed Al 2 O 3 and
MgO-doped Al 2 O 3 . While as-printed Al 2 O 3 green parts had a low density of 36%,
a high fired density of 97.8% was obtained after WIP, with a 4PB flexural strength
(ASTM C1961–90) of 231.5 MPa. Doping Al 2 O 3 with MgO resulted in even better
properties: despite a lower green density of 34%, a fired density as high as 99.2%
was obtained, as well as a 40% higher 4PB flexural strength of 324 MPa. Figure 6.9
shows a 3D printing BJ with ceramic.
   P-BJ was the first fast and cost-effective fabrication of highly porous ceramic
components from coarse powders. It started manufacturing porous molds for invest­
ment casting and biomedical scaffolds for tissue engineering. The P-BJ process is
characterized by its inability to produce dense struts and homogeneous parts, yield­
ing high levels of residual porosity, which tends to be beneficial for applications of
highly detrimental to mechanical properties.
   Generally, any raw ceramic material, such as aluminum oxide, zirconium oxide,
and silicon carbide, can be processed with BJ. Decisive factors are the particle size
distribution, the particle shape, the density, and the specific surface of the powders
used. On the one hand, these material properties indicate the flowability and com­
patibility of the powders. Fine powders with a high specific surface area are cru­
cial to ensure sufficient reactivity during the sintering process (https://wzr.cc/en/
binder-jetting-2/).
   In P-BJ, a coarse ceramic powder has been explored primarily for coarse powder
particle sizes (i.e., 25–150 µm in diameter) as feedstock and is typically spread into
thin layers by a roller. However, it is now feasible to process fine powder materials
having an average particle size of ~10 µm. This technology has been extensively used

sintering shrinkage was found to be highly anisotropic, with values of 8.75% in
the X-direction, 10.92% in the Y-direction, and 15.37% in the Z-direction. While
the sintering profile had a relatively minor effect on final density, it significantly
influenced the mechanical properties. Increasing the sintering time from 2 to
16 hours nearly doubled the maximum compressive strength (ASTM C773–88),
from 77.86 to 146.60 MPa. Similarly, Young’s modulus increased by 70%, from
31.25 to 54.14 GPa, and Vickers hardness exhibited a six-fold rise, from 240 MPa
to 1.51 GPa.

6.1.1.2   Slurry-Based Binder Jetting
Slurry-based binder jetting (S-BJ) was developed to enhance the BJ process by intro­
ducing colloidal ceramic processing into the technology. The powder bed is formed
by making layers of ceramic slurries instead of dry powders, thus enabling the use of
submicron powders to improve the powder bed packing density, therefore increasing
the green and sintered densities. The S-BJ three-dimensional printing (also called
S-3DP) process was developed by the same group that invented the BJ process at the
MIT in the late 90s.

6.1.1.2.1   Colloidal Ceramic Processing
It’s based on colloidal science, which deals with particles typically in the range of 1
nm to a few micrometers dispersed in a continuous medium. When integrated into
S-BJ, colloidal ceramic processing helps overcome limitations of P-BJ (e.g., poor
packing, low green strength), resulting in higher-quality ceramic parts.

6.1.1.2.2   Benefits of Colloidal Ceramic Processing Include
   •  Improve particle packing and green density
   •  Reduce porosity and anisotropic shrinkage
   •  Enhance final mechanical properties of printed parts
   •  Minimize the need for post-processing corrections

In S-BJ, a slurry layer is deposited by a doctor blade. The slurry is then dried, and the
binder is applied onto the dried powder bed. This technology is denoted as layer-wise
slurry deposition (LSD), where a liquid suspension of ceramic particles is spread as
a thin layer comparable to tape casting, while within this layer a cast is formed com­
parable to slip casting, Figure 6.10.
  The process results in powder compacts with densities exceeding 60% theoreti­
cal densities (TDs). The formation of a cast starts as soon as the slurry is in contact

For commercial silicate ceramic slurries, a speed of the doctor blade of 50 mm/s is
typically chosen. For technical ceramics, the speed of the doctor blade is increased
to 100 mm/s or higher. After the deposition of all layers required for building up the
desired geometry, the printed body is embedded in the powder bed, which is a block
of densely packed particles. For the release of the part, the powder compact must
be dissolved by a solvent. S-BJ has the potential to produce powder compacts with
high powder packing densities, typically exceeding 55% TD and with low content of
organic additives, typically below 5 wt.% (https://euroceram.org/en/eu/slurry-based).
  Ceramic slurries containing approximately 50 vol% Al 2 O 3 powders and small
amounts of sodium alginate were selectively gelled upon contact with droplets of
a saline solution. This approach enabled the fabrication of high-density alumina
components with fine-grained microstructures and flexural strengths exceeding 400
MPa. More recently, a research team at the BAM Federal Institute for Materials
Research and Testing in Germany developed its own version of the process under
the name LSD print (Zocca et al., 2017). This method has been employed to pro­
duce fully dense alumina and Si–SiC parts with mechanical properties comparable
to those of conventionally manufactured ceramics.
   In this process, an aqueous slurry of fine Al 2 O 3 powders containing 0.3 wt%
alginic acid sodium salt is spread into 50 μm-thick layers using a doctor blade. Each
layer is subsequently dried and crosslinked by the selective jetting of a binder solu­
tion composed of copper sulfate pentahydrate dissolved in ethylene glycol. The Cu2
ions in the binder induce gelation of the sodium alginate. In addition to promoting
gelation, the alginate enhances the slurry’s rheological behavior for layer deposition
and acts as a binder within the green layers, effectively preventing crack formation

6.1.1.3   P-BJ versus S-BJ
The downsides of P-BJ applied to advanced ceramics mostly stem from the require­
ment to use powders with an average particle size well above 10 μm to enable layer
spreading during the recoating step, which limits the resolution of the process, results
in high surface roughness, and leads to high porosity and poor sintering densifica­
tion. Therefore, the best applications for this technology used with ceramics remain
the production of non-structural porous components such as scaffolds for tissue engi­
neering and investment casting cores and molds. Nevertheless, post-processing den­
sification steps, such as CIP, WIP, and infiltration, can be used to increase density
and mechanical properties, although these additional steps result in increased labor,
manufacturing time, and overall costs.
   Finally, the main issues of P-BJ may be overcome by taking a  colloidal
slurry-based approach, which has been shown to enable the production of near-fully
dense parts without the need for pressure-assisted post-processing thanks to the
use of submicron powders. The resolution of the process and surface roughness of
as-printed parts are also greatly improved for the same reason. However, S-BJ results
in longer manufacturing time due to the need to dry out the powder bed before jet­
ting the binder for each recoated layer. Moreover, careful consideration must also be
given to the chemical and physical properties of ceramic slurries to ensure they have
the correct viscosity for layer spreading, to prevent drying cracks, and ensure that
parts can be successfully removed from the unbound powder bed.

6.1.2.1   Direct Powder-Based Selective Laser Sintering
It is complicated owing to the poor thermal shock resistance of ceramic materials.
Furthermore, the sintered parts have a low density and poor mechanical properties.
Slocombe and Li (2001) produced complex-shaped TiC – Al 2 O 3 ceramics via the
direct SLS combined with self-propagating high-temperature synthesis to overcome
the defect of a low density of direct sintered samples. Nevertheless, it is difficult to
avoid easy cracking in the direct SLS-manufactured parts because of the thermal
stresses during the sintering process that cause poor mechanical features in the final
products (Chen et al., 2018).
   In the SLS, shown in Figure 6.13, a laser source sinters/melts the top layer of pow­
der in a powder bed in a predetermined pattern. The powder bed is lowered in height,
and a fresh layer of powder is positioned on top via a leveling roller. The process is
then repeated. Direct SLS does not include a sacrificial binder phase, and the ceramic
parts are made by direct sintering or melting. Generally, direct SLS processes use
metal powders directly without any binder, while indirect SLS uses a polymer binder
to produce a green part. Figure 6.14 shows a part made by the SLS method.
   Powder-based direct selective laser sintering (P-dSLS) is a type of 3D printing
where a laser scans over a bed of ceramic powder, fusing it layer by layer to create
a ceramic part in one step. Unlike other methods that use a binder to hold the mate­
rial together, this process uses the laser to directly melt and fuse the ceramic pow­
der. In some cases, the laser can also cause a chemical reaction in a different type
of material, turning it into a ceramic during the process. Ideally, there is no need
for post-thermal treatment or additional densification steps after P-dSLS. However,
the high melting point, poor thermal shock resistance, and low ductility make the
P-dSLS of ceramics significantly more challenging than metals. Indeed, the very
short laser-powder interaction time during the P-dSLS process, combined with the
extreme temperature gradients, tends to result in poor ceramic sintering, incomplete
densification, and high thermal residual stress, causing crack formation. P-dSLS has
been applied to technical ceramics including Al 2 O 3, SiO2, reaction-bonded silicon
carbide (RBSiC), Al 2 O 3 -SiO 2, and Al 2 O 3 -ZrO 2 mixtures.

thermal debinding and furnace sintering steps. On the other hand, one of the process
limitations is caused by the thermal stresses occurring during P-dSLS of ceramic
materials, resulting in cracking and porosity. As a result, no large monolithic ceramic
parts can be produced. There are some limitations regarding material selection since
some high-performance oxide and non-oxide ceramics may remain challenging to
shape by P-dSLS due to their high melting point, poor resistance to thermal gradi­

6.1.2.3  Laser-Powder Bed Fusion
Over the past years, applying the laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) process to pro­
duce complex shape ceramic components attracted lots of attention. This technique is
similar to the SLS in using high-energy laser sources. However, L-PBF is a time-sav­
ing process that manufactures the parts by fully melting the powders, using higher
energy density of laser sources, and needs no binder or post-sintering process for
further consolidation. The L-PBF process is considered the only 3D printing process
to manufacture ready-to-use complex ceramic parts with higher purity, nearly full
density, and high strength in a single step and less time. This can be explained by
fully melting the powder into the liquid phase, ensuring fast densification instead
of heating the powder at a particular point where the particles are partially melted
and fused in the SLS process. Hence, products with lower porosity, superior control
over the crystal structure, and excellent final characteristics can be produced via the
L-PBF process (Chen et al., 2019).
   Nevertheless, the final properties of a ceramic part produced via the L-PBF pro­
cess depend on several factors, such as feedstock properties, orientation and position
of fabrication, and manufacturing parameters. Besides, the physical and chemical
properties of the interaction between the material and the source of energy and
post-processing of the printed part play a significant role in determining the final
features. One of the noticeable parameters is the layer thickness, which controls the

168168           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

production time and the part’s surface quality. A smaller layer thickness leads to less
surface roughness, even though it increases the build time. In contrast, a larger layer
thickness may cause a significant stair-step effect on the component’s surface (Chen
et al., 2019).
   Despite showing great potential, the L-PBF of ceramics is complicated compared
to metallic materials owing to some inherent problems related to the process; hence,
their applications are still very limited. This limitation can be attributed to the for­
mation of defects like porosity, rough surface finishes, low dimensional accuracy,
and densification of the final product. These defects lead to the hard achievement
of the isotropic ceramic body. In the L-PBF process, laser processing parameters
are crucial factors influencing the quality of fabricated parts. The balling effect can
happen when exposed to insufficient energy input, while excessive energy would
result in powder spattering. Nonetheless, direct melting consists of a high-tempera­
ture interaction between laser and powder during a short period, leading to large gra­
dients of temperature within small volumes of material and thermal stress, termed
as the drastic heating and cooling rates upon each laser scan. Since ceramics have
limited thermal shock resistance; thus, cracks and distortions form in the sintered
parts because of thermal stress.
   For instance, Shishkovsky et al. (2007) processed the ZrO2  parts using the
L-PBF process and found cracks and large open pores in the final parts. In another
work (Mercelis and Kruth, 2006) experimentally studied the origin of the residual
stresses in the L-PBF manufactured products. They developed a simple theoretical
model to predict the existence of residual stress. They also found that the scanning
strategy has a noticeable influence on the level of residual stresses. It is well doc­
umented that a powder bed preheating with precise control of powder morphology
can result in nearly fully dense parts. The pore size was reduced with the increase
in layer thickness. Moreover, most of the closed pores were mainly formed near the
external surfaces. Besides, the total porosity percentage of the glass–ceramic sam­
ples declined with increasing layer thickness, Gan and Wong (2017). These results
presented negative correlations between layer thickness, pore sizes, and porosity
content. In terms of mechanical characteristics, it is reported that the strength of
the as-printed samples was initially reduced by increasing layer thickness (Gan and
Wong, 2017).
   Recently, Shen et al. (2022) fabricated Al 2 O 3 / GdAlO 3 binary eutectic ceramics
at different scanning rates (4 – 60 mm/min) at a laser power of 200 W. It was revealed
that the hardness gradually increased by increasing the scanning rate, whereas the
fracture toughness first enhanced and then slowly declined (Figure 6.17).
   Further developments introduced some modified 3D printing methods derived
from the L-PBF process with the ability to manufacture complex shape ceramic parts,
such as slurry-based L-PBF (Gahler et al., 2006). Other forms of powder packing
have been developed instead of dry powder deposition to raise the sintered density
and prevent crack formation in the L-PBF ceramics. The slurry form offers the bene­
fits of a more homogeneous and highly packed nature. Gahler et al. (2006) used sta­
ble slurries loaded with an alumina-silica powder mixture (up to 63 vol%) and water
with high fluidity. Before drying, the materials are deposited layer by layer through

using a laser beam. The bond is an organic additive that, when irradiated by the laser
beam, melts, bonds powder particles, and creates a green body.
   Laser fuses the first layer or first cross-section of the model. A new layer of pow­
der is spread across the previous layer using a roller. Further layers or cross-sections
are fused and added. The process repeats until the entire model is created. Parts
produced through ceramic PBF often require post-processing. The initial surface
finish may not meet industry standards, necessitating additional steps to enhance
quality. Techniques like machining or polishing improve the surface but increase
production time and costs. L-PBF 3D printing technology enables the manufacturing
of a vast array of geometrically complex products using a heat source, mainly laser
beams, to fuse powder particles layer by layer, forming a solid part. L-PBF of oxide
ceramics is highly desirable for aerospace, biomedical and high-tech industries. One
promising application of the mature PBF process is the cost-effective manufactur­
ing of green bodies, which must be densified by conventional debinding and sinter­
ing. To achieve this, special powdery starting materials consisting of a composite

170170           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

of ceramic and polymer are being developed. During printing, powder layers with
typical thicknesses between 20 and 200 μm are successively applied by the squeegee
unit (recoater). In the process, energy is applied locally to a powder bed using a laser
beam. At this point, the material heats up (partly) melting or softening the polymer
binder to stick the powder particles together.
   Typical parameters for the laser sintering process are the laser power, laser type
(wavelength), hatch distance, laser focus/spot, line strategy, preheating of the powder
bed, layer thickness, and powder properties, such as the flow properties and melting/
sintering temperature (Vock Silvia et al., 2019). Typical laser systems installed in
polymer PBF printers are CO2  lasers with a wavelength of 1060 nm and power
from 15 W up to 240 W. As an alternative to CO2  lasers, fiber lasers with wave­
lengths of about 1.06 nm or near-IR range or lasers with wavelengths from 808 nm
to 976 nm and laser power from 5 to 30 W are used. Complex structures can be
produced cost-effectively and without the need for support structures, as the powder
bed fulfills this task, with high productivity by using relatively low-cost plant tech­
nology from the polymer PBF-LB sector. By modifying the technology from clas­
sic PBF-LB to μ-PBF-LB, a broad range of component sizes and resolutions can be
achieved (Berger Christian et al., 2024). Among others, the technique offers superior
productivity, which might be the central argument in the future for evaluating the
applicability of PBF-LB for industrial manufacturing. A novel approach to ceramic
PBF-LB is presented by Berger et al. (2024), using a thermoset binder for incorpo­
rating ceramic particles in the starting material that, due to the non-meltable nature
of the binder, improves the dimensional stability of the green parts during thermal
debinding and sintering. The production of large, complex structures opens up a wide
range of applications.
  One promising application for porous structures made of photocatalytic titanium
oxide is in the water treatment sector. Such printed, debinded and sintered filter mod­
ules enable the degradation of organic residues in water, thus contributing to safer
and higher water quality. Furthermore, high-resolution printing can be realized via

6.1.3   Directed Energy Deposition﻿

DED has the striking advantage over most other ceramic AM processes of being
a single-step AM process, meaning that the final geometry of the part and its final
physicochemical properties are defined directly during the AM process, removing
the need for post-processing heat treatment. Directed energy deposition technology
uses a high-energy-density heat source to melt high-purity ceramic raw materials
conveyed synchronously without a binder. The densification of microstructure and
direct forming of net-shaped structures are completed by melt growth and local
deposition. DED is typically used to work on metal parts; this process can also be
used with polymers and ceramics. Almost any weldable metal can be additively man­
ufactured using DED, including aluminum, inconel, niobium, stainless steel, tanta­
lum, titanium and titanium alloys, and tungsten. Extreme temperature gradients with
DED result in thermal cracking. Some advanced ceramics, particularly non-oxide
ceramics with high melting temperatures, may not be processable using the current
technology. Figure 6.19 summarizes the different DED categories.
  DED systems include powder-feed and wire-feed-based DED (depending on the
feedstock type), melt-based DED, and kinetic energy-based DED (depending on the
energy source). Melt-based DED could be further subclassified as laser-based DED,
electron-beam-based DED, plasma-based DED, and electric arc-based DED. The
powder-based DED system uses a laser beam as the heat source. Figure 6.20 shows
the coaxial and off-axial powder feeding methodologies of LAM-DED processes.
Wire-based DED processes provide a lower resolution than laser-beam powder-based
processes but have a higher deposition rate and the ability to build larger structures.
The DED process can be controlled through laser power, spot size, scan speed, and
powder feed rate. Figure 6.21 shows how a combination of ceramic and/or metal

   Laser-based DED process, also known as laser cladding, laser energy net shaping
(LENS), or laser metal deposition, was first commercialized in the mid-1990s. In
this technique, feedstock materials are directly delivered in a molten pool generated
by a heat source like an electron beam, laser, or plasma arc. In the DED process,
ceramic materials with a melting point up to 3000°C can be melted using a high-
power laser beam. During the deposition, the already deposited layers were exposed
to repeated thermal cycles and very high cooling rates. This thermal history in the
as-built parts depends strongly on the process parameters and Saboori and et al.,

and mechanical characteristics of as-deposited materials (Saboori et al., 2019 and
Moheimani et al., 2022). These parameters are classified into three main categories:
system (specifications) dependent, feedstock (powder, in this example) dependent,
and process (deposition) variables dependent (Svetlizky et al., 2021).
  So far, several efforts have been undertaken on the fabrication of different materi­
als using the DED method, such as steels, titanium alloys, cobalt alloys, nickel alloys,
aluminum alloys, high-entropy alloys, shape memory alloys, composites, and func­
tionally graded materials (Nedjad et al., 2022). Besides, this technique has also been
employed to build ceramic oxide parts such as alumina, zirconia, eutectic ceramic
composites, zirconia–alumina ceramics, alumina/aluminum titanate ceramics, mul­
lite ceramics, and magnesium aluminate spinel ceramics (Frazier, 2014).
   Recently, four different Al2O3–ZrO2 functionally graded ceramic (FGC) samples
were manufactured through the DED method (Wu et al., 2022). It was found that the
bonding strength was noticeably improved, and the interface fracture of FGC sam­
ples was altered to a transgranular fracture. Moreover, the samples’ microhardness
and flexural strength reached 25 GPa and a maximum of 160.19 MPa, respectively.
Highly dense (≥98%) Al 2 O 3 -YAG-ZrO 2 (AYZ) samples were successfully fabri­
cated by Fan et al. (2019) using the LENS technique. The LENSed AYZ specimens
presented refined eutectic microstructures and almost isotropic features. Figure 6.22

   Since larger powder particle sizes are used in the DED process, it offers both cost and
safety advantages compared to PBF. Despite these benefits, it has a lower-dimensional
resolution, lower powder efficiency/recyclability, and larger surface waviness (princi­
pally when printing a mixture of powders) concerning the PBF (Svetlizky et al., 2021).
   However, fast cooling rates and high thermal gradients (thermal conditions) in
the DED process can cause some defects such as complex phase transformations and
microstructural changes, non-uniform residual stresses, distortions, porosity, and
cracking, which finally result in fair corrosion resistance and mechanical behavior
degradation, and premature failure. Besides, it often needs post-fabrication machin­
ing to achieve an appropriate surface quality (Svetlizky et al., 2021).
  DED has the following advantages and limitations:

A.   Advantages

    1. DED is a single-step process; therefore, a post-processing sintering furnace
       is not required.

Powder-Based Deposition for Advanced Ceramics                        175

    2. Fast deposition rates and minimal material pre-processing make it the quick­
       est AM method for producing sintered ceramic parts.
    3. By using several nozzles, the process enables depositing multiple materials,
      allowing for the direct fabrication of ceramic–ceramic and metal–ceramic
      composites.
    4. The material composition can be adjusted by varying the powder feed rate,
      thus enabling fine control over both material and composition grading.

B.   Limitations

    1. High thermal gradients and fast cooling rates invariably result in thermal
      stresses with delamination and cracking. Therefore, the laser power, beam
      spot size, scan spacing, and scan speed must be perfectly controlled and
      optimized.
    2. The process parameter optimization is material-dependent and must be car­
      ried out every time the composition or morphology of the ceramic powder/
     wire feedstock is modified.
    3. Limited geometrical complexity, limited resolution, poor control over the
     shape of manufactured parts, and low dimensional and geometrical accu­
      racy, which require post-machining to achieve net shapes.
    4. Support structures cannot be generated, so five-axis capability is required to
     manufacture complex geometries and overhangs.
    5. DED enables the fabrication of fully closed empty cavities; however, a small
     amount of ceramic particles would always remain trapped in any closed cav­
       ity because not all of the feedstock powder is caught under the laser beam.
    6. There are limitations regarding material selection, and high-melting-point
     non-oxide ceramics, in particular, could prove challenging.

6.2  POWDER-BASED PROCESSES USING
    PRECERAMIC FEEDSTOCK

Polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs) represent a relatively new class of materials within
AM. PDCs enable the development of ceramic parts patterned via low-cost poly­
mer 3D printing methods, followed by pyrolysis in a high-temperature process in
which the polymer itself forms a ceramic, often in the absence of any ceramic filler.
PDCs have served as a feedstock for various 3D printing techniques, and a wide
range of physicochemical factors can be tailored to optimize ceramic manufacturing
processes. Also, powder-based processes are not an exception to using Preceramic
Feedstock to produce components through AM.

6.2.1   BJ or 3DP Technology﻿

BJ is an AM process that uses a liquid bonding agent that is selectively deposited
to bind powder material together and form a solid part layer by layer. This process
requires two materials: a powder-based material and a liquid binder material. A typi­
cal BJ process begins with creating a powder bed using a recoater. The powder bed is

then selectively bonded with a binder adhesive deposited through an inkjet printhead,
forming solid 3D components layer by layer, as shown in Figure 6.23.
  The BJ process can fabricate ceramic components using ceramic or preceramic
powders. In one study, Zocca et al. prepared preceramic feedstocks using a com­
mercially available PMS polymer powder for manufacturing solid parts with the BJ
process (Zocca et al., 2013). To cure the PMS powder, two crosslinking catalysts
(zirconium acetylacetonate (ZrAcAc) and tin-octoate (TinOc)) were employed in sep­
arate experiments. In one approach, the feedstock powder (~45–90 μm in diameter)
was made from a mixed solution, including PMS polymer powder, isopropanol, and
ZrAcAc. The feedstock powder was then selectively bonded by depositing isopro­
panol from the inkjet printhead and forming the solid green structures. In the other
approach, a binder solution was prepared with TinOc and a mixture of 1-hexanol and
hexylacetate. The prepared solution was then deposited on the PMS powder bed to
form a 3D green structure. The fabricated green structures were further crosslinked
and then pyrolyzed to obtain porous ceramic components.

6.2.2  Powder Bed Fusion﻿
Selective Laser Sintering: Using the SLS technique, a laser beam facilitates the
fusion or sintering of powdered materials together to build 3D structures. First, a
thin layer of powder is deposited on the build platform. A high-powered laser beam is
exposed on the powder bed, accurately tracing the desired object shape. Consequently,
particles stick together because of the material’s partial melting and selective fusion
in defined areas. After sintering each layer, the platform is lowered to prepare a
new layer of powder for sintering. Once the sintered 3D structure has undergone
cooling, it is taken out for subsequent processing, for example, removing the excess
powder and finishing the surface, followed by heat treatment, depending on the mate­
rial and desired specifications. The research from Friedel et al. in 2005 is the only
reported study on using SLS specifically for curing PCPs (Friedel et al., 2005). They
referred to this process as selective laser curing (SLC). Poly(methylsilsesquioxane)
(MK) mixed with a SiC passive filler was SLS printed and cured using a CO2 laser
beam at 400°C. MK was cured due to a condensation reaction between hydroxyl and
ethoxyl groups, transforming the resin from a thermoplastic resin into a thermosetting

6.3  REVIEW QUESTIONS

6.3.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. How does powder-based binder jetting (P-BJ) differ from slurry-based
     binder jetting (S-BJ) in terms of material properties and processing
     techniques?﻿
     Answer: P-BJ uses a dry powder – often metal or ceramic – that’s spread in
      layers. A liquid binder is then jetted to hold the powder particles together.
      After printing, the part is fragile and needs post-processing like drying,
      sintering, or infiltration to become strong. P-BJ is known for fast printing
     speeds and works well with high-strength materials. S-BJ works differently:
      the powder is mixed with a liquid to form a slurry, which is then jetted onto
      the build platform. Because the powder is already in suspension, S-BJ can
     produce parts with smoother surfaces and better material uniformity.

178178           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

﻿   2. What are the various application areas of ceramic binder jetting?﻿
     Answer: The various application areas of ceramic binder jetting are:﻿
       1. The orthopedic field (56%) uses ceramic binder jetting to make bone
         scaffolds and implants.
      2. The structural application has the second-highest number of applications
        (35%).
       3. A small number (3%) of dentures and crowns are also reported.
       4. Dielectric radio frequency filters and ferroelectric dielectric capacitors
         are fabricated for electronic applications (3%).
﻿   3. What are the advantages and limitations of powder-based binder jet­
      ting (P-BJ) for fabricating advanced ceramic components?﻿
     Answer: P-BJ offers key advantages like design freedom, fast production,
     and reduced material waste.  It can handle complex geometries without
      support structures and works with various ceramic materials. However, it
     comes with limitations. Parts need post-processing like sintering, and binder
     removal can be challenging. Also, final parts often have lower density com­
     pared to other methods like powder bed fusion, which may affect their
     performance.
﻿   4. What are the key differences between direct and indirect powder-based
      selective  laser sintering (P-dSLS  vs. P-iSLS)  in ceramic additive
     manufacturing?﻿
     Answer: The main difference lies in how the ceramic powder is processed.
      In P-dSLS, the laser directly fuses the ceramic particles, resulting in parts
     with higher density and strength. In P-iSLS, the laser sinters a binder mixed
     with the ceramic powder. The binder is later removed, and the ceramic is
      fully fused through additional heating. While P-dSLS offers better mechan­
       ical properties, P-iSLS is gentler on heat-sensitive ceramics.
﻿   5.  Define laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF)﻿
     Answer: L-PBF is a time-saving process that manufactures the parts by
      fully melting the powders, using higher energy density of laser sources,
     and needs no binder or post-sintering process for further consolidation.
     The L-PBF process is considered the only 3D printing process to manu­
      facture complex ceramic parts with higher purity, nearly full density, and
     high strength in a single step and less time. This can be explained by fully
     melting the powder into the liquid phase, ensuring fast densification instead
      of heating the powder at a particular point where the particles are partially
     melted and fused in the SLS process. Hence, products with lower porosity,
      superior control over the crystal structure, and excellent final characteristics
     can be produced via the L-PBF process. Some advanced ceramics, particu­
       larly non-oxide ceramics with high melting temperatures, may not be pro­
      cessable using DED.
﻿   6. What is directed energy deposition (DED) of advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: DED technology uses a high-energy-density heat source to melt
      high-purity ceramic raw materials conveyed synchronously without a
      binder. Therefore, DED has the striking advantage of being a single-step

     cochemical properties are defined directly during the AM process, removing
      the need for post-processing heat treatment. DED is used to work on metal
       parts, polymers, and ceramics.
      In the DED process, ceramic materials with a melting point up to 3000°C
     can be melted using a high-power laser beam. During the deposition, the
      already deposited layers were exposed to repeated thermal cycles and very
     high cooling rates. DED has also been employed to build ceramic oxide parts
     such as alumina, zirconia, eutectic ceramic composites, zirconia–alumina

     (AYZ) samples were successfully fabricated using the LENS technique.
     The LENSed AYZ specimens presented refined eutectic microstructures
     and almost isotropic features.
﻿   7. How does directed energy deposition (DED) work in the context of
     ceramic additive manufacturing, and what are its main advantages and
     challenges compared to metals?﻿
     Answer: In DED, a focused energy source, such as a laser or electron beam,
       is used to melt the feedstock material, which is often in the form of powder
      or wire. The material is deposited layer by layer, solidifying immediately
       after being melted. The key advantages of DED for ceramics include the
       ability to repair or add features to existing parts, high flexibility in material
      choices, and the potential to create complex shapes directly without the need
      for molds or tooling. DED also offers excellent control over deposition rates
     and material composition.
     Ceramic materials are generally more challenging to process in DED com­
     pared to metals due to their brittleness, low thermal conductivity, and ten­
     dency to crack during cooling. The high cooling rates in DED can lead to
     thermal stresses and defects like cracks or porosity. Additionally, ceramics
      require higher laser power to achieve melting or sintering, which can be
       difficult to control precisely, especially when using non-metallic powders.
     Achieving a uniform microstructure and desirable properties such as tough­
      ness and strength can also be more difficult with ceramics.
﻿   8. What are the advantages of using preceramic polymers in powder bed
      fusion (PBF) additive manufacturing?﻿
     Answer: Preceramic polymers are easier to process and can form complex
     shapes with lower sintering temperatures. They’re also highly tunable –
      properties like toughness, heat resistance, and porosity can be adjusted to fit
      specific applications.
﻿   9. What are the pros and cons of using polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs)
      instead of traditional ceramic powders in PBF?﻿
     Answer: PDCs allow for more complex designs and better control over
      the final ceramic structure. They can offer improved toughness and thermal
       stability. On the downside, they may have poor powder flow, require more
      careful post-processing, and can develop residual stresses during sintering.

180180           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

﻿ 10. How does ceramic powder particle size affect printability and part
      quality in binder jetting (BJ)?﻿
     Answer: Particle size plays a big role. A narrow size range improves pack­
      ing and surface finish but may reduce flowability if the particles are too fine.
     Coarser powders flow better but can cause weak bonding and defects like
      porosity. Balancing the distribution is key to high-quality prints.
﻿ 11. How can post-processing improve the quality of BJ-printed ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Post-processing steps like debinding and sintering are critical.
     Debinding must fully remove the binder without damaging the part, while
      sintering needs to be carefully controlled for temperature and time to ensure
      proper density and strength. Extra steps like hot isostatic pressing can fur­
      ther boost mechanical properties and reduce flaws.

As discussed earlier, bulk solid-based deposition technologies are classified into two
main categories: sheet lamination (SL) and material extrusion (ME). The ME cate­
gory is further divided into fused deposition modeling (FDM) and robocasting (RC),
also known as direct ink writing (DIW), as shown in Figure 7.1. On the other hand,
Table 7.1 illustrates that all of the bulk solid-based deposition technologies treated
in this chapter are all related to the multi-stage additive manufacturing processes.
Moreover, two approaches will be considered in this chapter, namely, conventional
filaments and preceramic feedstocks.

7.1  MATERIAL EXTRUSION

The various names used to refer to ceramic ME technologies can be somewhat con­
fusing. In particular, the terms extrusion freeform (EFF) and filament-based DIW
have both been used to refer to the entire family of processes. Although the former
acronym initially described a process more specifically similar to fused deposition
of ceramics (FDC), the latter is now mostly used interchangeably with robocasting.
An overview of ME technologies used to shape advanced ceramics is provided in
Table 7.1. There are two main types of ceramic ME processes:

   (i) Wax-Based Extrusion Processes: In wax-based ceramic ME processes,
     ceramic powders are suspended in a polymeric dispersion medium, and the
      resulting polymer/ceramic composite paste or filament is extruded through
     a small orifice onto a platform.
  (ii) Water-Based Extrusion Processes: To address the issues that arise during
     debinding when using large amounts of polymer as the dispersion medium
      for ceramic materials, most ceramic extrusion technologies use water-based
     ceramic pastes rather than polymer/ceramic feedstock. These aqueous
      pastes are typically characterized by a high ceramic powder loading and
     low organic content. Several variants of the ceramic extrusion process are
     based on this approach.

   Table 7.2 provides a rapid comparison of both technologies.
  The ME process (Figure 7.2) is an additive manufacturing (AM) process where
the raw material is extruded through an orifice. This is the most common and

7.1.2   Material Extrusion Using Conventional Feedstock Filaments﻿

7.1.2.1   Feedstock Preparation and Properties
Feedstocks for EFF have the following common requirements:

    1. A high solid loading to counteract shrinkage and cracking due to sintering
      or binder burnout.
   2. A homogeneous particle distribution to ensure a constant flow and to avoid
      flaws due to agglomerates.
   3. Entrapped air should be minimized.
   4. Solvent migration and sedimentation of particles must be prevented to
      ensure constant flow and storage stability.
   5. Suitable rheology for the applied process to ensure shape retention and good
     welding of the filaments.
   6. Suitable particle size and distribution for the applied nozzle dimensions.
   7. A binder phase that is easy to drain, dry, or burn out.
    8. Suitable solidification kinetics (e.g., vapor pressure, thixotropy, thermal
      conductivity and capacity, glass transition temperature (Tg), and melting
       points).
    9. Suitable interface properties for adhesion and fusion of filaments.

In FDC, mostly a dried and surfactant pre-coated powder (1 mm) is incorporated in
the organic binder vehicle at high temperatures (above Tm) and shear forces consist­
ing of an amorphous base binder, a tackifier to add tackiness and flexibility, wax to
lower the viscosity and add stiffness, and plasticizer to add flexibility. The process is
thus similar to the one applied when manufacturing a feedstock for injection mold­
ing. When homogeneity is achieved, the feedstock is extruded to form a filament

Bulk Solid-Based Deposition for Advanced Ceramics                     189

which fits into the liquefier of the FDM machine. Another approach is to generate a
pourable granulate by chopping the filament strand. Special attention has to be paid
to the mechanical properties of the feedstock. The wire-like extrudate must be flexi­
ble enough to wrap around spools, yet sufficiently rigid to function as a piston in the
liquefier without buckling.
  Most preparation routes for RC and freeze-extrusion fabrication (FEF) feedstocks
follow the same principle.

    1. The first step to obtain a feedstock is an aqueous or non-aqueous homoge­
     neous slurry of powder particles having a high solid loading (>50 vol.%).
      Therefore, particles are dispersed (mostly aided by electrostatic dispersants)
      in the solvent by agitation with shakers, ball mills, planetary mills, or ultra­
      sonic probes until homogeneity is achieved.
   2. A polymeric viscosifier/binder is added to prevent sedimentation and sol­
      vent migration, to ensure consistent extrusion and to provide green strength.
    3. After the complete dissolution of the viscosifier, the suspension can be
     degassed by vacuum or centrifugation and then filled into the cartridge.

To offer improved shape retention for the extrusion of free-spanning filaments, tubes,
or special filament geometries, a colloidal gel is applied to EFF such that the slurry
can be coagulated using van der Waals forces, bridging flocculation and depletion
flocculation mechanisms by adding salts and pH modifiers or polymers. Another
approach is to embed particles into a thermos-reversible hydrogel. This route is also
applied in bioplotting, which works similarly to FDC, where the liquid phase of the
feedstock is not frozen upon deposition but passes a gel point and thus solidifies in
a cooled bath.
   For UV/heat-curable inks, the powder is embedded and dispersed into a monomer/
oligomer liquid doped with UV-sensitive polymerization initiators. Shape retention
by crosslinking the binder molecules can be achieved by mixing two components
continuously in a mixing chamber shortly before exiting the nozzle during the depo­
sition (Table 7.3).
  The FDM process mainly relies on the following:

    1. The material composition should have a tackifier to provide the tackiness
     and flexibility of the material; an elastomer to provide elasticity, a plas­
       ticizer to provide the plasticity for the filament to the spool, and wax to
     reduce the viscosity.
   2. The strength of the entire filament is given by the base polymer, which is
      easily modifiable by the other constituents.
    3. In the FDC process, a binder system with low viscosity, high strength, high
       strain, high modulus, and easy burnout was developed.
    4. The binder system is composed of 55 vol.% of ceramic powders, like tita­
     nium dioxide, mullite, and fused silica.
    5. The printing process is initiated with the nozzle temperatures between
     200°C and 265°C, with suitable extrusion rate parameters.

7.1.2.2  Fused Deposition Modeling
Figure 7.3 illustrates the schematic of the FDM deposition technology with two raw
materials: filament and granule. In both cases, the feedstock is composed of the
ceramic powder (usually around 40–50 vol.%) and multicomponent binders usually
containing a thermoplastic (ethylene vinyl acetate), polylactic acid (PLA), polyvinyl
butyral, polyolefin, low-density polyethylene, surfactant (stearic acid and plasticizer
(polyethylene glycol)) De Camargo et al., 2022).
   This material is heated to just above the melting point of the polymer. So the mate­
rial is selectively extruded through a nozzle and deposited layer-by-layer according
to a pre-defined path. Figure 7.3a shows the fused filament fabrication operation,
which uses a ram extruder, with the filament pushing the softened material out of

be produced without cracks during the subsequent heat treatment. Efforts to produce
ceramic FDC were started in the late 1990s. On the other hand, equipment suppliers
and available systems have risen in the last three years. 3D printers for filament and
granules are available, and the difference between these feedstocks is discussed next
(De Camargo et al., 2022).

loading is a big challenge, and they are commonly brittle and difficult to handle
and nozzle blockages can occur due to particle agglomeration. The research group
from Empa (Switzerland) led by Dr. Clemens have shown that is possible to process

Using granules favors the application of FDC on a larger scale since

7.1.2.2.3  FDM Technologies
FDM is modified to fabricate ceramics and is often abbreviated by FDC. In the FDC
a liquefied ceramic–polymer suspension, similar to an injection molding feedstock,

7.1.2.4  Freeze-Form Extrusion Fabrication
Freeze-form extrusion fabrication (FEF) is a novel, environmentally friendly AM
process that builds a 3D part layer by layer using computer-controlled extrusion
and deposition of aqueous-based colloidal pastes (Mason et al., 2009). Unlike most
EFF processes, which use organic binders to bond the ceramic powders, the organic
binder content is only 2–4 vol.%, while the paste solids loading is 45–50 vol.% or
higher. While RC fabricates parts at room temperature, FEF builds green parts below
the water freezing point to solidify the paste after the deposition of each layer during
the fabrication process. FEF can be used for the following:

    1. Building relatively large parts compared with RC
    2. Fabrication of cones and other monolithic ceramic components, including

7.1.2.5  Multiphase Jet Solidification
MJS is an ME AM process where the extruded material consists of metal/ceramic
powder with a binder, used to create parts in multiple steps, or phases. After a green
part is built, the binding material is removed with chemicals or heat, and a green part
is created that can then be sintered. In this process, low viscous materials (liquefied
substances or powder–binder pastes) are extruded through an X–Y–Z controlled jet,
and parts of different materials are fabricated layer by layer up to the final shape
(Figure 7.11). Subsequently, the binder is removed, and the green part is sintered to
reach the final density. Figure 7.12 shows fast, functional prototypes built by MJS.
The advantages of the MJS-process are as follows (Geiger and Wilhelm, 1994):

then ball-milled at 100°C to ensure homogeneity. The resulting suspension is loaded
into a heated cartridge and extruded through a nozzle. This technique supports both
continuous and droplet-based deposition strategies and is also applicable to shap­
ing hard metals and cemented carbides. For example, Al 2 O 3 and ZrO2 suspensions
with solid loadings of 67 and 45 vol%, respectively, were successfully extruded to
form simple stacked geometries. After sintering, the parts achieved densities exceed­

successful processing of only certain ceramics, such as alumina and zirconia, has
been reported. T3DP has also been used for the production of multi-material parts
by combining different ceramic powders, as well as combining ceramics and metals.
Studies presented show the potential of T3DP in producing high-quality ceramic
parts. It is also shown that this method has the potential to be further improved,
possibly by processing different types of ceramic powders as well as different com­
binations of these powders.
  T3DP feedstock should possess high solid loading, as high green densities result
in lower shrinkage and cracking during sintering, as well as lower porosity in the
final part. The homogenous distribution of particles is also crucial as it results in
the improvement of the Weibull distribution of strength. The feedstock should have
high enough strength (yield stress) to be processed with high solid loading without
facing problems during debinding. The yield stress of the suspension is dependent
on the particle size, size distribution, and interparticle forces. These parameters also
affect the viscosity of the feedstock, which needs to be low at the processing tem­
perature and pressure. The use of low-melting-point wax is important for achieving
low viscosities of molten suspension, while the use of surfactant helps to achieve the
low viscosities with high solid loading. The suspension needs to be pseudoplastic
(shear-thinning); that is, its viscosity needs to decrease with increased shear rates
to be processable at process conditions and to maintain the shape after the process.
For shear rates below 10 1/s, viscosity below 100 Pa s is acceptable, while for shear
rates below 100 1/s, viscosity below 20 Pa s is acceptable (Weingarten et al., 2019).
The melting temperature and the viscosity of T3DP feedstocks are lower compared
to FFF feedstocks (Scheithauer et al., 2017a, 2017b).

7.1.2.7  Ceramic On-Demand Extrusion
Ceramic on-demand extrusion (CODE) process is a freeform water-based AM
process in which ceramic particles like zirconia powder in aqueous suspensions
are deposited in layers and then radiated by infrared radiation after each layer to
form parts having high density. The CODE process extrudes and deposits aqueous
pastes onto a substrate to print each layer sequentially. The substrate is placed
inside a tank designed to hold a fluid medium (normally oil). Once one layer is
deposited completely, the oil is pumped into the tank to surround the part, prevent­
ing undesirable water evaporation from the perimeters of the deposited layers. The
oil level is maintained just below the topmost layer of the part being fabricated.
Infrared radiation is then applied in a direction perpendicular to the top surface
to uniformly dry the deposited layer so that the fabricated part will be partially
dried and stiffened (Figure 7.13). This enables the printed body to sustain the
weight of the subsequently deposited layers without deformation. After the parts
were printed, the oil in the tank was drained, and the parts were moved out of the
tank with the substrate attached for post-processing, which includes bulk drying
to eliminate the remaining water content inside the parts and oil on the surface
of the part, followed by debinding and decomposing of support material and sin­
tering (Li et al., 2017). Figure 7.14 shows a final turbine-blower housing part after
sintering.

7.1.3  ME Using Preceramic Feedstocks﻿

ME is a 3D printing process for fabricating ceramic components using various feed­
stocks. Preceramic resins have particularly drawn attention because of their ver­
satile precursors, including solid filaments or pastes (Gorjan et al., 2019, Zhao et
al., 2021, and Solís Pinargote et al., 2020). Solid filament containing preceramics
can soften when heated and harden upon cooling, allowing for subsequent layer-by-
layer deposition and solidification. Typically, paste materials are used in DIW where
their rheological properties play a crucial role in printing high-quality components
and ensuring that parts maintain their solid structure and integrity during and after
fabrication. Solid-phase preceramic polymers, such as powders or those with high
viscosity, may require solvents or other lower-viscosity materials to improve flow
properties (Franchin et al., 2018). On the other hand, if the viscosity of the prece­
ramic polymer is too low, particles, fibers, or high-viscosity resins are added to adjust
their flow behaviors (Kemp et al., 2021). Once printed, solid green structures are
converted to ceramics after pyrolysis, such as the VP process. Different feedstocks
containing preceramic precursors for FDM and DIW are summarized in Table 7.5.

7.1.3.2  DIW or RC Using Preceramic Polymers
As previously discussed, the rheological properties of preceramic polymers play a
critical role in the success of a DIW process. Therefore, the rheological properties of
the preceramic ink need to be carefully adjusted to achieve high-quality printed solid
structures. Different feedstock designs have been employed for the DIW process.
Among them, a typical approach is to incorporate fillers into the materials to improve
flowability, reduce volumetric shrinkage, and eventually enhance the properties of
the pyrolyzed ceramic components. For example, adding fillers to a preceramic paste
usually results in a significant increase in the viscosity of the paste. However, the
viscosity decreased rapidly upon the application of the shear stress, indicating a shear
thinning behavior (Shear thinning behavior refers to a property of certain feedstock
materials, where the viscosity of the material decreases as the shear rate increases).
This behavior can be explained by the Herschel–Builkley model. Non-Newtonian
colloidal gels exhibit shear thinning flow behavior due to the attrition among filler
particles, as described by the Herschel–Builkley equation:

where τ is the shear stress, τy is the yield shear stress, K is the viscosity parameter,
γ is the shear rate, and n is the shear thinning exponents (Shahzad and Lazoglu,
2021). The shear thinning effect of feedstock containing solid fillers can significantly

materials for DIW processes has also been studied. Chen et al. (2023) recently inves­

The solid structure could successively experience controllable shape transformation
and then be transformed to ceramic structures after pyrolysis (Chen et al., 2023).
   Typically, DIW-printed  solid green  structures using preceramic feedstocks
require an additional thermal curing process to become completely solidified before
they are pyrolyzed into ceramic components. This thermal curing step is necessary

respectively. In this research, a 50 wt.% of Si 3 N 4 powder was selected as an inert
filler because it has good light transmission in the UV region.

7.1.4   Advantages and Limitations of Ceramic ME

The primary advantages of ceramic ME processes are as follows (Lakhdar et al., 2021):

    1. Relative ease of operation.
    2. Low manufacturing costs as the processes do not involve any high-energy
     beams.
    3. Water-based extrusion techniques RC, FEF, and CODE make use of highly
     loaded aqueous slurries with minimal binder content, which have several
      additional advantages compared to wax-based extrusion.
    4. High green densities.
    5. Simplified debinding schedule.
    6. Low sintering shrinkage.
    7. Environmentally friendly.
    8. Low cost of feedstock and hardware.
    9. Unlike wax-based extrusion processes, RC and FEF enable the production
      of thick cross-sections with appreciable densities due to the low amounts of
      organic additives in the feedstock formulation.
  10. FDC, EFF, and other wax-based extrusion processes may provide more free­
    dom than water-based extrusion in terms of geometrical complexity when
     manufacturing small components due to the use of a thermoplastic polymer

      as the structural matrix, which enables the formation of stiffer struts for the
      production of small overhangs without the need for a secondary support
      material.

Some disadvantages include the following:

    1. The mechanical properties of extruded parts are highly anisotropic and
      largely depend on the raster printing orientation strategy.
   2. Surface bumpiness and stair casing effects remain an aesthetic issue. The
      surface finish, geometrical accuracy, and enhanced shape retention can be
      substantially improved using finer nozzles. The latter has some drawbacks,
     such as much longer printing times, which increase the printing defects and
      the possibility of nozzle clogging.
   3. Surface roughness is also a source of critical defects that limit the mechani­
      cal reliability of as-printed parts, and mechanically strong parts are obtained
       after post-process machining and grinding.
   4. Extrusion-based processes are also inherently restricted regarding the print­
      ing throughput, since fabrication time increases linearly with part volume,
     although this issue can be partially addressed by using a larger extrusion ori­

      effect on layer thickness and resolution, and a compromise must be made
     between productivity and resolution.
    5. AM is relatively unsuited to produce large components with a good surface
      finish without resorting to post-processing.

7.2.1   Laminated Object Manufacturing﻿

LOM processes are the AM processes in which sheets of material are bonded to form
an object. The history of LOM started in 1986 when the Helisys Corporation devel­
oped the LOM process for creating three-dimensional parts from sheets of paper,
plastic, or metal. The process was patented in 1987, while the first LOM machine
(LOM-1015) was commercialized in 1991. Two LOM technologies can be differenti­
ated: traditional LOM and computer-aided manufacturing of laminated engineering
materials (CAM-LEM) (Deckers et al., 2014).

7.2.1.1   Traditional LOM
The traditional LOM process deposits green ceramic tape-cast layers. These layers
are unrolled onto the working platform, where a CO2 laser beam cuts the outline
of each layer of the part. A heated roller is then passed over the layer to thermally
activate the tape’s binder system and laminate the sheet to the previous layer. The
high ceramic powder load in the tapes (> 40 wt.%) requires the use of double-sided
adhesive tape or a diluted binder solution to promote the interconnection between the
adjacent tapes. Using the roller compression, the boundary between the tapes should
be undetectable. After debinding and sintering the green object in a furnace, the
final ceramic (e.g., alumina and silica 24) or glass–ceramic is obtained by (Deckers
et al., 2014).
  Ceramic LOM works by sequentially stacking, cutting, and bonding ceramic green
tapes produced by tape casting or preceramic paper, to form the desired geometry.

208208           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

For each layer, the outline of the part is first cut with a computer-controlled knife or
CO2 laser, and a heated roller is then applied onto the surface to activate the binder
to promote bonding between adjacent layers thermally. LOM works at low tempera­
ture and rolling pressure, which minimizes warping and delamination. LOM has
been used to produce monolithic components with a 250 μm layer thickness that
could be fabricated using a solvent-assist spray technique. Unpolished specimens
had a flexural strength of 150 MPa, which was quite low compared with commercial

green parts obtained are then subjected to debinding and pressureless sintering to
densify the parts. The pores occurring during the sintering process can be filled by
infiltration methods to cover the gaps and increase the strength properties of the final
objects. The infiltration can be done by liquid silicon material at 1500°C for 1 to 7 h

7.2.1.2  Computer-Aided Manufacturing of Laminated Engineering Materials
The CAM-LEM process is identical to that of LOM, but instead of the layers being
stacked and then cut, each layer is pre-cut and robotically stacked onto the working
part for lamination. This method has some advantages over traditional LOM, for
example, internal voids within each layer can be easily produced (Deckers et al.,
2014).
  The CAM-LEM process uses a cut-then-stack approach, where each ceramic
green layer is pre-cut before lamination. As a result, unlike in LOM, there is no
waste material within the build, and, therefore, additional support material  is
required for overhanging structures. However, the fact that tapes are pre-cut allows
for the production of hollow geometries. It also enables in-layer spatial mixing of
materials as well as the implementation of tangent cutting for enhanced surface
quality. Liu et al. (1997) used aqueous slurries of Si 3 N 4 with 10 wt% sintering aids
(3:5 Y2 O 3 / Al 2 O 3 ) and PVA as the binder to prepare 150 μm thick tapes that were
then dried, cut, and stacked layer by layer under 50 MPa with isostatic pressing at
room temperature for 2 min to form green bodies. After debinding and pressureless
sintering (1800°C, 60 min, and nitrogen atmosphere), a relative density of 93.7% and
total linear shrinkage of 23.2% were possible. For each sample, at least five speci­
mens were cut, ground, polished to a 1 μm finish, and chamfered; an average flexural
strength of 34 MPa was obtained, which was lower than for injection-molded and
extruded parts.
  CAM-LEM was applied for more complicated parts with angular surfaces or hol­
low structures, where the single sheets were cut, and the waste material was removed
before stacking and lamination. The staircase effect was avoided by inclining the
laser during cutting. In this way, alumina parts with internal channel structures were
produced. Internal structures for electronic devices have also been prepared with
low-temperature co-fired ceramics containing Sio – Al 2 O 3 – RO glass and Al 2 O 3
particles. In contrast to the Helysis device, these tapes were cut using a milling
plotter (LPKF Laser & Electronics, Garbsen, Germany) and cold laminated with a
double-sided adhesive tape with a thickness of 12 mm. Binder decomposition was
finished at 425°C and sintering at 870°C led to a density of 99%. The advantages
of this method are that the slight lamination pressure at room temperature enables

  CAM-LEM is commonly applied in electronic ceramics technology, especially
for the use of ceramic green tapes has the following advantages;

    1. The low-temperature lamination prevents distortion and deformation due to
     low thermal stresses.
    2. The material, machine, and process costs are lower than those of other sol­
      id-form fabrication techniques.
    3. About part sizes up to a volume of 500_800_500 mm3, accuracy over the
     work envelope is 0.25 mm.
    4. Hollo structures can be produced using the CAM-LEM method.

Disadvantages are the following:

    1. The decubing of the parts prevents the creation of very detailed surfaces.
    2. In post-processing the organic binder material has to be removed between and
      within the single layers, which results in anisotropic mechanical properties.

To improve the LOM process and eliminate disadvantages, the lamination and cut­
ting process and the waste removal strategy should be considered. In this respect,
Wang et al. (2019),

   •  Bigger rollers lead to better lamination of the sheets, while small rollers
      enable shorter process times due to concentrated stress distribution at the
      interface.
   •  Applying heating temperatures up to 450°C, before pressing, increases the
       roller moving speed.
   •  The laser energy has to be adapted to the material system and layer thickness.
   •  Normally, waste material volume is cubed for easier removal.
   •  The waste volume should be divided into two sections: coarse cubes in the
      outer sections and fine cubes in the inner region, which saves laser energy,
      protects the part, improves the process efficiency, and shortens the decubing
      time.
   •  Laser energy decomposes the adhesive in the working zone up to a critical
      inclination angle, where the overlap zone between the cuts of two layers
     becomes too large.
   •   If horizontal or areas with inclination below a critical angle are avoided,
     decubing time can be significantly reduced and surface quality improved.
   •   If the waste material is removed during the process, hollow shapes can be
     produced.
   • A self-adhesive sheet material with shielding paper is required to remove waste
      material, with the adhesive on the top of the sheet areas that have to be removed
      are printed with graphitic powder on the layer below to prohibit fixing.
   •  Bridging elements can be inserted to create freestanding parts, which have
      to be removed after decubing.

7.2.2   Advantages and Limitations of SL

LOM and CAM-LEM have been successfully used to manufacture parts from a
wide range of oxide and non-oxide advanced ceramic tapes, showing the versatil­
ity of SL regarding the type of ceramic materials that can be processed. However,
SL processes are limited in terms of surface quality due to the creation of surface
defects during the decubing step, although this issue can be largely minimized by
using adaptive laser crosshatching strategies or surface burnishing. Parts made by
LOM are usually characterized by a high surface roughness caused by stair cas­
ing effects, which are difficult to minimize. The use of non-negligible amounts of
binder to promote layer bonding can be detrimental to the final density of the sintered
parts and results in the formation of pores. The presence of interfacial discontinuity
and defects is the main disadvantage of LOM, leading to delamination, differential
shrinkage, and interfacial porosity. Nevertheless, LOM and CAM-LEM have been
used to produce parts with good mechanical properties. As expected, there is usually
a significant difference in mechanical properties and shrinkage between the stacking
direction (Z) and the tape plane (XY). This anisotropic behavior must be taken into
account during the design phase.


7.3  REVIEW QUESTIONS

7.3.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. What  is fused deposition modeling (FDM), and how  is  it used in
     advanced ceramics?
     Answer: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is a 3D printing method where
      material is extruded layer by layer to build up a physical object. When it
     comes to advanced ceramics, the process uses a special feedstock made
     from ceramic particles mixed with a polymer binder. This allows the ceramic
      material to be printed like plastic. Once the object is printed, it goes through
     a sintering process that burns off the polymer and solidifies the ceramic into
        its final, strong form.
   2. What’s the difference between fused filament fabrication (FFF) and
     fused deposition modeling (FDM)?
     Answer: Technically, there’s no real difference between FFF and FDM –
      they describe the same process. The main distinction is in the naming: FDM
       is a trademarked term from the company Stratasys, while FFF is the open-
      source, more generic term used by the wider 3D printing community. Both
      involve melting and depositing filament material in layers to create an object.

﻿   3. What are the key FDM process parameters that affect ceramic part
      quality?﻿
      Several settings in the FDM process can significantly influence the final
      quality of ceramic parts. These include:
       •  Extrusion Temperature: Needs to be just right for smooth flow and
        good bonding.
       •  Layer Thickness: Affects surface finish and detail resolution.
       •  Print Speed: Influences both print quality and time.
       •  Deposition Temperature: Ensures consistent layering and adhesion.
       •  Build Orientation: Can impact mechanical strength and finish.
      Post-printing processes, like sintering temperature and cooling rate, are also
       critical for the final properties of the ceramic.
﻿   4. What types of FDM technologies are used in ceramic 3D printing?﻿
     Answer: Ceramic additive manufacturing has evolved to include several
      variations of FDM-based technologies, such as the following:
       •  Ceramic Slurry Extrusion: A thick liquid mix of ceramic is printed
          layer by layer.
       •   Direct Ink Writing (DIW): Uses printable ceramic inks, allowing for
         very fine detail.
       •  Composite Filament Extrusion: Involves standard FDM printers but
         with filaments filled with ceramic particles.
     Each method comes with its own strengths in terms of resolution, material
      behavior, and post-processing needs.
﻿   5. What is robocasting (RC), and how does it help in ceramic 3D printing?﻿
     Answer: Robocasting is a specialized form of 3D printing that uses a
      paste-like ceramic slurry extruded through a nozzle to build parts layer by
       layer. These printed parts are called “green bodies” and are later sintered to
     become dense, solid ceramics. Robocasting is especially good for producing
     complex ceramic shapes and is used in industries like aerospace, healthcare,
     and electronics.
﻿   6. How does freeze-form extrusion fabrication (FEF) work with ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Freeze-form extrusion fabrication (FEF) involves extruding a
     ceramic slurry into a cold environment where it instantly freezes as it’s
      deposited. This frozen structure is then freeze-dried to remove moisture
      before being sintered. FEF is great for creating dense, precise ceramic parts
     with minimal distortion or shrinkage.
    7. What is multiphase jet solidification (MJS), and how is  it used in
     ceramic 3D printing?
     Answer: Multiphase  jet solidification (MJS)  is a cutting-edge method
     where multiple materials – such as ceramic slurry and a binder – are jetted
      together and solidified layer by layer. This approach allows for combining
      different materials in a single print, enabling the creation of functionally
     graded ceramics or parts with region-specific properties. MJS offers more
      design flexibility than traditional techniques.

﻿   8. What are the advantages and limitations of ceramic extrusion in 3D

     Answer:﻿
     Advantages:﻿
       •  Can produce highly complex, custom geometries
       •  Minimizes material waste
       •   Ideal for rapid prototyping and near-net-shape manufacturing
       •   Offers good design flexibility
     Limitations:
       •  Requires specialized materials and careful post-processing
       •  Removing binders and sintering can lead to shrinkage or defects
       •   Resolution and mechanical uniformity can be challenging
       •  Limited availability of ceramic-compatible extrusion materials com­
         pared to other 3D printing processes
