8.1  CHALLENGES OF ADVANCED CERAMICS
    IN AM TECHNOLOGY

Additive manufacturing (AM) of ceramic parts is relatively more challenging con­
cerning polymer and metallic parts, owing to their high melting temperatures and
inherent brittleness. For instance, the melting points of alumina and tungsten carbide
are 2050°C and 2870°C, respectively. For this reason, most of the ceramic parts
are produced using indirect AM processes that need post-processing steps such as
debinding and sintering for further consolidation. Although in selective laser sinter­
ing (SLS), laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF), and directed energy distribution (DED)
processes, ceramics are directly sintered or melted, high thermal stress generally
causes crack formation in printed parts. Compared with these methods, SLC is more
famous for creating ceramic components in an indirect way, where the material
selection, post-processing, and controlling processing parameters are more critical.
Besides, due to ceramic materials’ low thermal expansion coefficient and inherent
brittleness, the full-scale industrial AM techniques for mass production and printing
large parts are still challenging (Dadkhah et al., 2023).
  One of the main concerns of using these AM processes is printing large ceramic
objects. 3D printing of large parts is not direct; they are cut into smaller pieces and
assembled later. Nevertheless, the produced parts often lack strength. Furthermore,
large ceramic parts possess problems during binder removal and sintering, which can
be attributed to significant variations in sectional thickness and differences in ther­
mal features and shrinkage. Another major challenge is the formation of porosity and
voids between the layers and beads. Depending on the used AM process, the volume
of voids in the printed part is different, which can lead to delamination of parts in
extreme cases. Ceramic objects produced using extrusion-based AM processes are
prone to such limitations. These defects can be minimized by loading high solids in
the feedstock, accurate control of the feedstock viscosity, temperature of the built
environment, and changing the nozzle design (Paul et al., 2017). The same incon­
veniences and solutions to limit them can be reported for digital light processing
(DLP), with the exception of the nozzle design.
   In all the parts produced via single-step AM processes, anisotropy in mechanical
properties and microstructure is intrinsic. By producing parts layer by layer, when
high thermal gradients and repeated heating/cooling cycles are generated, they result
in microstructure variation and anisotropic mechanical features in various directions

(Vrancken et al., 2012). The anisotropy property can be addressed by applying proper
post-printing techniques, such as sintering and hot isostatic pressing (HIP) of printed
ceramic parts. FDC-created objects have the required strength for many ceramic
engineering applications. However, due to the poor mechanical properties, the pro­
duced parts using SLS, L-PBF, and sheet lamination (SL) are handicapped. Other
than the fused deposition, all other AM technologies are restricted by the volume
of specimens and printing speed. Meanwhile, SHL and the fused deposition are not
able to produce complex products with high resolution (Oropallo and Piegl, 2016).
   Ultimately, the development of a single-step AM process able to produce defect-
free, fully dense ceramic parts while retaining the freeform fabrication feature that
characterizes AM can be considered the ultimate goal, although such an objec­
tive is probably far from being realistically achievable in the near future. Instead,
most research teams currently focus on the development and optimization of viable
ceramic systems and processing methods for exploitation in multi-step AM. Research
has mostly moved toward the use of slurry-based processes instead of dry powders
to enable the fabrication of pore-free and crack-free components with a high surface
finish and a fine microstructure.


8.2  COMPARISON REGARDING AMC PROCESSES

In this section, we conclude and summarize the main characteristics and capabilities
of AM processes that have been used to shape advanced ceramic materials.
   Despite plenty of research methods exhibiting high-quality advanced ceramic
parts, there are not many successful companies using AM techniques for fabricating
advanced ceramic materials. Table 8.1 provides information about the commercial
AM systems available worldwide. It is observed that oxides are the most commonly
used advanced ceramics, and most of the AM techniques are suitable for fabricating
oxide materials, specifically alumina and zirconia.
   Table 8.2 compares different ceramic AM categories and their characteristics,
regarding build size, resolution, surface quality, manufacturing cost, and the type
of printed ceramic. Table 8.3 compares the main AM techniques for manufacturing
ceramics, merits, demerits, and applications (Dadkhah et al., 2023).
   In many AM approaches, heating and cooling are essential steps. Figure 8.1 com­
pares the fabrication speed, achieved resolution, and the energy needed in the seven
main AM categories as defined by ISO/ASTM 17296. Many AM technologies, like
BJ technology (BJT), use various binders for processing using relatively lower heat.
The selection of a proper binder, its durability, and its applications can be challeng­
ing. The DED process uses the maximum energy in the fabrication of ceramic com­
ponents at the highest speed, while the generation of ceramic parts using BJT needs
the minimum energy.
   Generally, a versatile range of feedstocks can be processed by SL techniques,
such as fiberglass or ceramic fillers. In contrast, other AM approaches use powdery
or liquid raw materials. Within the AM techniques, the sheet lamination (SL) process
can accelerate the large-scale production of parts. SHL (SL in Figure 8.1) possesses
a printing resolution compatible with all other AM approaches.

      slurry-BJ are the use of expensive lasers and an inert environment, which
      increase the overall manufacturing cost and require more stringent health

      material to another, potentially affecting the effectiveness of the LS process

          Direct laser sintering (dLS) uses similar expensive high-power lasers,
      but the part is shaped by directly processing the ceramic material itself rather
      than a binder, making it a single-step AM process, since ceramic materials
      are sintered as they are being shaped, removing the need for post-process
      binder burnout and furnace firing. However, the extreme temperature gra­
      dients of ceramics arising from the laser have so far prevented the fabrica­
      tion of crack-free parts taller than a few millimeters and have also limited
      the printed materials to a few specific oxide ceramics. Furthermore, poor
      control over dimensions of the melt pool typically results in high surface
      roughness. Nevertheless, the dLS process has been applied to the follow­

      nical ceramic powders without using any sacrificial binder due to the very
     high melting point of this class of materials. Solid-state fiber lasers such as
      the Nd:YAG laser with a wavelength of ~ 1 μm are often used for dLS of
     ceramic powders because of their higher power and smaller beam spot size
     compared to CO2  lasers. Less technical ceramics such as silicates (e.g.,
      ﻿SiO2 and ZrSiO4 ) can be sintered using a CO2 laser to manufacture low-

          The most significant advantage of dLS in particular over most other
     ceramic AM processes is its single-step nature, where the ceramic material
       is directly melted and sintered as it is shaped, removing the need for the
      lengthy post-AM thermal debinding and furnace sintering steps. However,
      thermal stresses that occur during dLS remain a critical issue for ceramic
      materials, resulting in cracking and porosity, and, as a result, no large mon­
       olithic ceramic parts have been demonstrated to date. So far, dLS has been
     demonstrated mostly with some oxide ceramic materials or specific ceramic
      blends such as the eutectic Al 2 O 3  ZrO 2 mixture, but there may however
     be some limitations regarding material selection: some high-performance
     oxide and non-oxide ceramics may remain extremely challenging to shape
     by dLS due to their very high melting point, poor resistance to thermal gra­
      dients, and low plasticity.
   • DED , also known as laser cladding, direct laser fabrication, or Laser
     Engineered Net ShapingTM (LENS®), is a single-step AM method and
     has the potential to enable the rapid additive fabrication of simple ceramic
      shapes. Extreme temperature gradients are also an issue with DED and
      usually result in thermal cracking. Some advanced ceramics, in particu­
       lar non-oxide ceramics with high melting temperature, may not be pro­
      cessable using this technology. Furthermore, by using several nozzles,
   DED also enables depositing multiple materials at a time, allowing for
      the direct fabrication of ceramic–ceramic and metal–ceramic composites.
    Much like other AM processes, this process parameter optimization is
      largely material dependent and must be carried out every time the compo­
      sition or morphology of the ceramic powder/wire feedstock is modified.
     However, this process has a few significant limitations, such as the lim­
      ited geometrical complexity, limited resolution, and poor control over the
     shape of manufactured parts.

      controlled frequencies. As a result, ink droplets are deposited only when and

     (RC, DIW, ceramic on demand extrusion (CODE), FDC  . . .) have the
     advantage of being the cheapest ceramic AM technologies, the most versa­
        tile, and the easiest to scale, enabling the fabrication of very small compo­
      nents as well as much larger ones. Material grading is also possible using
      extrusion processes with multiple deposition orifices, although not with the
     same level of microstructural control as with DIP. Surface finish, however, is
      directly dependent upon the shape and size of the deposition nozzle, giving
       rise to a direct conflict between surface quality and fabrication throughput.
     Both DIP and extrusion technologies do not suffer the limitations of stereo­
      lithography (SLA) concerning the range of ceramics that can be shaped, and
     a wide range of oxide and non-oxide ceramics have already been demon­
      strated with both processes.

8.3  MAIN CRITERIA FOR SELECTING A SPECIFIC AMC PROCESSES

While manufacturers can utilize the full spectrum of AM processes to shape advanced
ceramic materials, the outcomes and performance vary significantly across different
processes, with each characterized by its own set of advantages and limitations. As
such, there is no single “best overall” ceramic AM process. Instead, the selection of
the most appropriate AM technology depends directly on the material being used
and the specific end-use application of the component. Therefore, before choosing an
AM process, it is essential to identify and specify the following requirements.

8.3.1   Type of Advanced Ceramic Material to be Printed﻿

The first and most crucial step in selecting any manufacturing process, including
AM, is identifying the ceramic material to be processed, based on the specific
requirements of the application and the desired properties of the final component.
While most oxide ceramics can usually be shaped using any AM process, as long
as proper material pre-processing is performed and printing parameters are opti­
mized, some restrictions can apply to non-oxide and polymer-derived ceramics
(PDCs) due to some of their specific physical properties. For instance, non-oxide
ceramics with high refractive index and absorption at UV and daylight wavelengths
(e.g., B4 C and TiC ) may prove significantly more difficult to shape using photopo­
lymerization-based processes than more transparent ceramics, for example, Al 2 O 3 ,
ZrO2 , and HA, because of excessive light scattering and insufficient cured depths.
Additionally, processes such as dLS and DED may face obstacles when working
with non-oxide ceramics due to their high melting points, low toughness, and poor

8.3.2   Printed Part Final Porosity, Density, and Mechanical Property﻿

8.3.2.1   Porosity and Selected AM Technology
To develop a more general understanding of the technical challenges associated with
additive manufacturing of ceramics (AMC), it makes sense to divide the 3D-printed
component porosity, as adopted in the three previous chapters, into two main cate­
gories, namely:

   •  Porous Components: It is well-known that the many AM technologies suc­
      cessfully applied to the manufacture of ceramics have been used to fabricate
     porous structures, for example, scaffolds for biological applications, filters,
     and lightweight structures. In these cases, the success of the respective tech­
     nology is based not only on its ability to exactly generate the desired porous
      structure but also on the fact that a certain amount of random and residual
      porosity in the solid ceramic part of the scaffold is tolerated or even desired,
      as it provides further functionality to the component.
   •  Fully Dense Monolithic Components : There are few AM technologies on
      the market capable of generating fully dense monolithic ceramic bodies.
   AM of monolithic ceramics, enabling the components to fully retain their
      superior physicochemical properties, is still a challenge and remains the
     most important task that needs to be solved to promote AMC to more than a
      specialized technology.

The property that most significantly affects the physical properties and mechani­
cal strength of ceramic parts is the final sintered density. This density is directly
influenced by factors such as green density, powder size, and the sintering method
and its schedule. Before choosing an AM process, it is important to consider the
requirements in terms of in-service mechanical properties of the end-use compo­
nent carefully, because these will directly impact the required part density. Dry
powder-bed processes, P-BJ and P-LS, are not suitable for producing high-density

Challenges, Comparison, and Process Selection Regarding AMC            231

parts due to the use of dry coarse powders that have a low sinterability and provide a
poor packing density, thus resulting in high porosity. Post-densification steps such as
WIP and infiltration can help improve density, but they result in extra manufactur­
ing time, added cost, and only partially solve the issue. High sintered densities can
be achieved using the slurry-based variants of these processes, namely, slurry-LS
and slurry-BJ, as well as other AM processes that use liquid ceramic feedstock,
such as aqueous-based extrusion (RC and CODE), ink jetting, and stereolithography
(Lakhdar et al., 2021). Both single-step processes, dLS and DED, have also been
used to produce monolithic specimens, although issues with cracking and limited
geometrical freedom still need to be addressed. It must also be kept in mind that,
in single-step processes, densification is performed in a very different manner than
with the more conventional solid-state sintering carried out at very low heating rates
in a furnace with dwell times of several hours at maximum temperature. Instead,
sintering in dLS and DED is carried out through the formation of a liquid phase,
the ceramic powder being melted in situ under a high-temperature laser and then
resolidified within a fraction of a second. As a result, the microstructure of mono­
lithic ceramics produced using single-step AM technologies differs significantly
from that of identical ceramics densified by furnace sintering, resulting in poten­
tially very different final physical, chemical, and mechanical properties (Lakhdar
et al., 2021).
  DED offers several significant advantages over PBF. One key benefit is that
porosity tends to be less critical in DED compared to PBF, where porosity can more
severely affect part quality. DED allows for the production of high-density samples
by optimizing process parameters and utilizing various laser configurations and
material combinations. Additionally, DED is better suited for manufacturing larger
components and typically delivers superior static and dynamic mechanical prop­
erties. The use of larger powder particles in DED not only reduces material costs
but also enhances operational safety. However, DED does have limitations, includ­
ing lower dimensional accuracy, reduced powder efficiency and recyclability, and
increased surface roughness – particularly when processing powder mixtures.
   However, the high cooling rates and steep thermal gradients inherent in the DED
process can lead to various defects, including complex phase transformations, micro­
structural changes, non-uniform residual stresses, distortions, porosity, and cracking.
These issues can ultimately compromise corrosion resistance, degrade mechanical
performance, and lead to premature failure. Additionally, components produced via
DED often require post-fabrication machining to achieve acceptable surface quality
(Dadkhah et al., 2023).

number of applications and has been widely demonstrated. However, for AM of
advanced ceramics to further develop and reach the same technological maturity
as metal AM, it is essential that it enables the manufacture of high-performance
ceramic materials into monolithic components with adequate mechanical properties.

8.3.3   Influence of Resolution and Dimensions
      on Selected AMC Technology﻿

The overall dimensions of the component to be manufactured have a decisive influ­
ence on the AMC process selection. On the one hand, certain AM processes may be
more suitable for manufacturing small components where high precision is essential.
On the extreme side of the spectrum, 2PP enables the production of micro-sized
objects with a resolution of a few hundred nanometers. SL, DLP, and DIP are also
very well suited to manufacturing small components for high precision applications,
with their excellent resolution and accuracy in the order of a few tens of microns.
Although all AM processes probably have the technical potential to eventually be
scaled-up to produce large parts, processes that tend to have a lower accuracy but a
higher throughput, such as powder-bed processes, may be easier and more cost-effec­
tive to scale up to produce medium to large parts. P-BJ is highly suited to producing
large-sized ceramic parts. In this regard, however, dLS does not (yet) offer the same
capability as other powder-bed processes due to the extreme thermal gradients that
limit the height that can be manufactured without the formation of pores and cracks.
Processes that use extensive amounts of polymeric binder such as SLA and FDC may
also experience limits regarding the maximum wall thickness that can be manufac­
tured for two reasons.

    1. Because binder burnout must be carried out at very slow heating rates,
         it may not be economically viable to run debinding schedules that could
      potentially take weeks to complete for thick-walled parts.
   2. Because the high amounts of volatile gaseous species trying to escape the
     bulk volume by diffusion are likely to result in the formation of pores and
      cracks.


8.3.4   Influence of Printed Part Surface Finish
      on Selected AMC Technology﻿

Usually strongly correlated to process resolution, surface roughness is mostly a func­
tion of two parameters: open porosity at the surface and the stair casing effect. On
the one hand, roughness resulting from open pores is directly related to the inability
of some AM processes to produce fully dense parts and to mitigate residual porosity,
and on the other hand stair casing effects arise when printing relatively thick layers
and are exacerbated by poor interlayer merging. While it is commonly accepted that
the best surface finish from AM processes can be achieved using SLA and DLP
vat photopolymerization technologies, excellent results have also been demonstrated
with DIW and S-BJ. Parts manufactured using these two processes usually do not
display any open porosity and can be optimized to be seemingly free of the stair cas­
ing effect. Slurry-based processes, S-BJ and S-iLS, also provide a good surface fin­
ish compared to their powder-based counterparts due to the significant reduction of
residual open porosity and the ability to form thinner layers. The often-poor surface

236236           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

quality obtained with ceramic extrusion technologies is caused by stair casing and
bumpiness due to poor surface merging of successive individual struts and is exac­
erbated when using large extrusion nozzles. As mentioned before, the surface finish
of extruded parts can be greatly improved by using smaller orifices (Figure 8.2),
although higher resolution comes at the cost of reduced manufacturing throughput.
  A comparison of dental crowns produced using two AM technologies is provided
in Figure 8.3 and shows the disparities in terms of surface finish that can be achieved
currently.

8.3.5   Influence of Printed Part Geometrical Complexity
      on Selected AMC Technology﻿

It is important to realize that not all AM processes have the same capabilities
and potential regarding geometrical complexity. The process with the most lim­
ited potential for improvement in this regard is, without doubt, DED since neither
self-supporting material nor support structures are present to accommodate over­
hangs. This, however, can be partly addressed by enhancing the DED process with
a five-axis deposition system. Conversely, LS and BJ powder-bed processes, in both
their dry powder-based and slurry-based variants, are naturally well-suited to the
manufacture of complex-shaped parts thanks to their self-supporting powder bed
that allows to produce intricate geometries and large overhangs without the need for
additional support structures. However, these processes do not allow the fabrication
of fully closed volumes since any excess support powder cannot be removed from
enclosed cavities and would remain trapped. While the same limitation applies to
LOM because the ceramic tape that acts as support would remain trapped inside any
closed volume, CAM-LEM addresses the issue thanks to its cut-then-stack approach.
Bedless AM processes, such as DIW, DIP, and DLP, may in theory allow the pro­
duction of fully enclosed volumes without the need for support structures by fol­
lowing specific design rules, although support material is most likely often going to

8.3.6  AMC Processes and Related Post-Processing Techniques﻿

The three  critical aspects  that ceramists improve through post-processing of
advanced ceramics are the final density, microstructure, and surface quality. These
three properties directly affect the overall performance of ceramic components and
their mechanical properties. The microstructure and density of advanced ceramics
are highly influenced by the sintering method, in particular, whether post-densifi­
cation is performed by pressureless or pressure-assisted sintering, but also by the

238238           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

selection of temperature schedule and atmosphere. These considerations are essential
since improving the final density by a few percentage points closer to 100% TD, and
reducing the average grain size, can result in a double or even triple digit percentage
increase in the mechanical properties. Furthermore, a high surface roughness is also
undesirable, first for aesthetic reasons, and second because surface features may ini­
tiate the formation of cracks under mechanical load, thus resulting in significantly
lower elastic modulus, flexural strength, and hardness.
   Ideally, ceramic parts produced by AM should be fully dense and have a fine
microstructure and a low surface roughness without the need for additional pres­
sure-assisted densification and surface modification, since these extra steps signifi­
cantly increase manufacturing complexity, time, and costs. Fully dense ceramics
were demonstrated using single-step AM processes, dLS and DED, although in both
cases careful consideration of material selection by choosing eutectic ratios of oxide
ceramics was necessary to produce crack-free dense parts. Both processes, however,
currently come with severe limitations regarding part size, as well as extremely high
surface roughness for dLS and limited geometrical complexity for DED.
  Some multi-step AM processes, followed by a suitable pressureless sintering, may
already enable the production of complex-shaped, crack-free, near-fully dense parts
with specific ceramic materials, such as vat photopolymerization of alumina and
material extrusion of silicon nitride, alumina, or zirconia. Other multi-step AM pro­
cesses would result in porous structures that require additional densification steps to
increase the density. For instance, while Costakis et al. (2016) could produce 98%
dense alumina samples using DIW followed by pressureless sintering, boron carbide
parts made using the same process reached only 82% TD without post-AM densifi­
cation (Rueschhoff et al., 2016, and Costakis et al., 2016). Therefore, in the current
context of ceramics AM, it remains essential to consider and investigate post-den­
sification methods and surface modification post-processing to produce highly
dense ceramic components with a suitable microstructure and the desired surface
roughness.

8.3.7   Printed Part Manufacturing Costs of AMC Technologies﻿

Costs related to the time taken by equipment, materials, pre-processing, process­
ing, and post-processing must be considered. Equipment costs include the purchase
price of the AM equipment, running costs (electricity, gases), and maintenance
charges from the equipment manufacturer. Materials costs include the price of feed­
stock materials as well as additional pre-processing costs for material preparation.
Processing costs depend mostly on whether costly equipment is required to run the
process, such as high-power lasers and inert gases. Finally, post-processing costs can
amount to a significant share of the total production costs due to high-temperature
heat treatments for debinding and sintering, as well as potential consolidation pro­
cesses such as cold isostatic pressing or HIP, and machining or polishing steps. Such
calculations are difficult to run accurately, especially so in AMC.
   For instance, while DIW is a relatively low-cost process overall, it still requires
post-processing heat-treatment at high temperature to sinter ceramic parts to full

Challenges, Comparison, and Process Selection Regarding AMC            239

density, which can become relatively expensive for some advanced ceramics, such as
high melting point carbides, requiring inert gas flow in furnace chambers and tem­
peratures more than 2000°C. On the other hand, dLS is in theory a significantly more
expensive process due to the use of high-power lasers and argon gas, but post-sinter­
ing would typically not be required since parts are already sintered to full-density
in-situ. Therefore, the time saved and lower number of post-processing steps may in
fact result in overall manufacturing cost savings. It thus becomes obvious that esti­
mating and contrasting the overall manufacturing costs of each process is a difficult
task, and further research dedicated to this topic is required.
   Accordingly, cost savings are one of the most important potential high-value
upside of AM for the ceramic industry. The mold-less nature of AM means that
substantial cost savings can be made on the manufacture of advanced ceramic com­
ponents, especially in the case of low-volume production. Negative AM, previously
discussed in CH2, also provides the ability to reduce production costs by 3D printing
molds for ceramic casting, thus lowering the costs and shortening the lead times
associated with manufacturing investment casting or gel-casting molds.
   In the long run, if single-step AM processes can be enhanced to match the per­
formance and reliability of multi-step AM and traditional ceramic forming methods,
they would likely become the dominant approach for producing functional advanced
ceramic parts, offering substantial time and cost savings. However, such develop­
ments are unlikely to occur in the near future due to the currently limited choice of
suitable ceramic materials, low performance of single-step AM technologies, and
the limited understanding of the science underlying these processes (collected by
Lakhdar et al., 2021).


8.4  REVIEW QUESTIONS

8.4.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. How does the printing speed of the additive manufacturing (AM) pro­
      cess affect the quality of advanced ceramic parts?
     Answer: Printing speed plays a big role in the final quality of ceramic
      parts. When printing too quickly, there’s a higher chance of defects like
      cracks, poor bonding between layers, or thermal stress. Ceramics are espe­
      cially sensitive to rapid changes in temperature. On the other hand, slower
      printing allows for better control over heating and cooling, which generally
     improves quality – but it also means longer production times and reduced
      efficiency.
   2. How does the thermal conductivity of ceramics affect AM in single-step
     processes?
     Answer: Ceramics typically have low thermal conductivity, which means
      heat doesn’t spread evenly during printing. This can create sharp tempera­
      ture differences in the material, leading to stress, warping, or cracking.
     Managing these temperature gradients is essential to maintain the integrity
      of the printed part.

240240           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   3. How  does  the  brittleness  of  ceramics  impact  the  handling  of
    AM-produced parts?
     Answer: Ceramics are naturally brittle, so they can easily crack or break –
      especially during or right after printing, when the parts are still fragile.
     This brittleness demands extra care during handling and often influences
      the design to avoid stress points that could cause failure.
   4. What are the primary challenges in applying additive manufacturing
    (AM) to advanced ceramics?
     Answer: Working with ceramics in AM presents several challenges. It’s dif­
       ficult to achieve high material density and maintain strength, and cracking
     can be a common issue during the build. Surface finish quality is another
      hurdle. Additionally, sintering – an essential step for ceramics – is tricky to
      control in AM setups, making the process more complex overall.
   5. How does selective laser sintering (SLS) compare with direct inkjet
     printing (DIP) for advanced ceramic fabrication?
     Answer: SLS uses powerful lasers to fuse ceramic powders layer by layer.
        It’s great for precision and part density but requires a tightly controlled envi­
     ronment and can be costly. DIP, by contrast, uses inkjet heads to deposit
     ceramic slurry, which makes it more flexible for complex shapes. However,
         it may not deliver the same resolution or density as SLS.
   6. In AMC, what are the disadvantages of slurry-LS compared to
     slurry-BJ?
     Answer: Slurry-LS relies on lasers and often requires an inert atmosphere,
     making it more expensive and complex. It also poses more health and safety
      challenges. In contrast, slurry-BJ (binder jetting) can use multiple nozzles to
     speed up the process, whereas adding multiple lasers in slurry-LS is techni­
      cally challenging and costly. Plus, how ceramics interact with lasers varies
     a lot depending on the material, which can affect how well slurry-LS works
      for different ceramics.
    7. What is the most significant advantage of direct laser sintering (dLS)
     over other ceramic AM processes?
     Answer: The main advantage of dLS is its single-step nature – it directly
     melts and sinters the ceramic material as it prints, eliminating the need
      for time-consuming post-processing steps like thermal debinding and
     furnace sintering. This makes the process faster and more streamlined
     compared to most other ceramic AM methods. However, the process
     comes with challenges. Thermal stresses during printing often lead to
     cracking and porosity, which so far has prevented the production of large,
     monolithic ceramic parts. dLS has mainly been demonstrated with cer­
      tain oxide ceramics and specific blends like eutectic Al 2 O 3 – ZrO 2 . But
      for high-performance ceramics with very high melting points or poor
      resistance to thermal gradients, dLS remains difficult due to material
      limitations.

Despite their many advantageous physicochemical and thermomechanical prop­
erties, nearly all advanced ceramic materials are plagued by the same drawback:
ceramics are brittle materials that desperately lack toughness and are prone to cat­
astrophic brittle failure. This critical limitation is one of the main factors that have
prevented advanced ceramics from replacing their more ductile metallic counter­
parts in most engineering applications. Ceramic matrix composites (CMCs) are com­
posite materials where ceramic reinforcements, such as continuous fibers, whiskers,
or nanoparticles, are embedded into a ceramic matrix phase; CMCs were developed
to enhance the properties of single-phase ceramics and address their lack of reliabil­
ity. Some CMCs have significantly better thermomechanical properties than their
single-phase ceramic counterpart, in particular, improved thermal shock resistance
and increased fracture toughness with higher elongation to rupture, leading to uses
as thermos-structural components for high-performance applications in demanding
service conditions. CMCs have great potential for applications in various fields such
as aircraft (combustion chambers, turbine blades), aerospace (aircraft surface heat
shields, rocket nozzles), military (nose cones and missile nozzles), and other fields
(Guo et al., 2009 and Deng et al., 2016), due to their excellent high-temperature per­
formance and low density.

9.1  CLASSIFICATION OF COMPOSITES BASED
   ON THEIR MATRIX MATERIAL

A composite material consists of two phases: a primary phase and a secondary phase.
The primary phase forms the matrix within which the secondary phase is embedded.
The embedded phase is sometimes referred to as a reinforcing agent (or similar term)
because it usually strengthens the composite. The reinforcing phase may be in the
form of fibers, particles, or various other geometries. The phases are generally insol­
uble in each other, but strong adhesion must exist at their interfaces.
  The matrix phase can be polymers, metals, or ceramics. The secondary phase
may also be one of the three basic materials, or it may be an element such as carbon
or boron. Based on the matrix material, Figure 9.1 classifies the composites into
polymer matrix composites (PMCs), metal matrix composites (MMCs), and CMCs.

9.1.1   Polymer Matrix Composites﻿

PMCs consist of a polymer matrix reinforced with high-strength fibers, designed
to transfer loads between the matrix and fibers. These composites offer several

and providing superior strength and rigidity along the direction of reinforcement.
Their diverse conventional manufacturing techniques include reaction molding, fila­

PMCs provide a high strength-to-weight ratio, strong fatigue resistance, inherent
resistance to corrosion, good electrical and thermal insulation qualities, and the abil­

of design choices. PMCs are suited for use in locations where they may be subjected
to severe chemicals because they have good chemical resistance, excellent impact
resistance, and a low coefficient of thermal expansion.
  PMCs have a variety of uses because of their characteristics. PMCs are exten­
sively used in the aerospace and aviation industries to create structural components
such as wings, fuselages, engine parts, and rotor blades because of their excellent
strength-to-weight ratio and fatigue resistance. In the automotive sector, PMCs are
utilized for various purposes, including structural parts, body panels, and interior
components. PMCs are also used as reinforcing elements to strengthen and extend
the life of concrete structures. Additionally, they are used to build facades, bridges,
and other structural elements. PMCs are extensively used in the marine industry to
construct boat hulls and other watercraft parts. Given that they are biocompatible,
solid, and effectively resist fatigue, PMCs are used in medical applications like den­
tal implants and prosthetic limbs.

9.1.2   Metal Matrix Composites﻿

This is a material class composed of a metal matrix reinforced by one or more sec­
ondary phases such as fibers, particles, or whiskers. These reinforcements increase
the base metals’ mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties, resulting in a com­
posite material with superior performance. MMCs have a range of attractive qual­
ities that make them useful in a variety of applications. They also have excellent
thermal conductivity, superior thermal stability, and customization capacity for spe­
cific purposes. Titanium–matrix composites, reinforced with either boron or silicon

9.1.3   Ceramic Matrix Composites﻿

The matrix material and reinforcing material are the two primary components of
CMCs. Each element is critical in determining the composites’ characteristics and
performance in achieving superior mechanical and thermal performance (Li, 2020).

9.1.3.1   Types of Ceramic Matrices and Their Properties
The selection of CMCs depends on the matrix material, which is categorized into
oxide and non-oxide-based matrices, as shown in Figure 9.2. Ceramic matrix mate­
rials, such as silicon carbide (SiC), aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3), and zirconium oxide
(ZrO2), are renowned for the unique properties that make them suitable for use in
high-temperature and harsh environments. These materials offer a combination of
high strength, thermal stability, and resistance to oxidation and corrosion, which are
crucial for applications in aerospace, automotive, and heavy industries.
   Silicon carbide (SiC)  is one of the most valuable ceramic matrices due to
its high thermal conductivity and melting point. These properties are ideal for

high-temperature applications such as gas turbine hot sections and rocket engine
components. Additionally, SiC exhibits low thermal expansion and high hardness,
enabling structural stability under extreme conditions. The oxidation resistance fur­
ther enhances the durability of SiC, making it a superior material for applications
requiring thermal and corrosion resistance. Reinforcement of SiC matrices with
fibers enhances toughness, making it suitable for applications demanding strength
and resistance to mechanical damage.
  Aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3), or alumina, is another widely used ceramic matrix
material. Its characteristics include high hardness, exceptional wear resistance, and
good thermal stability. These properties make Al 2 O 3 ideal for applications requiring
high wear resistance, such as cutting tools and abrasion-resistant coatings. Moreover,
its excellent electrical insulation properties provide additional advantages in elec­
tronic and insulation applications. Al 2 O 3  is often reinforced with materials such
as silicon carbide to enhance its toughness, enabling its use under high-pressure
conditions.
  Zirconium oxide (ZrO2), known for its high fracture toughness and thermal
stability, is widely employed in dental applications and as thermal barrier coat­
ings. ZrO2 can withstand high temperatures and has low thermal conductivity,
making it ideal for thermal insulation materials. Another advantage of ZrO2  is
its ability to undergo phase transformations at high temperatures, which adds to
its toughness and resistance to cracking under mechanical stress (Liu et al., 2024
and Lei et al., 2022). Stabilizers like Yttria are often added to ZrO2 to enhance its
properties further, allowing it to perform well in extreme environments. Table 9.1

9.2  AM OF CMCS

9.2.1  Basic Differences between AMCs and AM-CMCs Technologies﻿

Advanced Ceramics are focusing on achieving high purity, strength, and thermal
properties from a single ceramic material, typically requiring a more straightfor­
ward AM process, but with post-processing for density and surface finish. CMCs,
on the other hand, are designed to enhance mechanical performance by incorporat­
ing reinforcing fibers, making the AM process more complex due to fiber integra­
tion, and often requiring specialized processing steps for bonding the fibers within
the matrix. The production of advanced ceramics and ceramic-based composites
(CMCs) through additive manufacturing (AM) technologies involves distinct pro­
cesses and considerations. Here’s a summary of the basic differences between both
products:

    1. Material Composition:
       •  Compositions of AMC are typically made from pure ceramic materials
           like alumina (Al 2 O 3), zirconia (ZrO2), silicon carbide (SiC), or other
          single-phase ceramics; the focus is often on achieving high strength,
        wear resistance, thermal stability, and electrical properties in a pure
         ceramic form.
       •  The compositions of CMCs consist of ceramic matrices reinforced with
           fibers (often made of carbon, silicon carbide, or other ceramic mate­
            rials). The fibers provide additional mechanical strength and fracture
         toughness, and the focus is on improving properties like toughness,
        damage tolerance, and the ability to withstand high temperatures or
         extreme conditions.
    2. Process Characteristics:
       •  Common AM techniques of AMCs include selective laser sintering
         (SLS), direct ink writing (DIW), stereolithography (SLA), and binder
           jetting (BJ) for ceramics. After printing, advanced ceramics often
          require additional sintering and sometimes polishing or machining to
         achieve the desired density, surface finish, and properties.
       •  CMCs can be produced using similar AM methods (e.g., SLS, BJ, and
        DIW), but with additional steps to incorporate the fiber reinforcement
          (often done through pre-forming or composite processing). The fibers
         need to be properly embedded within the ceramic matrix during the AM
          process, which can be more challenging due to the differences in the
          rheological properties of ceramic slurries and fiber orientations. Finally,
          post-processing of CMCs typically undergoes densification processes
           like chemical vapor infiltration (CVI) or hot isostatic pressing (HIP) to
         improve the matrix–fiber bonding and achieve the desired mechanical
          properties.
    3. Property Enhancements:
       •  For advanced ceramics, the aim is often to achieve high hardness, wear
           resistance, electrical insulation, or high-temperature resistance. The

250           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

          material is typically brittle, and the primary concern is achieving high
          density and uniformity. The design considerations for advanced ceram­
           ics emphasize the material’s intrinsic properties without the need for
          additional strengthening phases.
       •  CMCs are designed to be tougher and more damage-resistant than pure
         ceramics by incorporating fiber reinforcement. The fibers improve the
          material’s ability to resist crack propagation, making  it suitable for
          applications requiring high strength and damage tolerance at elevated
          temperatures. The design considerations of CMCs focus on achieving
         optimal fiber orientation, matrix–fiber bonding, and overall mechanical
         performance, especially in applications like aerospace or automotive
         components.
   4. Applications:
       •  Advanced Ceramics are applied in fields requiring high-performance
          wear-resistant parts, thermal insulators, electronic components, cutting
           tools, and biomedical devices.
       •  CMCs are applied in fields requiring high-temperature structural com­
         ponents (e.g., turbine blades, aerospace parts), where resistance to ther­
        mal shock, high-temperature strength, and toughness are crucial.
   5. Manufacturing Complexity:
       •  Advanced ceramics are less complex (relatively straightforward) to pro­
         duce, as there is no need for fiber integration or complex composite pro­
          cessing steps. However, achieving the desired density and mechanical
          properties without porosity can be a challenge, requiring precise control
         over sintering and printing conditions.
       •  CMCs are more complex due to the need to integrate reinforce­
        ment fibers effectively and manage the matrix–fiber interface. The
         choice of fiber, matrix material, and reinforcement configuration can
        be critical. However, ensuring good fiber distribution, maintaining
         fiber–matrix bonding, and dealing with the different thermal expan­
         sion properties of the matrix and reinforcement materials represent
         challenges.
   6. Manufacturing Cost:
       •  Adding the cost factor into the comparison between advanced ceramics
        and CMCs produced via AM is crucial. Based on available research and

9.2.2   Challenges in Producing CMCs through AM Processes﻿

Producing CMCs through AM processes presents several key challenges:

    1. Fiber Distribution and Alignment: Achieving a uniform distribution of
      reinforcing fibers within the ceramic matrix is difficult. The alignment and
      orientation of fibers are critical for the material’s strength and performance,
     and controlling this during AM is challenging, especially with complex
      geometries.
    2. Porosity Control: AM processes often introduce porosity due to incomplete
      densification or non-uniform heating, which can compromise the mechan­
       ical properties and overall performance of CMCs, particularly under high-
       stress conditions.
    3. Bonding between Fibers and Matrix: Ensuring proper bonding between
      the ceramic matrix and the reinforcing fibers is a significant challenge. Inad­
      equate bonding can lead to weak points in the material, reducing its strength
     and thermal stability.
    4. Material Compatibility: Many AM techniques use different types of feed­
      stock materials that may not be fully compatible with each other, leading to
       difficulties in achieving desired properties such as high temperature resis­
      tance or durability in the final CMC part.

252           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   5. Thermal Management: CMCs typically operate under extreme thermal
      conditions. During AM, controlling the heat flow and thermal gradients is
      crucial to avoid cracking, distortion, or phase transformation of the ceramic
      materials.
   6. Complexity in Process Control: AM of CMCs often requires precise con­
       trol over multiple parameters (e.g., temperature, deposition rate, layer thick­
      ness) to ensure the desired microstructure and mechanical properties are
      achieved. Any variation can affect the quality of the composite.
    7. Post-Processing Requirements: CMCs often require extensive post-pro­
      cessing steps like sintering or infiltration to achieve full densification and
     optimize the fiber–matrix interaction. These post-processing steps can be
     time-consuming and challenging to integrate with AM workflows.

9.2.3  AM Viable Techniques for Fiber Reinforced CMCs﻿

Since its invention, AM has been used to fabricate polymers, metals, ceramics, com­
posites, and others. Compared to polymers and metals, the application of 3D printing
to the production of ceramics and CMCs is still in an early stage. Following the tech­
nology roadmaps of AM, these techniques can be described as follows (Sun Jinxing,
Ye Daoron et al., 2022):

   • SLA
   • SLS
   •  Laminated object manufacturing
   •  Inkjet printing (IJP) and BJ
   •  Laser engineered net shaping (LENS)
   • DIW

All these techniques have been comprehensively reviewed to serve as a simplified
introduction to AM viable CMC techniques.
   However, Wang et al. (2022) had classified AM technologies to prepare FRCMCs
into four categories, which are commonly used (Figure 9.4):

   •  Vat photopolymerization (VP) (SLA and digital light processing (DLP))
   •  Powder bed fusion (PBF) (usually including SLS and selective laser melting
     (SLM))
   •  BJ
   •  Material extrusion (ME) (usually including fused deposition modeling
     (FDM), extrusion free forming (EFF), and DIW)

9.2.3.1   Stereolithography
SLA is one of the earliest and most extensively studied technologies within the
domain of AM. It operates on the principle of photopolymerization, wherein a pho­
tosensitive material – typically a liquid photopolymer resin – is selectively cured by
light in a layer-by-layer fashion to form a three-dimensional object. SL technology
primarily comprises two variants: SLA apparatus, illustrated in Figure 9.4a, and

DLP, shown in Figure 9.4b. Both techniques utilize light-induced polymerization to
fabricate complex geometries with high resolution. A key advantage of SL lies in its
exceptional dimensional accuracy and surface quality, making it particularly suitable
for applications requiring fine detail and precision.
  SL is mainly used for the fabrication of fiber-reinforced oxide CMCs, such as
short fiber-reinforced Al 2 O 3 CMCs, short fiber-reinforced SiO2 CMCs, and contin­
uous fiber-reinforced ZrO2 CMCs (Sun JX and Yu SX et al., 2022). However, it is
difficult to prepare FRCMC components by SL when the colors of ceramic powders
and fibers are darker due to the high absorbance of ceramic powders and fibers at
ultraviolet wavelengths. The SLA-based AM technique is one of the most popular
AM processes, capable of producing CMCs thanks to its excellent printing accuracy
and surface finish, as well as relatively fast build speed. However, ceramic and rein­
forcement materials with high refractive index and light absorption, such as boron
carbide (B4 C) and graphene (G), as well as carbon nanotubes (CNTs), are more chal­
lenging to fabricate as these materials allow low cure depth under UV exposure.
Furthermore, a large amount of organic can result in significant volume shrinkage
and therefore lead to part deformation and cracking during debinding. Therefore,
it is challenging to make thick-walled parts without excessive porosity or cracking.

9.2.3.2  Powder Bed Fusion
SLS represents one of the most extensively utilized PBF AM technologies for the
fabrication of CMCs. As depicted in Figure 9.4c, SLS employs a high-power laser –
typically a carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) laser – as the energy source to selectively scan and
fuse powder particles according to cross-sectional data derived from a digital model.

254           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

The process is carried out in a layer-by-layer manner, wherein each layer of powder is
selectively sintered to form the desired geometry. The unsintered powder surround­
ing the scanned regions serves as a self-supporting medium, which eliminates the
need for additional support structures and facilitates the fabrication of parts with
complex and intricate geometries.
   However, due to the existence of the heat-affected zone, the surface of the CMCs
fabricated by SLS is rougher and the accuracy is lower compared with SLA. And, it
should be pointed out that the melting points of ceramics are too high for SLS tech­
nology. Most importantly, due to the large temperature gradient and thermal stress
during the laser sintering process, it is easy to induce defects and cracks into the final
CMC products. At present, SLS is mainly used to fabricate short fiber-reinforced
non-oxide (such as SiC and Si 3 N 4) CMCs.
  The variant of SLS, SLM, is regarded as a direct AM process, in which the
ceramic part can be obtained by direct laser melting without debinding and sin­
tering. However, the mechanical properties of the SLM-manufactured parts are
not comparable to those obtained by indirect AM techniques since ceramics are
subject to cracking because ceramics have high melting points, low thermal shock
resistance, and low thermal conductivity (Zhang and Jung, 2018). SLS is one of the
most established due to its high potential for the manufacturing of a wide range of
CMC parts. However, the components prepared by SLS still exhibit high porosity,
leading to relatively low densities and poor mechanical properties, and it has lim­
ited part resolution, compared to SLA. Additionally, the SLS process is relatively
fast because of the high-layer thickness printing. The advantages offer SLS make
it a robust AM technique for producing porous composite parts, for example, in
the application of bone scaffolds, catalyst supports, and heat exchangers (Shuai
et al., 2014).

9.2.3.3  Binder Jetting
BJ is a powder bed-based AM technique that, unlike SLS, uses a liquid binder
deposited by an inkjet print head to selectively bond powder particles, as shown
in Figure 9.4d. Successive layers are joined through binder infiltration, forming a
three-dimensional structure without the application of heat. As BJ does not involve
powder melting, it avoids residual stress formation, offering improved dimensional
stability. The advantages of BJ are very close to those of SLS, such as fast build
speed, the lack of a need for a support structure, easy to produce porous structures,
a wide range of materials choices, and a large printing envelope. However, the CMC
produced by BJ is porous and has relatively low geometric accuracy due to low pow­
der packing density. Hence, post-densification processes are needed. Materials used
in BJ are mostly ceramics and reinforcements, such as chopped fibers, CNT, and par­
ticulates. Currently, BJ has been successfully used to fabricate short fiber-reinforced
Al 2 O 3 CMCs (Mei et al., 2019).

9.2.3.4   Material Extrusion
ME is among the earliest and most widely adopted AM techniques. The process
involves the extrusion of semi-fluid feedstocks through a nozzle, followed by layer-
by-layer deposition and solidification to form three-dimensional green bodies.

AM of Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs)                             255

   In  the  context  of  fabricating  fiber-reinforced  ceramic  matrix  composites
(FRCMCs), ME technologies are primarily categorized based on the physical form
of the feedstock material:

   •  Wire-based feedstocks, as utilized in FDM
   •  Paste-based feedstocks, employed in techniques such as EFF and DIW

DIW, also known as robocasting, relies on the extrusion of a ceramic paste or a ceram­
ic-loaded filament from a small nozzle through layer-by-layer deposition. The DIW
system is significantly cheaper and able to build continuous CMCs owing to the relative
simplicity of the setup and elimination of an expensive laser source. The advantage of
DIW lies in its flexible materials requirements, and it offers the broadest spectrum of
printable materials at present. Moreover, the incorporation of a reinforcement phase
such as chopped fibers can be controlled in terms of their orientation via optimizing the
extrusion parameters. However, the quality and resolution of the parts are much lower
than those produced by SLA. The introduction of fillers raises the issue of nozzle clog­
ging, which also limits the filler content of the resultant composites (Croom et al., 2021).
  The most outstanding advantage of ME technologies is their wide range of raw
materials. At present, ME technologies have been used to fabricate short fiber-rein­
forced silicate composites, short fiber-reinforced SiC CMCs. It should be pointed out
that ME technology is currently the only AM technology that can integrate continu­
ous fiber-reinforced CMCs.
   Distinct from other ME methods, FDM relies on thermal processing to induce
material fluidity. In this technique, a thermoplastic filament is heated until molten,
enabling its extrusion through a nozzle. Upon deposition, the material undergoes
rapid cooling, which increases its viscosity and leads to solidification (Figure 9.4e).
In contrast, other ME approaches – such as extrusion free-forming or DIW – do not
rely on thermal transitions for solidification. Instead, these methods utilize alterna­
tive mechanisms such as solvent evaporation, chemical curing, drying, or dehydra­
tion to achieve structural integrity (Figure 9.4f). As illustrated in Figure 9.5, during

However, there is not a “best overall” ceramic AM technique but rather the most

for CMCs and end-use applications should be carefully considered, based on the
significant advantages and limitations, as well as issues such as build volume and
resolution. In general, the latter contradictory relation between build volume and res­

requires reducing the build volume to a smaller one. SLM and LENS do not involve
time-consuming thermal treatment, yet the extreme temperature gradients prevent
the fabrication of highly dense parts. Other 3D printing methods, such as DIW, IJP,
and BJ, allow the broadest spectrum of printable materials selection. Therefore, for
specified ceramic materials and applications, the selection of the best AM candi­
dates should be based on a comprehensive investigation of all AM techniques.

9.2.4   Indirect AM and Direct AM of FRCMCs﻿

Currently, there are usually two types of reported AM technologies for FRCMCs:
indirect AM and direct AM. As shown in Figure 9.7a, the indirect AM always con­
sists of three main steps:

    •  Preparation of the templates (including ceramic template and fiber template)
     by common AM technologies
    •  Fabrication of the composite green part by traditional methods (including
      slurry replication, CVI, PIP, and LSI)
    •  Debinding and sintering of FRCMCs to obtain the final body

Different from indirect AM, as illustrated in Figure 9.7b, direct AM of FRCMCs
can usually be divided into two main steps, including fabrication of the composite
green part by AM, debinding, and sintering. Whether there is debinding or sintering
mainly depends on which AM technology is used.
   Considerable progress and breakthroughs have been made in the AM of FRCMCs.
Typical short fiber-reinforced oxide CMCs, such as Al 2 O 3 , SiO2 , and matrix com­
posites; short fiber-reinforced non-oxide CMCs, such as SiC and SiCN ; and con­
tinuous fiber-reinforced CMCs such as ZrO2 and SiC have been reported using
different AM technologies, Mei et al. (2019) and Yunus et al. (2017).
   In the following two sections, the basic concept, differences, challenges, and
advantages of indirect AM and direct AM techniques are described.

9.2.4.1   Indirect AM of FRCMCs
Indirect AM for FRCMCs is a sophisticated process that combines the advantages of
AM with traditional ceramics and composite manufacturing techniques. This hybrid
approach allows for the production of complex parts with a high degree of design
freedom, tailored material properties, and high performance, especially in high-tem­
perature and mechanical applications.

9.2.4.1.1  Indirect AM Process for CMCs Step-by-Step
    1. The first step in indirect AM is to create a sacrificial mold or preform. This
     mold is crucial because it serves as the temporary structure in which the
       fibers and ceramic matrix will be placed and consolidated. The mold is
       later removed through processes like thermal degradation, dissolution, or
     combustion.
    2. AM, such as SLA, FDM, or BJ, is typically used to create this mold. The
     advantage of using 3D printing here is that it allows for the creation of
      highly intricate, complex geometries, which would be difficult or impossi­
      ble to achieve through traditional mold-making methods. The material for
      the mold is often polymeric, wax, or even metal in some cases. The choice
      of material is important because it must be easily removable without affect­
      ing the final FRCMC part. For example, wax molds can be melted away,
     while polymers may be dissolved in a chemical solvent. The key benefit of
      using AM for mold creation is the ability to fabricate complex internal fea­
       tures, channels, and intricate designs, which are not possible with traditional
     molding techniques. This ability to print hollow structures or parts with
      internal reinforcements significantly enhances the design freedom available
      for the final composite part.
    3. The next step is to introduce fibers (typically carbon, glass, or ceramic
       fibers) into the mold. The fibers provide enhanced mechanical properties
     such as strength, stiffness, and thermal resistance. The fibers are aligned in
      specific directions depending on the design requirements of the final part,
      ensuring that the material properties are tailored to meet the needs of the
      application. The alignment and distribution of fibers within the matrix is
     a crucial step. The fiber network is typically added manually or through
     automated systems like fiber placement machines. In some cases, this step
    may involve weaving or braiding fibers into a preform structure that is then
      placed into the mold. The fibers’ orientation can be optimized to resist spe­
       cific types of stresses (e.g., tensile, compressive, shear).
    4. Once the fibers are placed in the mold, a ceramic slurry or powder is
     introduced to form the matrix that will hold the fibers in place and pro­
      vide the final material properties (e.g., high-temperature stability, wear
      resistance). The ceramic matrix can consist of various ceramic materi­
      als like silicon carbide (SiC), alumina (Al 2 O 3), zirconia (ZrO2), or other
     advanced ceramics. These materials are chosen for their excellent thermal
      properties, chemical stability, and high mechanical strength at elevated
      temperatures.

260           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

    5. The infiltration of the ceramic matrix can occur via several techniques:
       •   Slip Casting: The fibers in the mold are impregnated with a ceramic
          slurry (a suspension of ceramic powder and liquid), which is then
         allowed to set or dry. After drying, the slurry forms a green body that
         encapsulates the fibers.
       •  Powder Injection Molding: In this process, ceramic powder mixed with
         a binder is injected into the mold, where it is consolidated around the
            fibers. The binder helps hold the matrix in place before it is sintered and
         removed.
       •  Sol–Gel Process : A solution or gel-like precursor to the ceramic matrix
            is applied to the fibers. This precursor is then dried and subjected to heat
          treatment to form the final ceramic matrix.
   6. After the ceramic matrix  is applied, the mold and composite material
     undergo a curing or drying process to harden the ceramic matrix and help
      the binder set. This step solidifies the matrix and ensures good bonding
     between the fibers and the ceramic material.
    7. The sacrificial mold, which was used to shape the FRCMC part, must now
     be removed. This step is critical because the mold material must not inter­
      fere with the final part’s structure or properties.
    Mold Removal Methods:
       •  Burnout: If the mold is made of wax or polymeric materials, it can be
         burned out in a furnace at high temperatures. This allows the mold to
        decompose and leave behind only the FRCMC structure.
       •  Chemical Dissolution: In some cases, the mold may be made from a
          material that can be dissolved in a chemical solvent. This is particularly
          useful when the mold material is soluble in specific chemicals without
          affecting the ceramic matrix.
       •  Thermal Decomposition: For some mold materials, the mold material
            is broken down at high temperatures, leaving only the desired ceramic
          fiber-reinforced part behind.
   8. Post-Processing Step:
            Once the mold has been removed, the composite part may undergo sinter­
      ing. Sintering involves heating the part to a temperature where the ceramic
      particles begin to bond and densify, forming a strong, solid structure.
            High-Temperature Sintering: During sintering, the ceramic matrix
       is fired at high temperatures, typically in a kiln or furnace, to consolidate
      the particles and eliminate any remaining binder. This process increases
      the part’s density and strength and enhances its thermal and mechanical
      properties.
             After sintering, the part may require further processing to meet the final
      specifications. These post-processing steps are typically conventional tech­
      niques used in ceramic manufacturing.
            Machining: If the part requires precise dimensions or surface finishes, it
    may undergo grinding, milling, or polishing to achieve the desired geometry
     and surface quality.

AM of Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs)                             261

             Coating: Sometimes, FRCMCs undergo additional surface treatments or
      coatings to improve properties like wear resistance, oxidation resistance,
      or to enhance thermal shock resistance. Coatings may also be applied to
     improve the interface between the ceramic matrix and the fibers.

Advantages of Indirect AM for FRCMCs:

    1. Complex Geometry: Indirect AM enables the creation of complex and
       intricate structures with internal features that would be challenging or
      expensive to produce using traditional methods.
   2. Tailored Properties: By carefully controlling the fiber orientation, matrix
      composition, and processing conditions, indirect AM allows for the custom­
      ization of material properties (such as strength, thermal conductivity, and
      resistance to wear).
    3. Material Efficiency: The use of a sacrificial mold reduces material waste
     compared to traditional molding techniques, as only the necessary material
       is used in creating the final part.
    4. Design Flexibility: Since the mold is 3D printed, designers have signifi­
      cant flexibility in terms of the shapes and geometries that can be produced,
      enabling optimization for weight, strength, and other performance factors.

Challenges of Indirect AM for FRCMCs:

    1. Process Complexity: The multi-step process, involving mold creation,
       fiber placement, matrix infiltration, mold removal, and sintering, can be
     time-consuming and complex.
    2. Material Compatibility: The choice of mold material must be compatible
     with the ceramic matrix and fiber materials, and it must be easily removable
      without damaging the final part.
    3. Cost: While the process can be cost-effective for complex geometries, the
     use of high-temperature processing and the need for specialized equipment
        (e.g., furnaces for sintering) can make it more expensive than direct meth­
     ods in certain cases.

Finally, indirect AM for FRCMCs is a versatile and effective approach for producing
high-performance parts with complex geometries. The process combines the flexibil­
ity of AM with traditional ceramic and composite processing techniques, resulting in
materials that are optimized for high-strength, high-temperature applications, with
the ability to tailor the structure and properties to meet specific needs.

9.2.4.2   Direct AM of FRCMCs
Direct AM of FRCMCs is an advanced manufacturing technique that eliminates the
need for a sacrificial mold and directly builds the final part layer by layer. Unlike
indirect AM, which involves creating a mold and then adding fiber reinforcement and
ceramic matrix material, direct AM allows for the direct deposition of ceramic and
fiber materials into the desired shape.

262           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   This method integrates the deposition of the ceramic matrix and fiber reinforce­
ment in a single, continuous process. It offers significant advantages, such as reduced
process complexity, increased design flexibility, and the ability to create parts with
highly customized material properties.

Considerations Regarding the Direct AM Process for FRCMCs:

    1. Material Preparation
      In direct AM for FRCMCs, the material preparation is a crucial first step.
     Unlike traditional ceramics, FRCMCs require the integration of fibers (e.g.,
     carbon fibers, glass fibers, ceramic fibers) and ceramic matrices (e.g., sili­
     con carbide, alumina, zirconia) in a form that can be deposited by an AM
      process.
           Fiber Selection: Fibers provide the primary reinforcement for the com­
      posite material, improving its mechanical properties such as strength, tough­
      ness, and resistance to thermal shock. The fibers are selected based on the
      required performance characteristics for the specific application. Common
      fibers used include carbon fibers (for high thermal and mechanical perfor­
     mance) and ceramic fibers (for applications requiring high temperature
      resistance).
           Ceramic Matrix Selection: Ceramic materials are chosen based on the
      application’s temperature, chemical, and mechanical requirements. These
    may include silicon carbide (SiC) , alumina (Al 2 O 3) , zirconia (ZrO2) , or
      other advanced ceramics.
           Feedstock Materials: In some direct AM techniques, the feedstock is
     a mixture of ceramic powders, fibers, and binders (e.g., resins, polymers)
      or a slurry. These feedstocks must have the right rheological properties to
     be extruded, printed, or deposited effectively. The feedstock must also be
      stable during processing to ensure good bonding between the fibers and the
     ceramic matrix.
   2. Direct AM Techniques Used for FRCMCs :
     There are various AM techniques that can be used to build up the FRCMCs
       directly, and each has its own advantages in terms of material control, res­
      olution, and application. Here are the main Direct AM techniques used for
    FRCMCs:
       a. DIW
       b.  Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF)
       c.  Direct energy deposition
   3. Sintering and Consolidation:
      After the fiber-reinforced ceramic part is built layer by layer, it needs to
     undergo sintering, Binder Removal, and Final Densification to achieve the
       final material properties:
       •   Sintering: This process involves heating the part to a temperature below
             its melting point, causing the ceramic particles to bond together and the
         matrix to densify. This is a crucial step because the sintering process
         determines the strength, density, and thermal properties of the FRCMC.

AM of Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs)                             263

       •  Binder Removal: In some cases, there may be a binder (e.g., polymer or
           resin) used in the feedstock material. This binder must be removed before
          the sintering process, usually through heating or chemical dissolution.
       •  Final Densification: Sintering further increases the density of the part
        and enhances the ceramic matrix, ensuring a strong bond between the
           fibers and the matrix. The fiber reinforcement helps to prevent crack
         propagation and improve the overall toughness of the material.
    4. Post-Processing and Surface Treatments:
      After sintering, the final part may undergo additional post-processing steps
      to optimize its performance:
       •  Machining: The ceramic matrix might be too hard to achieve specific
         dimensions or surface finishes directly after sintering. In such cases,
         machining, grinding, or polishing is used to refine the part.
       •  Coatings: In some applications, FRCMCs may require protective coat­
          ings for improved performance, such as oxidation resistance or wear
           resistance. Coatings may be applied by spraying, dipping, or chemical
         vapor deposition (CVD) processes.
       •  Heat Treatment: Some parts may undergo additional heat treatment to
          further optimize material properties, such as enhancing thermal shock
          resistance or increasing crystallization in the ceramic matrix.

Advantages of Direct AM for FRCMCs:

    1. Complex Geometries: Direct AM allows for the production of highly
     complex and intricate structures that are not feasible with traditional man­
      ufacturing techniques. It enables the creation of internal features, lattice
      structures, and optimized geometries that reduce weight while maintaining
      strength.
   2. Tailored Fiber Distribution: The ability to control the fiber orientation
     and distribution within the ceramic matrix allows for the creation of parts
     with highly customized mechanical properties. For example, fibers can be
      oriented in specific directions to resist particular stresses.
    3. Reduced Material Waste: Direct AM uses only the material required for
     each layer, reducing waste compared to traditional manufacturing methods,
     which often involve cutting away excess material.
    4. Speed and Efficiency: Direct AM can be faster and more efficient than tra­
      ditional methods, particularly for small to medium-scale production runs.
     This is especially important for complex or custom parts.
    5. Design Flexibility: Designers can easily iterate on part designs and make
      modifications without the need for new tooling or molds, which is a signifi­
      cant advantage in industries requiring rapid prototyping or custom parts.

Challenges of Direct AM for FRCMCs:

    1. Material Development: While many ceramic materials are amenable to
    AM, developing suitable feedstocks that can effectively combine fibers and
     ceramics in the required forms for direct AM is challenging. The material

264           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

     must have the right rheological properties for deposition and strong bonding
      capabilities.
   2. Post-Processing Requirements: Parts made via direct AM often require
      extensive post-processing, including sintering, binder removal, and some­
      times machining, which can add to the cost and time required to produce the
       final part.
    3. Limited Fiber Integration: Integrating fibers directly into the ceramic
     matrix during deposition is technically challenging. The fibers must be
      evenly distributed, aligned properly, and well-bonded to the ceramic matrix,
       all while maintaining the properties of both the fibers and the ceramic
      material.

Concluding, direct AM for FRCMCs is an advanced and highly versatile process
that allows for the direct fabrication of fiber-reinforced ceramic parts with complex
geometries and customized material properties. While it offers significant advantages
in terms of design flexibility, material efficiency, and reduced lead time, the process
also faces challenges in material development, fiber integration, and post-processing.
However, it holds great potential for industries requiring high-performance materials
with tailored properties, such as aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors.

9.2.5  CMCs and Their Reinforcement Categories﻿

The introduction of reinforcements into the ceramic matrix can be implemented at
different stages of the 3D printing process, including:

   •  At the beginning (e.g., mixing the reinforcement material with raw ceramic
      matrix material),
   •  After a medium stage (e.g., infiltration of ductile phase into the ceramic
     green or brown bodies), and
   •  In the end (e.g., interpenetrating with reinforcement material after the
     ceramic is sintered).

Accordingly, the final CMCs can exist in many forms, either topologically contin­
uous, such as interpenetrating phase composite (IPC), or discontinuous, such as a
discrete  particulate/whisker/fiber-reinforced  composite. For  particulate/whisker/
fiber-reinforced CMCs, the reinforcement material is typically mixed, in a state of
discontinuous distribution, with the ceramic matrix to be prepared as ink for 3D
printing. On the other hand, in the case of IPC, commonly, porous or cellular ceram­
ics are produced as a preform, and the voids or empty spaces are then filled with a
second material to form a ceramic composite.

9.2.5.1  Reinforcement Categories of CMCs
Although 3D printing of ceramics offers the possibilities to fabricate ceramic struc­
tures with highly complex geometries and interconnected pores, the brittleness prob­
lem still exists for 3D printed pure ceramics, whether dense or porous, since this is
an inherited drawback associated with the material. A general route to overcome

have specific mechanical properties. For example, graphene, a single layer of sp2

200 times larger than that of steel and a Young’s modulus of 1 TPa (Lin et al., 2015).

However, they can be used to reinforce ceramics to form Carb-CMCs as well.

      exhibit improved toughness and impact resistance compared to single-phase
      ceramics, which mainly depend on extrinsic toughening mechanisms such

      the second-phase ceramic has been widely examined primarily through
     homogenous mixing of the matrix and reinforcement ceramic raw material
     (Zhu et al., 2023).
   2. M-CMCs: M-CMCs have many advantages. For example, carbon fibers
      are incredibly strong and lightweight, leading to high strength-to-weight
      ratios in composite materials, and they are immune to corrosion, unlike
    many metals. Ceramic/carbon fiber composites are suitable for applications
      in corrosive environments. However, metals can provide better toughness
     and impact resistance compared to carbon fibers, which can be brittle. The
     mechanical properties of metals can be better matched to ceramics, leading
      to improved compatibility and reduced stress concentration at the interface
     between the two materials. Ceramic/metal composites are suitable for appli­
      cations where elevated temperatures are involved, such as aerospace propul­
      sion systems and certain industrial processes.
    3. P-CMCs: Toughening ceramic with metal usually gets high strength
     ceramic composites. However, the processes are commonly involved with
      high-temperature infiltration, which makes the process very complex to

      usually impregnated into the 3D-printed sintered ceramic scaffold to form

demonstrates unique properties such as very high thermal conductivity (above 5000

and lubricants, which on many occasions produce defects during sintering (Li et
al., 2021). These defects can be related to the evaporation of the aforementioned
additives, which leads to volumetric shrinkage and crack formation, considerably

graphene (in other words, graphene oxide (GO)) was proposed to prepare an aqueous
