(2017) formulated free additives pastes of diverse materials, based only on the use

has a great similarity to clay, including its viscoelastic behavior. Clay has excep­

any other natural material. The special combination of surface chemistry and the

not collapsing during the 3D object forming process.

9.2.7  AM of Ceramic Reinforced C-CMCs﻿

Although ceramics can be reinforced by carbonaceous materials, polymers, and met­
als, the ultimate strengthening and toughening solution should come from C-CMCs.
Compared with Carb-CMCs, P-CMCs, and M-CMCs, C-CMCs tend to have higher
temperature stability and chemical compatibility. Certain ceramic/ceramic compos­
ites, especially those reinforced with ceramic fibers or particles, can exhibit improved
toughness and impact resistance compared to single-phase ceramics, which mainly
depend on extrinsic toughening mechanisms such as enhanced ability of resistance
to crack propagation, and reduced stress concentration at the crack tip (Bai et al.,
2022). For ceramic-based 3D printing, the introduction of the second-phase ceramic
has been widely examined primarily through homogenous mixing of the matrix and
reinforcement ceramic raw material.
   For whiskers/fibers strengthening strategy, one-dimensional (1D) ceramic-based
whiskers, fibers, or nanowires, such as SiC whisker (SiC w ), chopped quartz fiber
(SiO 2 f ), and alumina whisker (Al 2 O 3 w ), are routinely incorporated into the pho­
tocurable ceramic suspensions to fabricate the high-performance C-CMCs with
complicated architecture via VP 3D printing. The reinforcement mechanisms
of this strategy mainly include crack deflection, fiber/whisker debonding, pull­
ing-out, and bridging that consume the energy of crack propagation. Meanwhile,
thanks to its high hardness, high strength and modulus, and excellent abrasion
resistance, SiCw has gradually been regarded as the most extensively used two-
phase whisker applied for ceramic-based VP 3D printing (Xin M et al., 2023 and
Xing H et al., 2020).
  The reinforcement strategy of C-CMCs relies on several key mechanisms to
enhance toughness and resist crack propagation, which is crucial because ceramics
are typically brittle. Here’s a brief explanation of how each mechanism contributes:

    1. Crack Deflection: When a crack encounters a reinforcing phase like fibers
      or whiskers, it is forced to change direction rather than continue straight.
     This increases the path length of the crack and dissipates more energy, mak­
      ing it harder for the crack to propagate.
    2. Fiber/Whisker Debonding: Instead of the crack cutting cleanly through the
       fiber, the bond between the fiber and the matrix partially breaks (debonds).
     This debonding absorbs energy and prevents immediate catastrophic failure,
     while also allowing other mechanisms (like pull-out) to engage.
    3. Pull-Out: After debonding, the fiber or whisker may be pulled out of the
      matrix, which takes additional energy. This frictional pull-out process is
      highly energy-consuming and slows down crack growth.
    4. Bridging: Some fibers span across a crack and act like bridges, holding the
      material together even as a crack opens. This reduces the stress intensity at
      the crack tip, impeding further crack growth.

Together, these mechanisms increase the fracture toughness of CMCs by turning
crack growth into an energy-intensive, gradual process rather than a sudden, brittle
failure.

ing, and self-toughening, have been employed to improve the mechanical properties
of 3D-printed C-CMCs.
  Feng et al. (2014) fabricated porous hydroxyapatite (HA) whisker toughened cal­
cium silicate (CaSiO3) scaffolds for bone regeneration and tissue engineering appli­
cations. HA whiskers ranging from 0 to 30 wt% were added to the CaSiO3 matrix.
The mechanical properties were promoted with increased HA whiskers, and reached
a maximum value when the HA whisker content was at 20 wt%. The improvement
of mechanical properties was attributed to whisker pull-out, crack deflection, and
crack bridging.


9.2.7.4   BJT-Fabricated C-CMCs
Ceramic/ceramic composites can be fabricated through a strategy involving the 3D
printing of a porous preform, followed by subsequent infiltration and pyrolysis pro­
cesses. This method is especially compatible with ceramic AM technologies that
utilize ceramic powders directly as raw materials, such as binder jetting technology
(BJT). During infiltration, ductile phases – such as silicon carbide (SiC) powders,
aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3) powders, or SiC whiskers – may be incorporated into
the ceramic matrix to enhance mechanical performance via particulate or whisker
toughening mechanisms. Furthermore, various precursor solutions, including silica
sol or polymer-derived precursors, can be introduced into the matrix. Upon pyroly­
sis, these precursors undergo in-situ transformation into reinforcing and toughening
ceramic phases, thereby contributing to improved structural integrity and mechanical
properties. Hence, many parameters, including infiltration temperature, infiltration
pressure, infiltration time, and solid loading of precursor solution, have significant
influences on the performance of BJT-fabricated C-CMCs.
  Lv X et al. (2019) successfully fabricated dense SiCw/SiC composites by integrat­
ing spray drying, BJT, and CVI. The feedstock used for BJT consisted of spray-dried
silicon carbide whiskers (SiCw), which exhibited enhanced flowability, facilitating
uniform printing. The CVI process introduced the SiC matrix into the porous SiCw
preforms, leading to dense SiC w / SiC composites with improved mechanical proper­
ties due to four main toughening mechanisms from the whiskers. Duan et al. (2015)
prepared SiC nanowires reinforced Si3N4 ceramic structures by using BJT technol­
ogy combined with polymer precursor infiltration and pyrolysis, and achieved good

AM of Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs)                             279

strength and toughening effect through in-situ generation of SiC nanowires. The
78% porous Si3N4 was first fabricated via BJ with pressureless sintering. The speci­
mens were then dipped into the organic liquid composed of polysiloxane and 5 wt%
ferrocene by vacuum infusion. The Si 3 N 4 ceramics with polysiloxane were cross­
linked at 300°C for 2 h and annealed at 1400°C for 2 h with an Ar atmosphere. The
sequenced process was repeated several times if more SiC nanowires were wanted
in the composite.
   In summary, the 3D printing of C-CMCs is generally more favorable compared
to carbon, polymer, and metal-based materials. However, when evaluating different
3D printing technologies for C-CMC fabrication, VP imposes significantly greater
constraints on the incorporation of strengthening and toughening phases. These lim­
itations arise from the distinct photopolymerization mechanism of ceramic suspen­
sions, which must concurrently fulfill rigorous rheological criteria (e.g., appropriate
viscosity and shear-thinning behavior) and photocuring demands (e.g., sufficient light
penetration and suitable curing kinetics). In contrast, other AM methods typically
allow for more straightforward integration of reinforcement phases. Nonetheless, key
parameters such as the printability of ceramic feedstocks (e.g., particle size distribu­
tion and dispersion stability), as well as the mechanical and functional performance
of the sintered composites, must be comprehensively optimized to ensure both man­
ufacturability and end-use reliability.

9.2.8  AM of M-CMCs﻿

Carb-CMCs have many advantages. For example, carbon fibers are incredibly strong
and lightweight, leading to high strength-to-weight ratios in composite materials,
and they are immune to corrosion, unlike many metals. Carb-CMC composites are
suitable for applications in corrosive environments. However, metals can provide bet­
ter toughness and impact resistance compared to carbon fibers, which can be brittle.
The mechanical properties of metals can be better matched to ceramics, leading to
improved compatibility and reduced stress concentration at the interface between
the two materials. Ceramic/metal composites are suitable for applications where ele­
vated temperatures are involved, such as aerospace propulsion systems and certain
industrial processes.

9.2.8.1  ME-Fabricated M-CMCs
ME-based 3D printing is one of the main processes used for architected ceramic/
metal composite fabrication, as its simplicity to pattern porous preforms for further
infiltration or impregnation processes. Soundararajan et al. (2001) fabricated intercon­
nected-phase mullite-aluminum metal–ceramic composites using an indirect FDM
process. Mullite is a rare silicate mineral with the chemical formula 3Al 2 O 3  2SiO 2,
or sometimes represented as Al 6 Si 2 O13. First, the porous mullite preform was fab­
ricated using FDM printed negative mold as a lost mold. The mechanically strong
porous mullite was obtained via two-stage sintering, including the polymer removal
and the porous mullite sintering. To get the mullite/aluminum composite, the pro­
duced porous mullite preforms were infiltrated with aluminum metal by pressureless
reactive metal infiltration (Soundararajan et al., 2001). A cylindrical porous preform

using ME is infiltration of liquid metal after a porous ceramic structure is fabricated.
The reinforcement mechanism lies in the plastic deformation of the ductile metal
phase, causing crack blunting, deflection, and so on.

9.2.8.2  SLS Fabricated M-CMCs
Stevinson et al. (2008) synthesized porous refractory ceramics by SLS/melting from
a mixture of zirconium oxides and aluminum. The porous SiC preforms were fabri­
cated by indirect SLS using a phenolic thermosetting binder, and the porous struc­
tures were then infiltrated with silicon.
  Wu et al. (2022) printed SiC triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structures
via L-PBF. SiC and epoxy resin powders were mixed to serve as the powder bed. The
green parts were carbonized under an Ar atmosphere and infiltrated with phenolic
resin. Later, the parts were carbonized again to increase the carbon yield. Si / SiC
TPMS composite structures were then obtained by the LSI process (Figure 9.19).
When the volume fraction of gyroid structures increased from 25% to 55%, the elas­
tic modulus of Si/SiC lattice structures increased from 121.9 to 932.0 MPa, and the
compressive strength increased from 2.3 to 16.3 MPa.
   Silicon is not strictly a metal – it’s classified as a metalloid. That means it has
properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals. For  that, Si-contained
ceramic composites are discussed in this section as ceramic/metalloid composites.

Specifically, silicon shows ductile fracture like metal when the temperature is above

Silicon is used as an infiltration medium in M-CMCs for the following reasons:

    1. Reactive Infiltration: Silicon can react with carbon to form silicon carbide
      (SiC) , a desirable ceramic phase. Infiltrating molten silicon into a porous
     preform (usually containing SiC and free carbon) results in SiC forma­
       tion, strengthening the composite.
    2. Excellent Wettability: Molten silicon wets carbon and SiC well, enabling
     good penetration into porous ceramic preforms.
    3. High-Temperature Stability: Silicon remains stable at high temperatures
     (~1414°C melting point), making it suitable for structural and thermal pro­
      tection systems (e.g., in aerospace applications).

Steps of AM of M-CMCs are as follows:

   •  Preform Fabrication: A porous ceramic “green body” is created using AM
      techniques like ME or BJ.
   •  Pyrolysis/Sintering: The preform is often heat-treated to remove binders
     and enhance structure.
   •  Silicon Infiltration: Molten Si is infiltrated into the porous ceramic at high
      temperatures. Free carbon in the preform reacts with silicon to form addi­
      tional SiC: Si  liquid   C  solid   SiC  solid  ﻿

Challenges with Si Infiltration are as follows:

   •  Residual Silicon: Unreacted Si can remain in the final product, which may
     reduce oxidation resistance or thermal shock resistance.
   •  Dimensional Control: Reaction with carbon causes volume changes that
     must be managed.
   •  Brittleness: While strong, the resulting composite may still be brittle

9.2.9  AM of P-CMCs﻿

Toughening ceramic with metal usually gets high strength ceramic composites.
However, the processes are commonly involved with high-temperature infiltration,
which makes the process very complex to implement and expensive. In comparison
to metal, the toughening of ceramics with polymer is less complicated in the process
since many of them can be done at room temperature. In addition, the polymer tough­
ening phase is usually impregnated into the 3D-printed sintered ceramic scaffold to
form a P-CMCs, which can not only sustain the material’s lightweight but also reduce
interface effects between the hard ceramic phase and the toughening phase. These
three-dimensional structural P-CMCs exhibit huge potential in dental, armor, and
energy-absorption applications.

9.2.9.1  VPP Fabricated P-CMCs
Zhang et al. (2023) fabricated Al 2 O 3 / polyurea (PU) dual-phase composite by VP
and a simple infiltration process. The cellular ceramic structure was printed using a
DLP-based 3D printing system, and PU was infiltrated into the cells of the ceramic
structure by immersion. The composite showed extraordinary load-bearing capacity
and significantly improved energy-absorbing ability under quasi-static and impact
compressive loading.
   Sajadi et al. (2021) reported the fabrication of damage-tolerant architected SiO2
ceramic structures via VP, followed by a conformal polymer micro-coating. The
polymer-coated architected structures showed multifold improvement in strength
and toughness upon the uniaxial compression test. As shown in Figure 9.20, the poly­
mer coatings significantly delayed the damage propagation and structural failure.
   Finally, there is less literature in P-CMCs compared to other CMCs; this is par­
tially because there is a temperature processing gap between ceramic and polymer.
However, there is still a broad range of research for 3D printed bioceramic/biocom­
patible polymer composite in the application area of bone tissue engineering (Du X
et al., 2018).

9.3  SUMMARY, CONCLUSIONS, AND PROSPECTS
    OF AM TECHNOLOGIES FOR CMCS

In summary, CMCs possess not only the excellent properties of ceramic matrix mate­
rials but also the toughness of the fibers and therefore are widely used in different
engineering fields. AM technologies provide a new approach for fabricating CMCs
and structures. However, the performance of CMCs fabricated by AM technologies
is far from meeting the application requirements.
   Although 3D printing technology includes several different specific processes,
the ceramic composites are commonly fabricated using ME (e.g., DIW), PBF (e.g.,
SLS), BJT, and VP. The first three processes are used mostly due to their inher­
ent capabilities to build porous structures. For example, the DIW process is able to
fabricate woodpile-like structures by fast patterning of filaments. PBF and BJT are
powder bed-based processes which are porous in nature due to the larger particle
size of the raw ceramic materials. Due to the fast development of ceramic VP (also
termed as ceramic SLA) for broad ceramic materials, VP is largely used via a prece­
ramic polymer route to fabricate SiC and SiOC-based ceramic composites, together
with the excellent ability to fabricate densified ceramic composites with complicated
architectures.

9.3.1  DIW as an Ideal Process for AM-CMCs﻿

Researchers have explored several printing techniques within AM that allow the fab­
rication of materials at high speeds and precision over customizable build volumes.
Of these, DIW has emerged as one of the most versatile AM methods that enables a
wide range of materials to be utilized for creating complex and/or periodic 3D struc­
tures (Smay et al., 2002). Typically, DIW, also known as Robocasting, can be divided
into two classes: droplet and continuous ink extrusion (Lewis et al., 2006). The low
cost, simplicity, and ability to combine different materials in a single processing
step in DIW have attracted a large number of research organizations and universities
worldwide to be involved in the state-of-the-art development of the technique. First
patented by Cesarano and Calvert (1997) at Sandia National Laboratory in 1997,
DIW emerged as a printing technique for complex ceramic structures. Since then, the
number of researchers using this technique has expanded worldwide into a myriad of
fields beyond structural ceramics. The published literature on DIW has also grown
exponentially since 2006, as seen in the trend shown in Figure 9.21, with major engi­
neering and scientific contributions coming from a wide range of disciplines. DIW is
distinct from other AM technologies in that it is not limited by material class as long

9.3.2   Issues Regarding AM-CMCs﻿

Although AM of CMCs has achieved significant advances, there are still many chal­
lenges and issues to be tackled. Restricted fiber orientation and achieving homoge­
neous fiber dispersion within the matrix present limitations in tailoring anisotropic
mechanical properties. Ensuring robust interfacial bonding between reinforcement
and matrix phases remains a critical area of investigation. The inherent complexity
of AM processes can introduce microstructural defects, necessitating advanced pro­
cess optimization. Scalability for high-volume production and cost-effectiveness are
ongoing economic considerations. Furthermore, effective non-destructive evaluation
techniques and suitable post-processing methodologies, including surface finishing
and environmental barrier coating integration, require further research and develop­
ment to realize the full potential of AM-fabricated CMCs.
   Although 3D printing of CMCs has achieved significant advances, there are still
many issues and conclusions to be considered, which:

    1. For polymer-infiltrated ceramic matrix composites (P-CMCs), applica­
      tions remain highly limited. Toughening ceramics with a secondary phase,
     such as a polymer, can compromise their inherent properties. Specifically,
     polymer infiltration significantly reduces the material’s thermal resistance,

AM of Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs)                             287

      rendering it unsuitable for high-temperature environments. As a result, the
     use of P-CMCs is restricted to niche applications that operate under mod­
      erate conditions, such as bone tissue engineering, where thermal stability is
      not a critical requirement.
    2. Compared to metals, toughening ceramics with polymers is a less complex
      process, often achievable at room temperature. Typically, the polymer phase
       is impregnated into a 3D-printed and sintered ceramic scaffold to form
     P-CMCs. This approach maintains the lightweight nature of the material
     while minimizing interfacial issues between the brittle ceramic phase and
      the toughening polymer phase. The resulting three-dimensional P-CMC
      structures demonstrate significant potential in applications such as dentistry,
      personal armor, and energy-absorbing systems.
   3. Carb-CMCs are well-suited for use in corrosive environments. However,
      metals offer superior toughness and impact resistance compared to the
      inherently brittle carbon fibers. Additionally, the mechanical properties
      of metals can be more closely matched to those of ceramics, enhancing
       interfacial compatibility and reducing stress concentrations. As a result,
      ceramic/metal composites are particularly advantageous for high-tem­
      perature applications, including aerospace propulsion systems and various
      industrial processes.
    4. Compared to Carb-CMCs, P-CMCs, and M-CMCs, ceramic–ceramic com­
      posites (C-CMCs) generally offer superior thermal stability and chemical
      compatibility. Specific C-CMCs, particularly those reinforced with ceramic
       fibers or particles, can also demonstrate enhanced toughness and impact
      resistance relative to monolithic ceramics. These improvements primarily
       result from extrinsic toughening mechanisms, such as increased resistance
      to crack propagation and reduced stress concentration at crack tips.
    5. Sintering is a critical step in fabricating CMCs, with Al₂O₃–Cf samples sin­
      tered at 1550 °C in argon, achieving 85% of theoretical density. Although
      this density is comparable to that obtained by CVI, extensive microstruc­
      tural cracking was observed. This damage is attributed to the thermal
     expansion mismatch between the Al 2 O 3 matrix and carbon fibers, leading
      to tensile stresses in the matrix during cooling. These stresses are believed
      to be the primary cause of cracking. In contrast, SiC–Cf CMCs exhibit
     fewer issues due to a lower thermal expansion mismatch. Therefore, SiC
       is recommended as a more compatible matrix material than Al₂O₃ for
     Cf CMCs.

9.4  REVIEW QUESTIONS

9.4.1  Solved Questions﻿
    1. What are the major challenges in applying direct AM to fabricate con­
     tinuous fiber-reinforced CMCs?
     Answer﻿: The primary challenges in using direct AM for continuous fiber-re­
      inforced CMCs include difficulty in accurately placing and maintaining the

288           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

     alignment of continuous fibers during the printing process. The high vis­
      cosity of ceramic slurries can hinder the smooth incorporation of fibers,
      especially when dealing with complex geometries. Moreover, controlling
      shrinkage and avoiding cracking during sintering remains problematic due
      to the anisotropic thermal expansion and poor interfacial bonding between
       fiber and matrix.
   2. How does indirect AM contribute to improving the design flexibility of
   CMC components, and what limitations does it still face?
     Answer﻿: Indirect AM enhances design flexibility by allowing complex
     geometries to be created using polymer-based molds or green parts that are
       later transformed into CMCs via infiltration or pyrolysis. This enables the
      production of components that would be challenging to machine or mold
      using traditional methods. However, limitations include potential distor­
      tion during the thermal conversion process, lower resolution in final parts
     due to mold degradation, and less precise fiber control compared to direct
     methods.
   3. Differentiate between direct AM and indirect AM of CMCs.﻿
     Answer﻿: The differentiation between direct additive manufacturing (direct
    AM) and indirect additive manufacturing (indirect AM) of ceramic matrix
     composites (CMCs) lies primarily in how the final composite part is pro­
     duced using additive techniques. In direct AM, the ceramic or ceramic-com­
      posite material is printed directly into its final shape (or near-net shape),
      layer by layer. In indirect AM, a mold, sacrificial template, or preform is
      created using AM. This is then used in a secondary process to form the final
   CMC part.
   4. What is the main motivation for introducing a polymeric or metallic
     second phase in AM of CMCs?﻿
     Answer﻿: The primary motivation is to compensate for the inherent brittle­
      ness of ceramics. While ceramics offer excellent thermal and chemical sta­
       bility, they lack ductility and fracture toughness. A polymer or metal second
     phase can introduce toughening mechanisms such as crack bridging, deflec­
       tion, and energy absorption. In AM, polymers also serve a dual function by
     enhancing printability and acting as binders or fugitive phases, which are
       later removed during sintering or thermal treatment.
   5. How does the incorporation of metals into ceramic matrices influence
     the mechanical properties of AM-fabricated composites?
     Answer﻿: Metals introduce ductility and plastic deformation zones that
     allow the composite to better withstand impact and thermal shocks. This
     toughening mechanism enhances fracture toughness and damage toler­
     ance – key properties for structural applications. For example, Ni- or
      Al-reinforced  ceramics show improved mechanical  behavior under
      cyclic loading compared to monolithic ceramics or ceramic/ceramic
    CMCs, making them suitable for aerospace engine components or heat
     exchangers.

AM of Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs)                             289

    6. What are the processing challenges associated with using metals as a
     second phase in AM of CMCs?﻿
    Answer: Challenges include:
       •  Thermal mismatch between metal and ceramic phases, leading to inter­
          nal stresses or delamination.
       •   Reactivity at the interface during sintering, which can form  brittle
           intermetallics.
       •  Oxidation of metallic phases at high sintering temperatures.
       •  Inhomogeneous distribution of metal particles in ceramic slurries or
         powders. These challenges require careful selection of compatible mate­
            rials and tailored processing strategies, such as spark plasma sintering
         (SPS) or infiltration post-AM.
   7. What  applications  benefit  specifically from polymer/ceramic AM
     composites?﻿
    Answer: Polymer/ceramic composites made via AM are particularly useful
       in:
       •  Biomedical implants: for example, biodegradable scaffolds where
         polymers enhance flexibility and biodegradability.
       •  Sensors and electronics: polymers provide electrical insulation or flexi­
          ble support in multifunctional ceramic components.
       •  Lightweight structural parts: in aerospace and automotive industries,
        combining ceramics’ stiffness with polymeric materials’ low density
        and toughness. These applications often prioritize design flexibility, bio­
          compatibility, or functional grading over extreme mechanical strength
          or temperature resistance.
   8. Why is it important to classify composites, and how does classification
      affect their application?
     Answer: Classifying composites is crucial because it helps engineers and
      designers choose the appropriate material for specific performance require­
     ments and environmental conditions. Each class – PMCs, MMCs, and
    CMCs – has distinct properties such as thermal resistance, strength, and
      corrosion resistance. For example, PMCs are ideal for lightweight struc­
      tural parts, whereas CMCs are suited for high-temperature environments.
     Proper classification ensures optimized material selection, efficient design,
     and cost-effective manufacturing.

10.1  IMPORTANCE OF POST-PROCESSING IN AM
     TECHNIQUES – GENERAL PERSPECTIVE

As previously discussed in Chapter 1, additive manufacturing (AM) includes three
steps. These are the pre-processing computer-aided design, converting to STL file,
slicing, the processing (3D printing), and the post-processing steps. According to
Wohlers Associates  (2021), www.materialstoday.com, post-processing accounts
for nearly 27% of the production cost of AM. The chart in Figure 10.1 presents the
cost segmentation between pre-processing, printing, and post-processing among
companies that offer both metal and polymer AM. Post-processing is often an over­
looked part of the AM process. It is a critical and final step, where parts receive
adjustments, such as smoothing and strengthening. Despite all the advantages of AM
over traditional manufacturing methods, it is still imperfect, and some post-process­
ing techniques are generally needed to enhance components or to overcome AM’s
limitations.
  Depending upon the AM technique and starting material used, the reason and
the type of post-processing vary. Additively manufactured parts can still have poor
surface quality and high porosity, which can affect the mechanical properties of the
component. The main objective of post-processing is to eliminate these potentially
dangerous defects. These processes can include heat treatment, which is needed to
reduce the stress on components before their removal from the build plate; separating
components from the support structure; and surface finishing procedures such as
computer numerically controlled (CNC) machining, blasting, and polishing.
  The post-processing of additively manufactured parts can be just as vital as the
fabrication itself. Some post-processing processes may involve thermal treatment to
eliminate residual and thermally induced stresses in the part to enhance the final
part properties. The residual stresses are the stresses that persist in a part even in the
absence of external loading. In contrast, thermal stresses are usually induced by any
change in a material’s temperature. Different AM processes have different results in
terms of accuracy, and thus, machining to final dimensions may be required. Some
AM processes produce relatively fragile components that may require the use of
infiltration and/or surface coatings to strengthen the final part. Finishing may include
media blasting, peening, sanding, abrasive flow machining, or grinding to smooth
surface features and allow visual inspection.
  Washing may be used to help remove powders from internal features. In cases
such as medical applications, sterilization may be specified. Coating and painting,
as used in plastic prototype finishing, may improve surface finish or appearance.

These operations may require specialized equipment and processes provided by
a dedicated service provider. Post-processing of printed parts may require a large
amount of skilled manual work in terms of machining, surface preparation, and coat­
ing. Post-processing operations may be manual, semi-automated, or automated, and
they can be performed through either batch or serial processing. Automation of the
post-processing step will be necessary to minimize labor and time costs for produc­
tion. Companies that can efficiently and accurately post-process parts to a customer’s
expectations can often charge a premium for their services, whereas those that com­
pete primarily on price may sacrifice post-processing quality in order to reduce costs.
   In conclusion, post-processing procedures vary by printing techniques and mate­
rials. Some AM processes may not require post-processing, but some processes
require careful and lengthy post-processing. For example, photosensitive resins
printed by stereolithography (SLA) require the component to cure under the UV
environment before the final application. If support structures are used during print­
ing, the removal of such support is required. The support can be removed mechani­
cally by cutting it from the printed object, or chemically by dissolving it in a solvent
that will not damage the target part.
   Finally, post-processing of 3D printed components offers many advantages:

   •  Higher cost-efficiency when automated post-processing operations are used
   •  Improved component performance due to an improved surface finish
   • New fields of application due to improved component performance
   •  Faster implementation of the 3D printing technology thanks to cost savings
      during the post-processing phase

10.1.1   Defects in Products Processed by AM
        That Need to Be Post-Processed﻿

The need for post-processing depends on the printing technology, materials used,
defects initiated, and print settings (Albright, 2021). This chapter presents the

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    297

different post-processing techniques used for 3D printed parts made of different
engineering materials, namely, polymers, metals, and ceramics, considering the
printing technology used.
  The defects of the 3D printed parts that need to be treated by post-processing
techniques may include the following:

   •  Pres
   •  Cracks
   •  Anisotropy
   •  Residual stresses
   •  Thermal stresses
   •  Laser spattering
   •  Inaccuracies, poor surface roughness, and stair-stepping effects
   •  Part distortion

These defects have a serious influence on the internal microstructure and mechanical
behavior of the final parts. Therefore, after the parts are manufactured, post-process­
ing operations are usually required to improve the mechanical properties and the
surface quality, thus achieving their intended utilization. There are many post-pro­
cessing technologies, such as the thermal post-processing method to release ther­
mally induced residual stress and laser peening to reduce micro-defects and improve
surface quality.
   Post-processing includes all processes performed after the parts are removed from
a 3D printer. It has two main categories:

    1. Primary post-processing includes the necessary steps that must be per­
     formed on all 3D printed parts to make them suitable to be used in any
      particular application. Primary post-processing activities generally include
      the removal of support as well as cleaning.
   2. Secondary  post-processing  includes  optional  finishing  processes  that
     improve the properties, performance, functions, or even aesthetics of the
       part. Secondary post-processing activities are those that are not necessary
      but would depend on the needs and purposes of the user, such as painting
     and vapor smoothing. Secondary post-processing plays a significant role in
     improving mechanical, chemical, and aesthetic properties, meeting tight tol­
      erances, providing near-injection molded finishes, and achieving added dura­
       bility. Additionally, it improves the surface properties of prints beyond the
       initial print, such that it controls wetting behavior, gloss, scratch resistance,
     and other properties. These essential surface characteristics allow post-pro­
      cessing to significantly extend the range of applications (Ryan et al., 2021).

10.1.2   Stair-Stepping Effect and Resolution in AM Processes﻿

The stair-stepping effect (also called layered surface roughness) in AM refers to the
visible layers that are formed as a result of the layer-by-layer construction process.
Since most 3D printers build objects by adding material in horizontal layers, each

layer is slightly offset from the layer below it, creating a “staircase” appearance on
the surface of the printed object, especially for steep or curved surfaces.
   This effect is more prominent when the print resolution (layer thickness) is
larger, as the layers are thicker, and thus the “steps” are more noticeable. However,
it can be reduced by using finer resolutions (smaller layer thickness) or employing
post-processing techniques like sanding or polishing. The stair stepping is a natural
consequence of the AM method, and while it doesn’t typically affect the structural
integrity of the object, it may impact the aesthetic quality of curved or sloped sur­
faces, especially for objects requiring high surface smoothness.
   Figure 10.2 shows the staircase effect on a 3D-printed part (Pandey et al., 2003).
Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most common process where stair-stepping
is most prominent due to its layer-by-layer nature. SLA and selective laser sintering
(SLS) tend to have smoother surface finishes and may show less noticeable stair-step­
ping effects than FDM. Ultimately, the stair-stepping effect is a trade-off between
print time, quality, and finish.
   Resolution in AM refers to the ability to produce fine details and precise layers in
the final printed part. It’s typically defined in terms of layer resolution (layer thick­
ness) and XY resolution (or lateral resolution).

    1. Layer Resolution (Z-Axis): This refers to the height of each layer of mate­
       rial deposited during the build process. The thinner the layer, the higher
      the resolution in the Z-direction. High-resolution printers can produce finer
      layer heights, typically in the range of 10–100 microns, while low-resolution
      printers might have a layer thickness of 200 microns or more.
   2. XY Resolution: This refers to the smallest feature that can be resolved on
      the horizontal plane (i.e., the precision with which the printer can deposit
      material in the XY direction). It depends on the nozzle diameter or laser

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    299

      spot size, with smaller nozzles or lasers allowing for finer resolutions. For
    FDM, XY resolution is often around 100–200 microns, while SLA or SLS
     can achieve much finer details, sometimes down to 50 microns or less.

10.1.3   Considerations for Setting Up a Post-
         Processing System for an AM Process﻿

Most AM companies aim to increase the printing speed, printing resolution, size,
and other aspects. For AM to be adopted in the industry mainstream, several factors
related to post-processing must be considered, including part quality, cost, time, uni­
formity, repeatability, workforce skills, safety, sustainability, and automation.
  The following items provide some important considerations for the selection of
post-processing techniques:

    1. Methods: Automation would address most of these factors. Automation
     would increase efficiency and productivity. Moreover, an interconnected
     hardware and software solution that can trace parts (with vision systems)
     throughout the workflow is ideal for manufacturing activities.
    2. Type of Material: The type of material is the first determining factor when
      designing post-processing operations. The development of new polymer
      3D-printing materials will warrant new post-processing methods for these
      materials. Materials (metals, polymers, or ceramics) for different applica­
      tions would need different post-processing techniques, such as in electron­
       ics, biomedical applications, oil and gas, aerospace, and many others.
    3. Part Features: In addition, the size, geometry, structure, complexity, and
     purpose of the part, dimensional accuracy/tolerance, and the number of
      parts to post-process should also be considered, as these factors are deci­
      sive for the selection of the post-processing operation and, consequently, the
      properties of the printed part. Knowing these would aid in the optimization
      of the post-processing operations. After analyzing these factors, the next
      step is to identify the technologies/machines and materials/solutions that are
     needed to set up a post-processing system.
    4. Targeted Properties: Further, different post-processing techniques are
     needed to enhance different properties (e.g., mechanical, electrical, and sur­
      face roughness) to cope with the intended applications. For example, 3D
      printed sorbents for oil–water separation (for the oil and gas industry) will
     need to enhance their hydrophobic/oleophilic properties (Tijing et al., 2020).
    5. Quality: For newly developed materials, where no post-processing devices
     have yet been developed, manual processing results in varying properties, as
      the quality depends on the skills of the worker. For such cases, the workforce
     should be trained in this industry, or dedicated devices and facilities should
     be developed to ensure part quality, especially in the case of mass production.
    6. Safety: Post-processing operations are accompanied by corresponding haz­
      ards in all aspects of operation, handling, storage, and disposal. Considering
      safety in all these aspects entails additional costs not usually previously
      considered during planning.

10.2  POST-PROCESSING TECHNIQUES IN AMC

10.2.1   Challenges of Post-Processing Techniques in AMC

The main post-processing challenges are removing support  structures, binder
removal, and densification or sintering. Processes like SLA require additional cur­
ing steps, or binder jetting (BJ) needs drying and depowdering, which are unique.
Removing the support structure without damaging the part can be an issue for fused
deposition or direct ink writing (DIW) parts, as those parts do not have high mechan­
ical strength in the green state. Binder removal of SLC or FDC is challenging due to
low solids loading. In most cases, thermal debinding is used, where a slow heating
rate removes the binder from the part, followed by high-temperature sintering. If
binder chemistry can be designed such that solvent extraction can be used to remove
a part of the initial binder volume, then faster heating can be used to remove the
remaining binder. Naturally, designing polymer chemistry becomes essential not
just for the pre-processing steps but also for the post-processing. The sintering of
3D-printed parts is sensitive to the materials’ chemistry. While the oxide ceramics
can be sintered in air, nitrides, carbides, or borides require unique sintering envi­
ronments to prevent degradation. Unfortunately, cracking, delamination, and warp­
ing are common in 3D-printed ceramic parts, which are evident after the sintering
cycles. This not only is frustrating but also makes ceramic 3DP expensive. Sintering
multi-material green bodies requires that the constituents be chemically compatible
and have similar densification temperatures. Densification of parts with anisotro­
pic particulates is also challenging due to the anisotropic shrinkage of platelets and
fibers and the tendency to create “overhang” porosity. Even when densification can
be achieved, residual stresses from the coefficient of thermal expansion mismatches
can cause cracking or spallation. Future research should investigate novel co-sinter­
ing or additive methods that avoid the need for green body densification to minimize
these issues. Methods are also needed to model the residual stresses more accu­
rately when designing and sintering multi-material ceramics. Ceramic 3DP’s future
is headed in directions that offer capabilities beyond the traditional shape-control of
AM techniques, with increasing demand for and research on capabilities enabling
multi-material and microstructurally controlled parts (Chaudhary et al., 2022).
   Although this book is focused primarily on pure ceramic part fabrication, signif­
icant work has been done over the years on ceramic-based composites that involve
ceramic printing. The 3DP of metal–ceramic composites, where ceramic preforms
are infiltrated with liquid metals, can greatly improve their mechanical properties. In
recent years, L-DED has been used to print ceramic-metal or functionally graded com­
posites offering unique location-specific properties or naturally architected designs.
Future research with ceramics and composites using 3DP has the potential to transform
ceramic processing as it did to metals and polymers and is expected to enable innovative
product designs offering location-specific properties and on-demand manufacturing.

10.2.2   Types of Post-Processing Techniques in AMC

During the printing processes, internal defects such as balling, porosity, cracks, pow­
der agglomeration, and thermal stress would appear between different printing layers.
These defects have a serious influence on the internal microstructure and mechanics

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    301

of the final parts. Therefore, after the parts are manufactured, basic post-processing
operations are usually required to improve the mechanical properties and the surface
quality, achieving their intended utilization. There are many post-processing tech­
nologies, such as the thermal post-processing method to release thermally-induced
residual stress and laser peening and polishing to reduce micro-defects and improve
surface quality. Other types of post-processing operations are optional, such as infil­
tration, sealing, coating, shrinkage compensation, surface texturing, assembly and
joining, quality control and inspection, and so on (Figure 10.3).

10.2.2.1   Basic Post-Processing Operations
Basic post-processing is typically essential to ensure the part’s structure, integrity,
and dimensional accuracy. These can be categorized into the following post-process­
ing steps:

10.2.2.1.1  Mechanical Methods
These include the following.

   a. Powder Removal (Depowdering): First, the powder that remains on the
      build plate after the printing process needs to be removed. This can be
     achieved with standard cleaning procedures. Excess powder is often saved
      or sent back to the supplier for recycling purposes. Depowdering is per­
     formed by water or air blasting. Depowdering is related to the mechan­
       ical post-processing category. Excess powder can be removed manually,
      but automated solutions have arrived on the market that vibrate or rotate to
     remove excess powder (Figure 10.4). This 3D printing post-processing tech­
     nique works like a sort of centrifuge, rotating the part in all three dimen­
      sions. Models printed using powder bed fusion (PBF) are fabricated using
      plastic or metal powders. Residues of powder, especially in the case of holes
      or more complex internal channels inside the model, can cling to or remain
      in the model.

GmbH in collaboration with Siemens.)

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    303

   b. Support Removal : This is a mechanical post-processing category. Many
      pieces need a support structure to be printed, so before any heat treatment
      or finishing can be affected on the piece, support structures need not be
     removed to help reduce distortion of features on the part; without supports,
      there is a risk of having a build failure if the part warps too much and causes
     an issue. Although a band saw or files might be enough to remove parts and
      support structure, in the case of harder materials that resist intense strain, it
     might be necessary to use CNC machining.
    c. Abrasive Finishing or Grinding: Abrasive finishing and grinding are con­
      ventional manufacturing techniques to improve the form accuracy and sur­
      face finish of advanced ceramic parts in various industries. They are used
      as common post-processing methods for AMC parts because of their high
      maturity and good accessibility.
   d. Mechanical Super-Finishing Post-Processing Operations: The mechan­
       ically based technologies comprise abrasive flow machining (AFM), water
       jet peening (WJP), and oil jet peening (OJP).
       • AFM : This is a purely mechanical process that finishes surfaces and
         edges by extruding a viscous abrasive medium flowing under pressure
         through or across a workpiece. This process provides a high level of
          surface finish and close tolerances with an economically acceptable
           rate of surface generation for a wide range of industrial components.
      A common setup is to position the work part between two opposing
          cylinders, one containing media (visco-elastic polymer) and the other
         empty. The polymer has the consistency of putty. The medium is forced
         under pressures ranging between 0.7 and 20 MPa to flow through the
          part from the first cylinder to the other, and then back again, as many
         times as necessary to achieve the desired material removal and finish.
      AFM is capable of removing electrical discharge machining (EDM),
       EBM, and laser beam machining damaged surfaces and significantly
         improving surface roughness  ( Youssef et  al., 2020 ). For advanced
         ceramic parts, AFM can be a valuable post-processing technique, espe­
           cially for improving surface roughness and achieving a smoother fin­
           ish. However, there are several factors to consider. AFM can access
          internal features, holes, and intricate contours that are hard to reach
         with traditional machining methods. This makes it a good option for
          post-processing advanced ceramic parts with geometrically complex
         shapes or fine features. While AFM can provide a smoother surface, it
         might not achieve the same level of precision as laser-based methods
           (like laser polishing (LP)) in terms of surface smoothness. However, it
         can still improve surface quality to a satisfactory level for many appli­
          cations. The abrasive slurry used in AFM must be carefully selected to
        match the hardness of the ceramic material, as too coarse an abrasive
         could damage the surface.
       •  WJP uses high-pressure water jets to impact a surface, creating local­
          ized surface deformations and compressive stresses. Unlike shot peen­
           ing, WJP does not involve solid media, which might make it less likely

304           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

          to cause cracking in brittle materials like ceramics. The process could
         induce compressive residual stresses, improve surface finish, and reduce
         roughness. Moreover, the absence of solid abrasives minimizes the risk
          of inducing fractures in the ceramic material. WJP could be a more suit­
          able post-processing method for advanced ceramics compared to shot
         peening or cavitation peening, provided that the process parameters are
         optimized to avoid damaging the material.
       •  OJP is similar to WJP, but it uses oil as the medium instead of water.
        The use of oil allows for the lubrication of the surface during peen­
          ing, potentially reducing the risk of damaging the surface compared to
        WJP. OJP offers a gentler alternative to WJP and may be more suitable
          for advanced ceramics, provided that the process is fine-tuned to avoid
          over-stressing the material.

Mechanical  super-finishing  post-processing  operations  not  applicable  for
AMC are:
   Shot peening (SP) involves bombarding the surface of a material with small,
spherical media (shots), typically made of steel or ceramic, at high velocity. This cre­
ates plastic deformation on the material’s surface, which induces compressive resid­
ual stresses that improve fatigue life and surface durability. SP is most commonly
used for metals, where plastic deformation is easily induced. Advanced ceramics,
due to their brittleness, have limited capacity for plastic deformation. This makes SP
more challenging and potentially damaging if not carefully controlled. The energy
of the shots could cause microcracking or surface damage on brittle ceramic parts.
Cavitation peening (CP), which is a process that uses the formation and collapse
of bubbles (cavitation) in a liquid medium to create shock waves that impact the
material’s surface. This process is typically used to improve the fatigue resistance of
metals but has also been considered for ceramics. Ceramics are much more brittle
than metals, so cavitation-induced shock waves could cause microcracks or surface
damage. The high-energy impacts generated by cavitation could be too aggressive
for advanced ceramics, leading to degradation rather than improvement. In conclu­
sion, CP may not be an ideal method for advanced ceramics due to the risk of damage
from shock waves. Its use would require stringent control of parameters like inten­
sity, duration, and fluid type.

10.2.2.1.2  Thermal Methods
These include the following.

10.2.2.1.2.1  Thermal Treatments
Post-processing heat treatment is a common method used to modify the tensile prop­
erties of 3D-printed parts. Heat treatment involves subjecting the printed parts to
controlled temperature conditions for a specific duration, resulting in changes in
the material’s microstructure, crystallinity, and mechanical behavior. The effects of
post-processing heat treatment on the mechanical properties of 3D-printed parts can
vary depending on several factors, such as the material type, printing process, heat
treatment parameters, and part geometry.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    305

    a. Curing: Curing refers to a post-processing step where the printed material
     undergoes a controlled thermal or chemical treatment to improve its final
      properties, such as strength, hardness, and stability. In the case of advanced
      ceramics, curing is typically used to ensure that the material undergoes solidi­
       fication or bonding processes that are essential to achieving the desired ceramic
       characteristics. The curing process can vary depending on the specific AM
      technique, but it is often necessary when the printing process involves mate­
       rials that are not fully solidified during printing or that require additional pro­
      cessing to achieve the desired ceramic properties. Curing is mostly needed for
      processes that use photopolymers, binder-based materials, or ceramic pastes
      (such as SLA, DIW, BJ, and material jetting (MJ)). The main goal of curing
      in these processes is to stabilize the printed parts before they undergo further
      processing steps, like sintering, to achieve the final ceramic properties.
   b. Debinding: It is defined as the removal of binder materials used during the
   AM process. Most advanced ceramics are printed with a binder to hold the
     ceramic powder together. Debinding is the process of removing the binder
      before sintering. It eliminates organic binders and avoids defects during sin­
      tering, ensuring proper part formation and density. While it may involve
      heat, it is not always classified as a full “heat treatment” in the traditional
      sense because it primarily focuses on removing binders rather than altering
      the material’s microstructure or properties. However, it can be considered a
      preliminary heat treatment step in the broader context of powder-based AM
      processes.
        There are two types of debinding, namely, thermal debinding, in which
      the part is heated in a furnace to burn off organic binders without caus­
      ing damage to the ceramic part, and solvent debinding, in which the part is
     immersed in a solvent to remove the binder before further processing.
       The green parts produced by AM usually undergo debinding to remove
      the binder or other organic residue from the printed part. This leaves behind
     a fragile ceramic structure with poor mechanical properties. Debinding is
     followed by sintering at elevated temperatures (up to 2300°C), leading to
      further shrinkage.
    c. Stress Relieving: Stress relieving is considered an important post-process­
      ing operation in AM of advanced ceramics. During the AM process, such as
     BJ or DIW, internal stresses can develop due to factors like thermal gradi­
      ents, cooling rates, and uneven material deposition. These stresses can lead
      to warping, cracking, or failure of the printed part.
         Stress relieving helps to mitigate these internal stresses and improves the
      overall mechanical properties and dimensional stability of the ceramic parts.
        It is typically done through stress relieving, which allows the material to
      gradually relax and reduce residual stresses that have developed during the
      printing or processing phase. The ceramic material is heated to a tempera­
      ture below its sintering temperature, typically between 500°C and 1000°C
      for a specific time interval, allowing the material to gradually relax and
     reduce the internal stresses. The part is then cooled slowly (often by turning
      off the furnace and keeping it cool at a controlled rate).

306           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   d. Sintering: Sintering is a heat treatment process where the ceramic part is
      heated to a temperature below its melting point, causing the ceramic particles
      to bond together, reducing porosity, and enhancing the mechanical properties
      of the material. Sintering mechanisms play a critical role in transforming a
     “green body” (shaped by a multi-step process, unsintered part) into a dense,
     mechanically strong final component. In sintering, the part is heated in a fur­
     nace in the presence of a controlled atmosphere (e.g., air, vacuum, or inert gas)
      for a set period. During this process, particles within the ceramic part diffuse
     and coalesce, increasing density and strength. There are two types of sinter­
      ing, namely, solid-state sintering (SSS) and liquid-phase sintering (LPS).

      1. SSS: involves densification without the formation of a liquid phase. At
        high temperatures (but below the melting point of the primary phase),
        atomic diffusion causes particles to bond and densify. It is characterized
       by the following:
          •  Involves diffusion mechanisms: surface, grain boundary, and lattice
             diffusion.
          •  Grain growth occurs as densification progresses.
          •  Requires high temperatures and long dwell times.
          •  Typically results in good mechanical properties.

       SSS is common in powder-based AM of ceramics like lithography-based
        ceramic manufacturing or BJ, where parts are printed in a loose or bound
       powder form and then sintered. It is also used for materials with high melt­
         ing points and no additives that form liquid phases at sintering temperature.
      2. LPS: is another valuable post-processing step in the AM of advanced
        ceramics, enabling improved densification, mechanical strength, and
          reliability of ceramic components. By introducing a secondary liquid
        phase during the sintering process, ceramic parts printed using AM
         technologies can achieve higher quality, stronger, and more functional
         materials suited for demanding applications in industries like aerospace,
        automotive, and medical devices. In LPS, a liquid phase forms during
          sintering, aiding particle rearrangement and enhancing densification at
        lower temperatures. LPS is characterized by:
          • A liquid forms at the sintering temperature (e.g., from additives or
            impurities).
          •  Capillary forces pull solid particles together.
          •  Enhanced diffusion and mass transport.
          •  Usually faster and can achieve higher final densities.

    LPS is common in ceramic composites, or systems like SiC with sinter­
      ing aids (e.g., Al₂O₃-Y₂O₃). It is used when complete densification is diffi­
      cult with solid-state mechanisms alone. However, it is more prone to grain
     growth and phase changes depending on composition.
    e. Ultrafast High-Temperature Sintering (UHS): In UHS, the part is rap­
      idly sintered (in seconds) by heating up to temperatures as high as 3000°C.
    UHS has been demonstrated to achieve densities greater than 95% while

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    307

      yielding uniform compositions and favorable microstructures for a broad
     range of ceramics that can be difficult to densify with the same results using
      conventional sintering approaches.
     f. Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP): HIP is a thermal post-processing operation
     used to consolidate and densify materials such as metals, ceramics, and
     composite materials. It involves subjecting the material to high temperatures
     and pressure in a gastight container, typically an inert gas such as argon,
      helium, or nitrogen. The material undergoes high-pressure isotropic com­
      pression, which helps eliminate voids or defects in the material. The tem­
      perature used during the process is typically close to the melting point of the
      material, which allows the material to achieve a maximum level of density
     and uniformity. HIP is often used for the production of parts with complex
      geometries that are difficult to produce by other methods such as casting or
      forging, and is used for high-performance materials. It is also used in the
      production of high-performance materials that have high density and uni­
      formity requirements, such as aerospace components and medical implants.
     HIPs are widely used in aerospace, medical, and automotive applications to
     produce high-quality, dense parts with excellent mechanical properties.
         Parts produced by various additive technologies are prone to poros­
       ity due to the layer-by-layer deposition process. This can lead to defects
     such as voids, cracks, and inclusions that can weaken the part and reduce
        its mechanical properties. HIP can be used to reduce porosity and improve
      hardness by applying high temperature and pressure to the part. The high
      pressure forces the gas to diffuse out of the part, while the high temperature
     promotes plastic deformation and defect healing, resulting in a denser and
     more uniform microstructure.
       HIP thermal treatment can improve the mechanical properties of AM
      parts by eliminating or reducing defects such as porosity, inclusions, and
      microcracks. This leads to an increase in strength, ductility, and hardness,
     making the parts more suitable for demanding applications. In addition, HIP
      treatment can be used to improve the surface finish and aesthetics of AM
      parts by applying high temperature and pressure to the part, resulting in
      plastic deformation of surface irregularities and creating a more uniform
      surface. This can make the part more visually appealing and suitable for
      applications requiring a smooth surface finish.
         Parts produced using additive technologies often contain residual stresses
     due to the thermal cycling involved in the printing process. These stresses
     can affect the mechanical properties of the part and lead to deformation or
      failure under stress. HIP treatment can be used to remove residual stresses
     by applying high temperature and pressure to the part, which promotes plas­
       tic deformation and stress reduction.
    g. Difference between Sintering and HIP: While both processes are cru­
       cial in the fabrication of advanced ceramics, HIP is often employed when
      parts require near-perfect densification, such as in high-performance appli­
      cations, while sintering remains the baseline technique for ceramic AM
     manufacturing. The primary goal of sintering is to consolidate the ceramic
      material by promoting particle bonding and reducing porosity, leading to

10.2.2.1.2.2  Thermal Super-Finishing
Thermal-based technologies comprise laser shock peening (LSP) and LP.

   a. LSP: In LSP, a laser beam is used to create a plasma shock wave, which is
      reflected on the surface of the component, inducing a compression residual
      stress (CRS) that deeply penetrates the material, as shown in Figure 10.5.
   A transparent layer is required, although a non-transparent (opaque) layer

Ye, 2006.)


       is also often used. The transparent layer (usually water) is used to reduce
      the plasma produced on the surface and increase the shock wave intensity.
     The temperature at the heating point reaches up to 10,000°C, and the pulse
      length is about 0.15 to 0.30 ns. After the laser beam passes through the
      transparent layer, it hits an opaque layer, usually made of aluminum, zinc, or
      copper, which is also called a sacrificial coating. The opaque layer is used to
      prevent direct laser ablation on the surface. An impulse of laser reaches the
      absorption layer, and then ionization occurs in the heated zone, and a shock
     wave is generated, which plastically deforms the material. LSP is an appro­
      priate method for improving the surface quality and mechanical properties
      of additively manufactured components. Sun (2018) studied the microstruc­
      tural and mechanical properties of wire arc additively manufactured 2319
     aluminum alloy subjected to LSP. LSP was able to impart a maximum CRS
      of 100 MPa up to a depth of 0.75 mm, which significantly improved the
      tensile properties. It significantly improved the microstructure and micro­
      hardness. LSP is widely utilized to improve the fatigue life of compressor
      blades, jet engine fans, and aircraft structures. It has also been applied to
     improve the surface properties of processed maraging steels.
   b. LP: LP is considered a potential method for improving the surface roughness
      of AM parts. It is a noncontact surface finishing process that uses laser irra­
      diation to achieve subsequent surface smoothening, as shown in Figure 10.6
     (Marimuthu et al., 2015). In this process, a laser beam is used to melt the
      surface of the workpiece to reduce the surface roughness. During LP, mor­
     phology apexes can reach the melting temperature. The liquid material redis­
      tributes because of the effect of gravity and surface tension. Once the laser
    beam stops scanning the surface, the temperature of the heat-affected zone
    (HAZ) drops rapidly, resulting in the solidification of the molten pool, and
      the surface roughness reduces accordingly. LP is an automated process that
     changes surface morphology by re-melting without changing or affecting the
     bulk properties.

  During the past 20 years, LP technology has been extensively utilized to post-pro­
cess different materials. Mai and Lim (2004) applied LP to reduce the roughness of
